MODULE 1 — Retrieval, Agency, and Multi-Agent Architecture

Compiled: 4 September 2026. All vendor names, versions, GA status and prices retrieved and date-stamped; nothing quoted from memory. CONTEXT block: not supplied. Written for general purpose, with decision boundaries expressed as thresholds you can substitute your own numbers into (corpus size, QPS, p95 budget, $/1k requests). Where a recommendation flips on a context variable, that variable is named explicitly.

Confidence tags: ESTABLISHED replicated/consensus · EMERGING thin evidence · CONTESTED practitioners actively disagree · VENDOR CLAIM asserted by a seller, not independently replicated.

#1A — RETRIEVAL ARCHITECTURE

#1A.0 The decision, up front

Build this, in this order, and stop when your eval stops moving:

  1. Fixed-size or recursive chunking, 400–800 tokens, ~10–15% overlap. Do not start with semantic chunking.
  2. Hybrid retrieval: BM25 + dense, fused with RRF (k=60). This is the single highest-value component after chunking.
  3. Cross-encoder reranking over 50–100 candidates, returning top 5–10.
  4. Contextual prefixes on chunks (LLM-generated, 50–100 tokens) if your chunks lose their referent when split — SEC filings, contracts, transcripts, code.
  5. Query rewriting only where measured: it helps a lot on non-question-shaped queries and multi-turn, and can hurt on well-formed domain questions.
  6. Everything else — GraphRAG, agentic loops, ColBERT, SPLADE, multimodal — is a targeted fix for a named failure mode, not a default.

Steps 1–3 are where nearly all the recall lives. Steps 4–6 are where nearly all the budget goes.

#1A.1 Chunking

#Decision table

Strategy Choose this when Avoid when Cost Evidence strength
Fixed-size / recursive (400–800 tok, 10–15% overlap) Default. Prose, docs, wikis, mixed corpora. Any corpus where you have not yet built an eval set. Documents where a chunk is meaningless without its parent (single-line clauses, table rows) ~0 ESTABLISHED
Semantic (breakpoint/clustering) Corpora that are genuinely concatenations of unrelated topics per file (scraped dumps, merged reports) Anything resembling a normal document. Costs embedding passes for inconsistent gain 1 embedding pass over corpus + tuning ESTABLISHED that it usually doesn't pay
Late chunking You already run a long-context, mean-pooling embedding model (Jina v2/v3, nomic) and documents are long (>2k tok) CLS-pooling models, short-context encoders, or if you'd have to change embedding vendor to get it ~0 at query time; longer encode pass at index EMERGING — small, consistent
Contextual retrieval (LLM-generated prefix per chunk) Chunks lose entity/time/section referents when split: SEC filings, contracts, medical notes, code, meeting transcripts Self-contained chunks (FAQ entries, product records, forum answers); or when the generated prefix would just paraphrase the chunk 1 LLM call per chunk at index (cacheable); +50–100 tok storage per chunk VENDOR CLAIM headline; EMERGING in third-party replication
Hierarchical / parent-child Retrieval precision needs small units but generation needs large ones — legal, technical manuals, codebases Corpora where the parent is huge and mostly irrelevant (you re-import the noise you chunked away) 2× index storage; trivial compute ESTABLISHED as an engineering pattern, thin comparative benchmarking

#Evidence

Semantic chunking does not reliably beat fixed-size. Qu, Tu & Bao evaluated breakpoint-based and clustering-based semantic chunkers against fixed-size across document retrieval, evidence retrieval and answer generation, and found the compute cost unjustified by consistent gains; the gains that appeared clustered on stitched synthetic datasets with artificially high topic diversity, and on realistic documents fixed-size performed as well or better. (Findings of NAACL 2025, pp. 2155–2177; arXiv 2410.13070, Oct 2024.) ESTABLISHED This is the most cost-effective finding in this section: it removes a step most teams add reflexively.

Late chunking is real but small, and model-dependent. Günther et al. embed the whole document first, then pool per-chunk, so each chunk vector carries document context. Averaged across three embedding models and four datasets: +3.63% relative (≈+1.9 points absolute) nDCG@10 over naive sentence-boundary chunking, and +3.46% (≈+1.8 abs) for fixed-size boundaries. (arXiv 2409.04701v3, 7 Jul 2025; OpenReview 74QmBTV0Zf.) The critical constraint is architectural: HeteRAG reproduced late chunking and found it improves on long-context mean-pooling models (Jina v2) but degrades on standard encoders (E5-v2, BGE-v1.5), because full-document encoding mismatches their sequence limits, and it does not work on CLS-pooling models at all. (arXiv 2504.10529.) EMERGING — replicated, but the benefit is conditional on your encoder, not universal.

Contextual retrieval: strong vendor numbers, weaker independent picture. Anthropic reported, on 1−recall@20 with Gemini text-004 embeddings retrieving top-20 across codebases, fiction, arXiv and science papers: failure rate 5.7% → 3.7% with contextual embeddings alone (−35%), → 2.9% adding contextual BM25 (−49%), → 1.9% adding reranking (−67%). Index cost with prompt caching was stated as $1.02 per million document tokens under their assumptions (800-token chunks, 8k-token documents, 50-token instruction, 100 tokens of generated context). (anthropic.com/engineering/contextual-retrieval, 19 Sep 2024.) VENDOR CLAIM — first-party, single eval suite, not independently replicated at that magnitude.

A 2026 legal-retrieval study is the useful counterweight. CRAwLeR audited Anthropic-style contextual prefixes on Polish legal text and found the failure mode is prefix quality: in every one of the four queries missed by both BM25 and BGE-M3, the generated prefix was a near-verbatim paraphrase of the chunk and injected no new context. Worse, the LLM-written context chunks themselves outranked the target chunk in 15/22 cases for BM25 and 17/22 for BGE-M3. (arXiv 2606.21676.) EMERGING A separate 2026 survey reports AWS and other engineering teams seeing 5–15% precision gains, an order of magnitude below the headline. (arXiv 2601.05265.)

#Chunk-size heuristic with a number attached

Smaller is not free. HeteRAG found that shrinking chunks from 128 to 16 tokens monotonically degraded naive-RAG retrieval, because the chunk stops carrying enough information to match anything. (arXiv 2504.10529.) Parent-child exists precisely to break the tie: index at 128–256, generate from 1024–2048.

#What most teams get wrong here

They tune the chunker instead of fixing the referent problem, and they never measure whether the generated context is informative. Semantic chunking is the most-A/B-tested, least-productive knob in RAG. The actual failure — "the company's revenue grew 3%" with no company and no quarter — is a referent problem, and the fix is prepending the referent (contextual retrieval) or carrying the parent (hierarchical), not moving the split point.

And when teams do adopt contextual retrieval, they ship it without the one check that determines whether it works: does the generated prefix contain tokens the chunk doesn't already have? Diff the prefix against the chunk at index time and reject prefixes with high lexical overlap — CRAwLeR's failures were all in that bucket. Second non-obvious trap: if you index the contextualised text, the context sentence becomes retrievable, and generic context sentences ("This section discusses revenue in the 2024 annual report") will outrank real answers across many documents. Index the prefix, but exclude prefix-only matches from the candidate set, or you build a distractor farm.

#1A.2 Indexing and search: dense, sparse, hybrid, fusion

#Decision table

Approach Choose when Avoid when Marginal cost vs dense-only Confidence
Dense only Short conversational queries, paraphrase-heavy, no identifiers in the corpus Any corpus with SKUs, error codes, statute numbers, ticker symbols, part numbers, names baseline ESTABLISHED insufficient alone for most enterprise corpora
BM25 only Small corpora, exact-match dominant, no budget for embeddings, or as a hard baseline you must beat Vocabulary-mismatch domains (users phrase things unlike the documents) ~0 (Lucene/OpenSearch/pg) ESTABLISHED — still beats dense on some real corpora
Hybrid + RRF (k=60) Default. Zero-config, no labelled data, no score calibration Nothing, really. This is the floor 1 extra index, +10–40ms, ~0 $ ESTABLISHED
Hybrid + convex combination (tuned α) You have ≥50–100 labelled query-doc pairs and can re-tune per corpus No labels, or corpus drifts weekly tuning time only ESTABLISHED small gain over RRF when tuned
SPLADE / learned sparse You need semantic expansion but must keep an inverted index (latency, explainability, existing search infra) You already run a good dense model + BM25 and are at the fusion ceiling index inflation, training/serving a sparse model EMERGING
ColBERT / late interaction High-recall requirement on domain-shifted corpora; you can pay 10–100× storage Cost-sensitive, large corpora, or when a cross-encoder reranker over 100 candidates gets you there cheaper multi-vector storage (thousands of vectors/doc) ESTABLISHED quality, CONTESTED cost-effectiveness

#Evidence

Hybrid beats both components, and BM25 beats dense more often than people expect. The cleanest recent primary source is a 2026 benchmark on text-and-table documents: RRF fusion of BM25 + dense improved over both constituents on all metrics and all dataset subsets, with the largest gain +8.1pp Recall@5 over BM25 on TAT-DQA. On the same benchmark, tuned convex combination at α=0.5 reached Recall@5 0.726 vs RRF's best 0.716 (k=10). Most striking: BM25 outperformed dense retrieval with text-embedding-3-large on every metric except Recall@20. (arXiv 2604.01733, "From BM25 to Corrective RAG", Apr 2026.) ESTABLISHED

The size of the hybrid gain is entirely domain-dependent, and that variance is the point. Reported lifts range from ~+1.7% on e-commerce product search (WANDS — product names already give strong lexical overlap, so BM25 adds little that dense missed) to ~+24% on BRIGHT Biology (researchers phrase queries nothing like papers, so dense needs a lexical anchor). (Compiled in premai.io, 17 Mar 2026, citing Weaviate search-mode benchmarking.) EMERGING — third-party compilation, not a single controlled study. A patent-domain benchmark of 22 embedding models found fusion gains consistent but modest, with optimal interpolation at α=0.7 (dense-dominant) for 4 of 5 models and a largest absolute gain of +0.0152 nDCG@10. (arXiv 2605.24297.) EMERGING

Practical read: you cannot predict your hybrid lift from anyone else's number. Run BM25 alone, dense alone, and RRF on 200 of your own queries before you decide the weights. That experiment costs a day.

#Fusion, concretely

RRF: score(d) = Σ_i 1 / (k + rank_i(d)), k = 60 by convention from Cormack et al. (SIGIR 2009). It needs no score normalisation, which is why it is the correct zero-config default — dense cosine and BM25 scores are not on comparable scales and min-max normalising them is a per-corpus calibration you will forget to redo.

Convex combination: score(d) = α·norm(dense) + (1−α)·norm(bm25). Better when tuned, worse when stale. Dynamic per-query weighting (DAT-style, adjusting α by score-distribution separation) is EMERGING (evaluated in arXiv 2604.03676) and not yet worth the complexity for most teams.

#What most teams get wrong here

They ship dense-only, then blame the embedding model when the system can't find "invoice #AZ-4471". Adding BM25 is a one-day change with the largest single recall payoff available, and most vector databases now do it natively.

The subtler error is at the other end: teams that do run hybrid retrieve only top-10 candidates and then rerank them. That destroys the reranker. On the TAT-DQA benchmark above, reranking 20 candidates gave Recall@5 of 0.458; 50 candidates gave 0.826; 100 gave 0.888 — while going from returning 10 results to 20 after reranking barely moved anything (0.826 → 0.878). Recall lives in the candidate depth, precision lives in the reranker. Retrieve deep, rerank hard, return shallow.

Adaptive rewriting (model decides whether and how to rewrite) Best measured configuration: avg 55.6 nDCG@10 vs 52.8 forced-HyDE vs 50.3 naive; +7.8 over forced HyDE on open-domain NQ 1 LLM call + decision tokens Heterogeneous query distributions Homogeneous query shapes — just hard-code the right transform

Step-back prompting No reliable production-grade measurement found 1 LLM call Conceptual/why questions over principle-heavy corpora —
Routing (retrieve vs. don't) Semantic router F1 84–96 across three domains; LLM agent 64.6–99.8 — better on tight domains, 28.8 F1 points worse on the loose one ~10ms (embedding router) or 1 LLM call (agent) Always. Retrieval on out-of-scope queries is a top-3 production failure —

#Evidence

The dominant recent primary source is Ferrazzi et al., an industry-track empirical comparison of "Enhanced" (fixed pipeline) vs "Agentic" (LLM-orchestrated) RAG across FiQA, NQ, FEVER and CQADupStack-EN. (arXiv 2601.07711v2, 20 Apr 2026; LREC 2026 Industry Day.) All query-rewriting and routing numbers above come from it. EMERGING but well-constructed: real BEIR-derived corpora, NDCG@10 against labelled qrels, published prompts, cost and latency tables.

Two findings deserve emphasis because they contradict common practice:

  • Forced HyDE is a net negative on domain QA. On FiQA, naive scored 45.3 and enhanced-with-HyDE 43.5. HyDE won big on FEVER (claims, not questions) and on open-domain NQ. The technique is a format fix for query-document mismatch, not a general improvement.
  • Routing is where agentic and non-agentic diverge hardest, in both directions. On tightly-scoped domains (finance, English grammar) the agent's routing hit 98.8 and 99.8 F1 against the semantic router's 95.7 and 96.6. On FEVER — a deliberately unrestrictive domain — the agent collapsed to 49.3 recall / 64.6 F1 versus 84.4/87.9, because it retrieved when it shouldn't have. The tighter your domain definition, the better the LLM routes; the looser it is, the more you need an example-based classifier.

A separately useful negative result: DoTA-RAG, the SIGIR 2025 LiveRAG production stack over 15M documents, reported dropping HyDE and Chain-of-Draft entirely after testing, because they decreased correctness and faithfulness and didn't generalise. (arXiv 2506.12571.) EMERGING

#Latency budgeting — where the time actually goes

From the same 2026 study's runtime breakdown of an Enhanced pipeline on valid queries: 45–50% of end-to-end latency is answer generation, a similar share is query rewriting, 0–5% is retrieval, and 0–2% is reranking. Every optimisation instinct that targets the vector index is aimed at 5% of your p95.

Practical implication: if you must cut latency, cut LLM calls — collapse rewriting into the generation prompt, cache rewrites for head queries, or run the un-rewritten retrieval in parallel with the rewrite and use whichever returns usable candidates first.

#What most teams get wrong here

They add query transformation as a global pipeline stage rather than a conditional one, and they pay for it on every single request. The measured picture is that each transform is a fix for a specific query shape, and applying it unconditionally makes the queries it doesn't fit worse. The correct pattern is a cheap classifier (or a small-model decision) that routes: conversational follow-up → rewrite; claim/keyword → HyDE; enumerable multi-part → decompose; well-formed domain question → pass through untouched.

The second, more expensive mistake: no out-of-scope route at all. A naive pipeline that retrieves on every query scores 66.7 F1 on intent handling by construction — it is wrong on 100% of out-of-scope queries. This is the cheapest large win in the entire query layer and almost nobody instruments it.

Sources: SciRerankBench efficiency analysis, arXiv 2508.08742 (per-question inference times, their config); arXiv 2602.15860 (TREC-COVID, LLM reranker 3.8s vs 4.5ms at +0.5% nDCG@3); Cohere pricing via OpenRouter model pages, retrieved 4 Sep 2026. Note on Cohere pricing: Cohere's own pricing page does not render rates in static HTML, and third-party sources disagree on the unit ($/1k searches vs $/1M tokens). The per-search figures above come from OpenRouter's listings and are consistent with the $2.00/$2.50 per 1,000 searches figures reported elsewhere; verify against a Production key before budgeting. One "search" is defined as a query plus up to 100 documents, with documents over ~500 tokens split into chunks that each count toward the 100 limit — so long documents silently multiply your billed searches.

#Cross-encoders vs LLM rerankers: the honest answer

CONTESTED, but the contest is lopsided on cost-effectiveness. Déjean, Clinchant & Formal ran a large comparison reranking SPLADE-v3 retrievers across TREC DL 19–23, BEIR and LoTTE, including GPT-4 listwise: GPT-4 was impressive zero-shot, but traditional cross-encoders remained competitive while being far more efficient, and in-domain the cross-encoders were hard to tell apart from one another. (arXiv 2403.10407.) The 2026 TREC-COVID head-to-head above puts a number on the trade: +0.5% nDCG@3 for ~840× the latency. ESTABLISHED LLM rerankers are a quality ceiling to measure against, not a production component for synchronous traffic.

#The result nobody publishes: rerankers can make things worse

A 2026 local-retrieval system reported that off-the-shelf cross-encoders (ms-marco-MiniLM, BGE-reranker-base) degraded nDCG by 0.3–3.1% while adding 560–2100ms, on technical and scientific corpora — the authors attributed it to a train/serve distribution mismatch, since those rerankers were trained on web-search relevance. They replaced the reranker with a recency boost. (arXiv 2604.15484.) EMERGING

This is consistent with the pattern in §1A.3: general-purpose relevance models are trained on a distribution, and if your corpus isn't in it, the model is a confident source of noise.

#What most teams get wrong here

They treat the reranker as a component you install rather than one you validate against a no-reranker baseline on their own corpus. The failure is silent: nDCG drops a couple of points, p95 goes up 600ms, and it looks like general system slowness.

Two specific errors: 1. Reranking too few candidates. Below ~50 the relevant document often isn't in the pool, and the reranker just reorders noise (Recall@5 0.458 at k=20 vs 0.888 at k=100 in the TAT-DQA study). Reranking 20 candidates is the worst of both worlds — you pay the latency and get almost none of the gain. 2. Billing surprise from long documents. Per-search pricing looks flat until a 4,000-token contract clause gets split into eight chunks and consumes 8 of your 100 document slots. Chunk before reranking, or budget by chunk count, not by query count.

#1A.5 Advanced patterns

#GraphRAG and knowledge-graph hybrids

Decision: Use a graph when your queries are global ("what are the main themes", "what changed across all the incident reports", "which entities connect X to Y") or genuinely multi-hop over entity relations. Do not use one for local factual lookup — the answer sits in one passage and graph traversal adds entities that crowd the context window without adding signal.

The cost picture is the deciding factor, and it has changed. Full GraphRAG runs an LLM over every chunk to extract typed entities and relations, then summarises communities. Microsoft's own follow-up, LazyGraphRAG, defers extraction to query time and reports: indexing cost identical to vector RAG and 0.1% of full GraphRAG; comparable answer quality to GraphRAG Global Search on global queries at >700× lower query cost; and at 4% of global search's query cost, outperforming all competing methods on both local and global queries — including vector RAG with a 1M-token context window. (Microsoft Research blog, LazyGraphRAG; BenchmarkQED blog, Jun 2025.) VENDOR CLAIM — and note what it implies: Microsoft's own successor system is a tacit statement that the original indexing budget is impractical for many deployments.

The evaluation is contested. GraphRAG's original wins (72–83% of comprehensiveness comparisons, 62–82% of diversity comparisons vs vector RAG) are LLM-judged win rates. An independent audit of that evaluation style found position bias capable of swinging win rates by more than 30 points depending on which answer is presented first, plus length bias and trial bias. (Reported in VentureBeat, 2 Aug 2026.) CONTESTED Treat LLM-judged comprehensiveness/diversity win rates as directional only; insist on a retrieval metric (Recall@k against labelled qrels) before committing to a graph.

Independent 2026 work also shows the extraction cost is real and attackable: LLM-based graph RAG systems consume roughly 10K tokens to index a single document on average, and LLM-free semantic-graph alternatives report ~10× faster indexing and ~100× faster querying than GraphRAG. (arXiv 2604.16350.) EMERGING

Practical shape in 2026: graph as one retriever among several behind a router, not as a replacement architecture. Route factual lookups to hybrid+rerank; route "themes/connections/across-the-corpus" to community summaries or graph traversal.

#Agentic / iterative retrieval, Self-RAG, Corrective RAG

Decision: agentic retrieval is worth it for routing and query reformulation, and is currently a poor substitute for a reranker.

The Ferrazzi et al. comparison isolates this cleanly. On document-list refinement (NDCG@10, FiQA + CQADupStack-EN average): naive 45.5, enhanced without rewriting 48.0, enhanced with rewriting 49.5, agentic 43.9 — the agent, allowed to re-retrieve freely, ended up below the naive baseline. The mechanism is diagnostic: the agent chose to re-retrieve only 10% of the time, and when it did, 53% of the retrieved documents were unchanged. Once the model commits to a retrieval decision it rarely reconsiders, and when it does, half the time nothing moves. (arXiv 2601.07711v2.) EMERGING

Cost of agency, measured: agentic RAG required 3.3× more input tokens, 1.9× more output tokens and 1.5× more wall-clock time on average versus the enhanced pipeline, up to 3.6× on cost — and that was with a hard cap of 3 turns. Uncapped loops go higher. (Same source, Table 9.)

Self-correction has a well-replicated ceiling that explains this. Huang et al. showed intrinsic self-correction — revising without external feedback — degrades reasoning: GPT-4 on GSM8K fell from 95.5% to 91.5% after one round and 89.0% after two; GPT-3.5 from 75.9% to 74.7%. The apparent gains in earlier self-correction papers came from using oracle labels to decide when to stop, which is oracle-guided filtering, not self-correction. (ICLR 2024; arXiv 2310.01798.) ESTABLISHED Tyen et al. localised the cause: models can fix an error once told where it is, but cannot find it. (arXiv 2311.08516.) ESTABLISHED

Design consequence: reflection loops only pay when the critic has external signal — a retrieval score threshold, a unit test, a schema validation, a compiler, a second retriever's disagreement. Corrective RAG works because the relevance evaluator is a separate scored judgment with a web-search fallback, not because the model reconsidered. A reflection loop with no external oracle is a token multiplier with negative expected value.

#Multimodal retrieval

Decision: go vision-first (ColPali/ColQwen family) when your corpus is charts, tables, scanned pages, forms or handwriting — and only if you have budgeted the storage.

ColPali renders each page as an image, embeds patches with a VLM, and scores with ColBERT-style late interaction (MaxSim), skipping OCR entirely. It substantially outperformed text-extraction pipelines on ViDoRe, the benchmark introduced alongside it. (arXiv 2407.01449; ViDoRe V2, arXiv 2505.17166.) ESTABLISHED for visually complex documents.

The cost is storage, and it is large. These models emit on the order of a thousand-plus patch vectors per page instead of one document vector; a 2026 survey notes multi-vector systems like Llama-Nemoretriever-Colembed hold top accuracy while severely worsening storage bottlenecks. (arXiv 2606.07654.) Mitigations are maturing: K-means quantisation to 1-byte centroid indices reports up to 32× storage reduction, and attention-guided pruning cuts late-interaction compute up to 60% with <2% nDCG@10 loss, yielding 30–50% lower query latency under HNSW. (HPC-ColPali, arXiv 2506.21601.) EMERGING

Budget the index before you prototype: vectors/page × dimension × bytes/value, times pages. The difference between model choices at a million pages is measured in hundreds of GiB.

#Structured + unstructured joins (text-to-SQL alongside vector search)

ESTABLISHED as a pattern, thin on comparative benchmarks. The decision rule that holds up:

  • Numbers, aggregates, filters, "how many / total / as of date" → SQL. Never ask a vector index to do arithmetic or a date range. Retrieval returns similar rows, not correct ones.
  • Explanations, policy, narrative, "why / what does the contract say" → vector + rerank.
  • Both → run in parallel, join on entity ID, and give the model the SQL result as ground truth plus the passages as justification.

The failure signature is unmistakable: the answer's numbers are wrong while the prose is fluent and well-cited. If you see that, a vector index is answering a question a GROUP BY should have answered.

Two production requirements: a semantic layer or view set the model queries (never raw schema — the model will join wrong), and a read-only role with a statement timeout and a row cap. Log the generated SQL as a first-class artefact; it's the only debuggable part of the pipeline.

#What most teams get wrong here

They adopt an advanced pattern to fix a problem that was actually a chunking or fusion problem, and the pattern buries the evidence. GraphRAG for local factual lookup is the standard example: the corpus needed BM25 and a reranker, the team built an entity graph, and now the failure mode is 10K tokens of extraction per document plus a context window full of loosely related entities.

The second, more specific error: treating "the agent can retrieve again" as equivalent to reranking. It measurably isn't — an agent with free re-retrieval scored below naive RAG on document-list quality while costing 3.3× the input tokens. The right composition is an agent that decides whether and how to search, feeding a deterministic hybrid + cross-encoder pipeline. Give the model the routing decision; keep the ranking in a scored, testable component.

#1A.6 The honest question: RAG vs long context vs fine-tuning

#The decision boundary

Regime Corpus Update frequency Approach Why
Fits in ~30–50k tokens after filtering < ~50k tok any Stuff the context. No retrieval Retrieval infrastructure buys nothing; you'd only be re-introducing recall risk
Fits in window but well past 30k ~50k–500k tok any Retrieve first, then stuff. Route hard queries to long-context Degradation with length is measurable well before the window limit
Larger than window > window any RAG. Not a judgment call —
Any size changes hourly/daily — RAG. Fine-tuning cannot track freshness Reindexing is minutes; retraining is not
Any size stable — Fine-tune for form, RAG for facts Fine-tuning teaches format, tone, schema adherence, domain vocabulary and tool-calling style. It is an unreliable way to install facts
Cost-bound, mixed difficulty large any Route (Self-Route pattern) Predictions from long-context and RAG were identical on >60% of queries

#Evidence

Long context wins on quality when you can afford it — and that's a real finding, not a strawman. Li et al. benchmarked RAG vs long context across public datasets on GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-Turbo and Gemini-1.5-Pro: long context consistently outperformed RAG when sufficiently resourced. But their predictions were identical on over 60% of queries, and their Self-Route method (let the model self-reflect on whether retrieval suffices, escalate only if not) cut cost by 65% for Gemini-1.5-Pro and 39% for GPT-4o at comparable performance. (EMNLP 2024; arXiv 2407.16833v2, 17 Oct 2024.) ESTABLISHED — note the model generation is now dated; the structure of the finding has held, the specific percentages should be re-measured on current models.

Long context degrades well before the window fills, which is why "just use 1M tokens" is not an architecture. NoLiMa extended needle-in-a-haystack with needle-question pairs that share minimal lexical overlap, forcing latent association rather than string matching. Across 12 models all claiming ≥128K: at 32K tokens, 10 of 12 fell below 50% of their short-context baseline, and GPT-4o dropped from a near-perfect 99.3% to 69.7%. (arXiv 2502.05167.) ESTABLISHED Chroma's "Context Rot" study tested 18 frontier models and found degradation with input length across all of them, including on trivially simple tasks. (trychroma.com/research/context-rot, Jul 2025.) VENDOR CLAIM — Chroma sells a vector database and the finding is commercially convenient for them; it is nonetheless consistent with NoLiMa, AbsenceBench and the older lost-in-the-middle literature, which is why it should be believed anyway.

The correct decision is usually "and", not "or". The architecture that follows from the evidence: retrieve aggressively to compress, hand the model a small high-signal context, and escalate the queries where retrieval self-reports insufficiency to a long-context call. This is Self-Route, and it is also what LazyGraphRAG's benchmark result implies — structure at index time beat raw context length at query time, using the same generative model.

#Where fine-tuning actually wins

ESTABLISHED: output format and schema conformance, domain vocabulary and tokenisation, tool-calling and routing calibration, latency/cost reduction by moving work to a smaller model, and style. CONTESTED: knowledge injection — it works, it is expensive to keep current, it is hard to attribute, and it cannot cite. If your users need provenance, fine-tuning cannot give it to them and RAG can.

The combination that consistently pays: fine-tune the small model to be a reliable component (router, rewriter, extractor, reranker), and use RAG for everything that has a freshness or citation requirement.

#What most teams get wrong here

They benchmark long context on their easy queries and conclude RAG is unnecessary — because on >60% of queries the two genuinely agree. The decision has to be made on the hard tail, and the hard tail is exactly where long-context degradation and retrieval recall failures both live. Evaluate on the queries your users complain about, not on a sampled distribution.

The second error is architectural rather than empirical: choosing between RAG and long context as a global setting. The cost-optimal system routes per query, and the routing decision is cheap. Teams that adopt 1M-token windows as a replacement for retrieval end up paying full input cost on every request for a quality profile that measurably worsens with the length they just paid for.

#1B — AGENT ARCHITECTURE

#1B.0 The decision, up front

Default to a single agent with a well-designed tool set and aggressive context management. Escalate to multi-agent only when you can point at one of three specific conditions:

  1. Parallel breadth — the task decomposes into genuinely independent search/read threads whose results are combined at the end.
  2. Context isolation as a feature — a second agent is better precisely because it hasn't seen the first agent's context (generator-verifier).
  3. Capability routing — different sub-tasks are best served by different models, and the routing decision is cheap relative to the sub-task.

If none of those apply, multi-agent buys you a token multiplier and a new class of coordination failures. Keep writes single-threaded. That is the one rule both sides of this debate now agree on.

#1B.1 Topology: single vs supervisor vs peer-to-peer vs hierarchical vs blackboard

Topology Choose when Avoid when Cost multiplier Confidence
Single agent + tools Default. Sequential dependencies, shared state, coding, anything where later steps depend on earlier decisions Task exceeds one context window even after compaction; genuinely parallel breadth 1× (≈4× a chat turn) ESTABLISHED
Supervisor / orchestrator-worker, read-only workers Breadth-first research, multi-source search, "find X for each of these 50 entities" Workers must write to shared artefacts ~15× chat tokens VENDOR CLAIM on magnitude, ESTABLISHED on shape
Generator-verifier (clean-context reviewer) Code review, policy compliance, claim checking — anywhere an independent second look has value The verifier has no external signal to check against ~2× EMERGING, strong practitioner evidence
Capability router ("smart friend") Heterogeneous sub-tasks, cross-model strengths, cost tiering The primary model is too weak to know when to escalate 1.1–2× EMERGING
Hierarchical (manager → children → grandchildren) Work spanning many artefacts over long horizons (a migration, a multi-PR feature) Anything smaller than a week of work; recursion without hard depth limits high, superlinear EMERGING, actively being figured out
Peer-to-peer / unstructured swarm — Essentially always, today unbounded CONTESTED, evidence unfavourable
Blackboard (shared state store, agents read/write) Systems needing durable shared state across agents and restarts As a substitute for explicit control flow varies EMERGING as infrastructure, not as a coordination strategy

#The two positions, at full strength

For multi-agent (Anthropic, Jun 2025). In internal evaluations of Claude's Research feature, an orchestrator-worker system with Claude Opus 4 as lead and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on their research eval, and token usage alone explained 80% of performance variance. The mechanism is context: subagents explore in parallel with their own windows and compress findings back to the lead. The stated cost is ~15× the tokens of a chat interaction (with a plain agent around 4×), which is why the pattern is only economic on high-value tasks. Anthropic also states plainly where it fails: tasks needing shared context, which includes most coding. (anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system, Jun 2025.) VENDOR CLAIM — first-party, internal eval, not externally reproducible.

Against multi-agent (Cognition, Jun 2025). Walden Yan argued that naive multi-agent violates two principles: subagents given only a summary lack the upstream context needed to interpret their task, and actions carry implicit decisions — parallel agents make incompatible choices about style, edge cases and patterns, and the orchestrator is left combining miscommunications. (cognition.ai/blog/dont-build-multi-agents, 12 Jun 2025.)

The 2026 synthesis, from the same author who wrote the case against. Cognition's April 2026 follow-up is the single most useful primary source in this section because it is a public update against a prior public position. Their conclusion: multi-agent works today when writes stay single-threaded and the additional agents contribute intelligence rather than actions. Specific findings:

  • Clean-context review beats shared-context review. Devin Review catches an average of 2 bugs per PR on PRs written by Devin, of which roughly 58% are severe (logic errors, missing edge cases, security vulnerabilities). Counter-intuitively this works best when the coding and review agents share no context beforehand — the reviewer skips hours of accumulated exploration context, reasons backward from the diff without the spec, and its shorter context makes it measurably sharper. They cite Context Rot as the mechanism.
  • Capability routing works between strong models; it fails with a weak primary. Their "smart friend" pattern (a smaller primary model calling out to a frontier model) did not work when the primary was too weak to know when to escalate or what to ask. It worked well across frontier models, where the delegation logic becomes a capability router rather than a difficulty escalator.
  • Unstructured swarms are a distraction. The practical shape is map-reduce-and-manage: a manager splits work, children execute, the manager synthesises.
  • On sharing context to the escalated agent: forking the full context of the primary was the pragmatic 80/20, and prompting the primary to ask broad questions beat narrow ones.

(cognition.com/blog/multi-agents-working, 22 Apr 2026.) EMERGING — practitioner report, no released benchmark, but from a team operating this at scale and publicly revising a prior claim.

The systematic failure data. Cemri et al. built MAST, the first empirically grounded taxonomy of multi-agent failures, from 1,600+ annotated traces across 7 popular MAS frameworks, developing the taxonomy on 150 traces with expert annotators at κ = 0.88 inter-annotator agreement. Fourteen failure modes in three categories: system-design/specification issues, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification. Their framing is blunt: MAS performance gains on popular benchmarks are often minimal, and the failures stem from system design, not model limitations — meaning better models will not fix them. (NeurIPS 2025; arXiv 2503.13657.) ESTABLISHED

A 2026 paper applying MAST to its own controller trajectories reports this distribution — useful as an illustrative prior, not as MAST's canonical numbers: system design issues 44.2% (step repetition 15.7%, unaware of termination conditions 12.4%, disobey task specification 11.8%, loss of conversation history 2.8%, disobey role specification 1.5%), inter-agent misalignment 32.3%. (arXiv 2601.17915.) Note that the two largest single modes are step repetition and not knowing when to stop — both are control-flow bugs, not intelligence problems.

#What most teams get wrong here

They adopt multi-agent for parallelism and then let the sub-agents write. Every coordination failure in the MAST taxonomy gets dramatically worse when two agents can both mutate the same artefact, because the conflict surfaces at integration time when the context that would explain it is gone. The rule that survives both sides of the argument: N agents may read, one agent writes.

The second error is subtler and costs more: treating a 15× token multiplier as an architecture decision instead of a unit-economics decision. Anthropic's own framing is that the pattern is viable when the output value exceeds the cost — which means the first artefact you produce should be a per-query cost model, not a graph diagram. If a query costs dollars and the answer saves an analyst ten minutes, that's a business; if it saves thirty seconds, you've built an expensive way to be slower.

#1B.2 Planning: ReAct, plan-and-execute, tree/graph of thought, reflection, compilers

Pattern Real-world reliability Choose when Avoid when
ReAct (interleaved reason/act) The workhorse. Reliable with ≤10–15 tools and a step budget Default for tool-using agents Long horizons without compaction — context grows monotonically
Plan-and-execute (plan once, then run) Better token economy, worse adaptivity. The plan is a durable artefact you can log, diff and approve Auditable workflows; human-in-the-loop approval gates; long tasks where re-planning every step is wasteful Highly dynamic environments where step 2's result invalidates the plan
Plan file / todo list as external memory Strong practitioner evidence; keeps the objective in context after compaction Any task over ~20 steps Trivial tasks
Reflection / self-critique, no external signal Negative expected value. Degrades reasoning accuracy — Always, in this form
Reflection with external verifier (tests, compiler, schema, retrieval score, second retriever) The version that works Code, structured output, anything with a checkable oracle Domains with no oracle — you're just paying for confidence
Tree/Graph of Thought Benchmark-strong, production-rare. Cost scales with branching; hard to bound p95 Offline/batch reasoning, puzzle-like search with a scorer Synchronous user-facing traffic
LLM compilers / parallel DAG execution Real latency wins when the dependency graph is genuinely wide Independent tool calls that can fan out Sequential dependencies (the common case)

The reflection result is the load-bearing one. Intrinsic self-correction degrades performance: GPT-4 on GSM8K 95.5% → 91.5% (one round) → 89.0% (two rounds); GPT-3.5 75.9% → 74.7%. Reported gains in earlier work came from oracle-labelled stopping conditions. (Huang et al., ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.01798.) ESTABLISHED The follow-up diagnosis: models can correct an error when told where it is; they cannot locate it. (arXiv 2311.08516.) ESTABLISHED

So the design rule is mechanical: every reflection loop must name its oracle. Test suite, type checker, JSON schema validator, SQL EXPLAIN, retrieval relevance score, a second retriever's disagreement, a policy checker. If you cannot name it, delete the loop and spend the tokens on better retrieval.

Benchmark reliability ≠ production reliability, and there's a metric for the gap. τ-bench introduced pass^k — the probability that all k independent trials succeed — precisely because pass@1 hides non-determinism. The published gap is severe: GPT-4o at 61% pass@1 on retail tasks fell to 25% at pass^8. (Yao et al., arXiv 2406.12045; gap cited in arXiv 2603.29231.) A 2026 study on τ²-Bench shows the same shape: a model at 81.6% pass^1 in the retail domain dropped to 56.1% at k=4, while pass@k rose toward saturation. (arXiv 2603.00540.) ESTABLISHED

Report pass^k in your own evals, not pass@1. If your agent takes an action with side effects — a refund, a ticket, a commit — a 90% success rate means roughly a 57% chance of eight consecutive clean runs. That is the number your on-call engineer experiences.

#What most teams get wrong here

They add a reflection step because it demos well, and never notice it made the system worse. Self-critique produces plausible, confident revisions, so the regression is invisible without a paired eval. Run the A/B: same 200 tasks, with and without the loop, scored on pass^k. In a meaningful fraction of deployments the loop is a pure cost.

The second one: evaluating an agent on single runs. Non-determinism is the dominant production failure mode of agents and it does not appear in a pass@1 number at all. Three trials per task tells you more than three hundred tasks run once.

#1B.3 Memory and context management

#The four stores, and what actually goes where

Store Contents Lifetime Implementation
Working state Current goal, plan/todo, last N tool results, active file set One turn/loop The context window itself — the scarce resource
Episodic What happened in prior sessions, decisions made, dead ends Across sessions Append-only event log outside the window, queried on demand
Semantic Facts about the domain, the user, the codebase Long Your RAG index — same retrieval stack as §1A
Procedural How to do recurring tasks; house style; playbooks Long, versioned Files in the repo (AGENTS.md-style), skills, prompt fragments — not learned

#Context management: three primitives, and when each applies

Anthropic's context-engineering guidance frames context as a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns and names three levers, in increasing order of invasiveness:

  1. Tool-result clearing — drop raw tool outputs once consumed. The lightest-touch form of compaction and the one to reach for first: there is rarely a reason for a raw 40K-token file read to remain in the window after the agent has extracted what it needs.
  2. Compaction — summarise a near-full window and reinitialise. Tune the compaction prompt by first maximising recall over complex real traces, then improving precision. Aggressive compaction loses subtle context whose importance only becomes apparent later.
  3. Structured note-taking — the agent writes notes to durable memory outside the window and re-reads them later. Claude Code's todo-list pattern is the canonical example.

(anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents; Claude Cookbook, context engineering: memory, compaction and tool clearing.) VENDOR CLAIM on efficacy, ESTABLISHED as practice.

The magnitude is worth internalising: in Anthropic's cookbook example, an unmanaged research agent's context reaches ~335K tokens over 5 turns, of which ~96% is file-read results. On a 200K-token model that run hard-stops mid-task. The fix is not a bigger window; it's not putting 322K tokens of raw file content in the window in the first place.

#"Context rot" — the failure mode, stated precisely

Performance degrades continuously as input length grows, well before the window limit, and on tasks that are trivially easy at short length. A model with a 200K window can show meaningful degradation at 50K. Every frontier model tested showed it. (Chroma, Jul 2025 — VENDOR CLAIM, corroborated by NoLiMa's 12-model result where 10 of 12 fell below half their short-context baseline at 32K, arXiv 2502.05167 — ESTABLISHED.)

The operational consequence, and it's counter-intuitive: a fresh agent with less context is often smarter than a continuing agent with more. This is exactly why Cognition's clean-context reviewer outperforms a shared-context one. Context isolation is a capability, not just a cost-control measure.

#What most teams get wrong here

They treat memory as a feature to add rather than context as a budget to defend, and they compact by token count instead of by task boundary. Compacting at 90% of the window means compacting at an arbitrary point mid-reasoning, which is where subtle-context loss does the most damage. Compact at natural task boundaries — after a sub-goal completes, before a new file set is opened.

The second failure is architectural: putting the session log inside the window. Once the agent's history is in context, every compaction is an irreversible decision about what to keep. Keeping the log external and letting the agent query it (rewind, re-read before a specific action, resume) turns an irreversible lossy decision into a retrievable one. That is a materially different reliability posture for long-horizon work.

Third: semantic memory is just RAG, and teams rebuild it badly. "Agent memory" products frequently ship a naive dense-only retriever over conversation history — reintroducing every failure mode §1A.2 solves. Use the same hybrid + rerank stack you use for documents.

#1B.4 Tool use

#Tool count: where accuracy actually degrades

This is the most actionable number in 1B, and there is now production data behind it.

A 2026 study of a production voice deployment measured tool-selection accuracy against human-confirmed ground truth, Wilson 95% CIs within ±4pp:

Model ~10 tools ~15 tools ~20 tools ~30 tools
Claude Haiku 4.5 91% @ 245ms median 87% — —
Claude Sonnet 4 95% @ 410ms median — ≥90% below 90%

Haiku drops below a 90% accuracy threshold between 10 and 15 tools; Sonnet holds ≥90% to 20 tools and drops below by 30. (arXiv 2606.30317.) EMERGING — single organisation, observational, production session logs not released, but it is real traffic with a real ground-truth process.

At larger scales the picture is worse. The same paper situates its threshold against Gan & Sun (tool-selection success above 90% only to ~30 candidate tools, degrading sharply beyond ~100) and Kate et al. (a 7–85% accuracy drop as the catalogue grows). Other 2026 compilations report accuracy falling from ~78% at 10 tools to ~13% at 100+, with a position bias: tools in the middle of long lists are selected less reliably — lost-in-the-middle, applied to your tool schema. EMERGING on the specific percentages, ESTABLISHED on the direction.

Design rule with a number: keep ≤10–15 tools visible in any single reasoning context. Support 200 tools if you must — but expose 10 per call, via one of: - Namespace routing — a cheap classifier picks a domain, then only that domain's tools are loaded. - Tool RAG — vector search over the tool registry, injecting the top-k schemas. Watch the relevance threshold: too high and the agent silently answers without tools; too low and you reintroduce the noise. - Hierarchical agents — co-used tools bundled behind a specialist agent that presents one interface upward. Note this is a legitimate reason to go multi-agent that is easy to miss: it's a tool-namespace decision, not a parallelism decision.

#Schema design that models actually call correctly

The failure modes are boringly consistent, and so are the fixes:

  • Distinctive names, no near-synonyms. search_orders and find_orders in the same context guarantees confusion. If two tools are hard for you to tell apart from their names alone, they're worse for the model.
  • The description is the prompt. Say what the tool is for and when not to use it. Anthropic's guidance names bloated tool sets with ambiguous boundaries as a top context-engineering failure mode.
  • Flat parameters, few required, enums over free strings. Deeply nested objects and free-form strings where an enum would do are where argument hallucination concentrates.
  • Validate at the boundary and return structured errors. The error message is a prompt: {"error":"invalid_date_format","expected":"YYYY-MM-DD","received":"March 3rd","hint":"use resolve_date first"} gets fixed; "400 Bad Request" gets retried identically until the step budget runs out.
  • Idempotency keys on every write tool. Agents retry. Without a key, a retry is a duplicate refund.
  • Return the smallest useful result. A tool that returns 40K tokens has just spent your context budget. Return a summary plus a handle the agent can expand.

On structured output cost: older work found requiring JSON output reduced GSM8K accuracy by 27.3pp versus natural language, with tighter constraints producing larger losses. (Tam et al., cited in arXiv 2510.14453.) CONTESTED and likely dated — current models are trained heavily on tool use and the gap has narrowed. But the underlying principle holds: do the reasoning in prose, then emit the call. Don't force the model to reason inside a JSON field.

#Parallel vs sequential

Parallel when calls are genuinely independent (fan-out reads, N lookups over N entities). Sequential when a call's arguments depend on a prior result. Models will happily parallelise dependent calls if you let them — constrain it in the schema (make the dependent tool require a field only the prior tool produces) rather than in the prompt.

#What most teams get wrong here

Tools accumulate. A three-tool agent becomes a forty-tool agent over two quarters, one reasonable addition at a time, and the accuracy degradation arrives as "mysterious failures that don't correlate with prompt quality or model version." Nobody attributes it to the tool count because no single addition caused it.

Instrument tool-selection accuracy from day one as a first-class metric, tracked against tool count. It is the leading indicator that tells you when to shard the namespace — and it is the specific measurement almost no team has when they need it.

Second: teams surface tool errors as opaque strings. The model cannot recover from what it cannot read. Error surfacing is the cheapest reliability work in the entire agent, and it is almost always skipped.

#1B.5 MCP and equivalents: current state

#Where the protocol is, as of September 2026

The current specification is 2026-07-28. The headline change is that the protocol core is now stateless, plus Multi Round-Trip Requests, header-based routing, cacheable list results, authorization hardening, and a formal extensions framework. Deprecations with a stated ~12-month offramp: Roots, Sampling and Logging (SEP-2577); Dynamic Client Registration in favour of CIMD; and the legacy HTTP+SSE transport. Tasks moved out of experimental core into the io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension with poll-based tasks/get and a new tasks/update (SEP-2663). Change notifications moved to a single subscriptions/listen stream clients opt into per notification type. All four Tier 1 SDKs support the spec as of release; the Rust SDK is in beta. (blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/, 28 Jul 2026.) ESTABLISHED

Adoption is not in doubt. The maintainers report close to half a billion Tier-1 SDK downloads per month, with the TypeScript and Python SDKs each past one billion total downloads. (Same source.) An academic threat-modelling paper counted 18,000+ servers listed on one MCP marketplace within a year, with OpenAI, Google, Meta and Microsoft participating. (J. Cybersecur. Priv. 2026, 6(3), 84; MDPI, 5 May 2026.) ESTABLISHED

Governance: MCP is a Linux Foundation project under the Agentic AI Foundation (contributed December 2025). A2A joined the same foundation on 17 August 2026. Each keeps its own maintainers, spec process and release schedule.

#The security model — this is the part to brief your security team on

Treat MCP as a supply chain, because that is what it is.

  • Tool descriptions are an unsanitized instruction channel. A malicious or compromised server can embed instructions in what looks like help text, and agents will follow them. Microsoft's June 2026 guidance classifies tool descriptions as supply-chain assets requiring production-code review rigour; OWASP lists tool poisoning at #3 in its MCP Top 10. (CSA research note, 1 Jul 2026.) ESTABLISHED
  • Empirical base rate. A study of 1,899 open-source MCP servers found 8 distinct vulnerability classes, only 3 overlapping with traditional software vulnerabilities: 7.2% contained general vulnerabilities and 5.5% exhibited MCP-specific tool poisoning; 66% showed code smells. (arXiv 2506.13538.) ESTABLISHED
  • Design-default flaws propagate. An April 2026 disclosure by OX Security described a systemic flaw in the official SDKs' defaults, with an estimated 200,000 vulnerable instances across a supply chain of >150M package downloads. (CSA research note, 4 May 2026.) EMERGING — vendor-disclosed, figures are estimates.
  • Government guidance exists. The NSA's AI Security Center published a Cybersecurity Information Sheet on MCP security design considerations on 20 May 2026, finding that adoption outpaced the security model, and naming uncontrolled automated actions and insufficient input screening among the risks. ESTABLISHED

Minimum controls, in priority order: 1. Allowlist servers. No dynamic discovery from public registries in production. 2. Treat MCP config changes as code changes — PR, review, sign-off. A config diff is a privilege change. 3. Pin versions and hash tool descriptions. Alert on drift. Rug-pull attacks change the description after you approve it. 4. Least privilege per server, scoped credentials, no shared service accounts across servers. 5. Assume tool output is hostile input. Never let a tool result flow into a privileged action without a policy check. 6. Namespace collision detection — cross-server tool shadowing is a live attack class.

#Where MCP fits, versus alternatives

MCP is the agent↔tool layer. Its main competition is a plain function-calling loop over your own OpenAPI clients, which remains entirely reasonable for a closed set of first-party tools. MCP earns its complexity when tools cross team or vendor boundaries, or when multiple different clients must consume the same tool surface.

#What most teams get wrong here

They onboard community MCP servers with the trust posture of an npm dev-dependency, and then give them production credentials. The base rate is roughly 1 in 14 open-source servers carrying a general vulnerability and 1 in 18 carrying tool poisoning. The relevant question at review time is not "does this server work" but "what is the blast radius when its tool description changes next Tuesday."

Second, and easier to fix: they aggregate servers to solve tool sprawl. Merging five servers behind one proxy makes the tool-count problem in §1B.4 strictly worse. The mitigation is scoped, per-context filtering — selective exposure, not aggregation.

#1B.6 Hand-off, shared state, and interop (A2A and friends)

#Layers, kept straight

  • MCP — agent to tools/data. Mature, huge adoption, active security work.
  • A2A — agent to agent across ownership/trust boundaries. Agents publish an AgentCard (JSON at /.well-known/agent-card.json) describing capabilities and endpoint; tasks have a lifecycle (submitted/working/completed/failed).
  • In-process handoff — your framework's own primitive (LangGraph edges, OpenAI Agents SDK handoffs, ADK routing). For agents you own, this is what you should use.

A2A status, September 2026: Linux Foundation project (donated by Google June 2025; moved under the Agentic AI Foundation 17 Aug 2026). At its one-year mark in April 2026 it reported >150 supporting organisations, integration across Google, Microsoft and AWS platforms, and production deployments in supply chain, financial services, insurance and IT operations. v1.0.1 (May 2026) added an extension mechanism; four official extensions exist (Secure Passport, Timestamp, Traceability, Agent Gateway Protocol). Roadmap items include an interoperability spec and registry consolidation. (Linux Foundation press release, 9 Apr 2026; arXiv 2606.31498.) ESTABLISHED on governance and support count.

The honest caveat: the announcement named verticals but published no production-deployment counts or usage metrics. Supporter counts and GitHub stars are not adoption. CONTESTED whether A2A is load-bearing in many production systems today.

Decision rule: if all your agents are in one codebase, A2A is overhead — use your framework's handoff. A2A earns its keep at exactly one boundary: agents with separate owners, separate tool access and separate trust domains. A vendor's agent talking to yours. A partner's fulfilment agent talking to your ordering agent. Inside one team, it is a distributed-systems tax with no distributed-systems benefit. A 2026 analysis of governance gaps notes what none of MCP, A2A or ACP currently express: which agent may read which data. Authorization remains yours to build.

#Shared state stores

The blackboard pattern is fine as infrastructure and dangerous as coordination strategy. Concretely:

  • Do put durable run state in a checkpointed store (this is what LangGraph checkpointing, Temporal-class engines and MAF sessions give you): resume-after-crash, human-in-the-loop pauses spanning days, and an audit trail.
  • Don't use shared mutable state as the way agents coordinate. That's how you get the implicit-conflicting-decisions failure, plus write conflicts with no transaction boundary.
  • Do give every message and tool call a correlation ID and emit OpenTelemetry spans. When a multi-agent run fails you need to reconstruct the execution path; log-diving across agents without correlation IDs is unrecoverable.

#1B.7 Termination, step budgets and loop prevention

Recall from the MAST-derived distribution that the two largest single failure modes were step repetition and unawareness of termination conditions. These are the cheapest failures to prevent and the most commonly unhandled.

A minimum viable control set — implement all of it:

Control Setting Why
Hard step budget 10–25 for task agents; surface remaining steps in the prompt The Ferrazzi agentic RAG evaluation ran with a max of 3 turns and still cost 3.3× input tokens; unbounded is unbudgetable
Wall-clock timeout p95 target × 3 Catches stalls the step counter misses
Token budget per run absolute ceiling, per run and per tenant The only cost control that actually binds
Loop detection hash (tool_name, normalised_args); on 2nd repeat inject a message naming the repetition; on 3rd, halt Step repetition is a detectable pattern — most systems simply never check
No-progress detector N consecutive steps with no state change → escalate or stop Catches semantic loops that vary arguments cosmetically
Explicit success criteria in the prompt "You are done when X. If you cannot achieve X, say so and stop." Models under-recognise completion. Say it in the prompt, not just in the harness
Recursion depth cap Sub-agents cannot spawn sub-agents (or depth ≤ 2) Anthropic reported early agents spawning 50 subagents for a trivial query
Graceful degradation On budget exhaustion, return partial results with provenance Partial results with sources beat a timeout error

Idempotency is part of termination. Retries and resumed runs will re-issue side-effecting calls. Every write tool takes a client-generated idempotency key derived from the run ID and step index.

#What most teams get wrong here

They set a step limit and treat it as done. A step limit bounds cost; it does not prevent the agent from burning all 25 steps repeating the same failing call. The loop detector is ten lines of code — hash the normalised tool call, count repeats, inject a message on the second, halt on the third — and it addresses the single largest failure mode in the multi-agent taxonomy. Almost nobody ships it.

The second, more insidious one: no budget for the failure path. Teams budget the happy path and discover their cost model was wrong when a malformed query sends an agent to its step ceiling. Your unit economics need to be computed at max steps, not average.

#1C — FRAMEWORKS

#1C.0 The decision, up front

Start with no framework. An agent is an LLM calling tools in a loop; the loop is roughly 200 lines. Write it, learn where it hurts, then adopt the framework that solves that pain. The most common expensive mistake in this space is adopting an abstraction before you know which abstraction you need.

Adopt a framework when you hit one of these, and pick for that reason:

  • A lost run is an incident (money moved, a ticket filed, a commit pushed) → durable execution and checkpointing → LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, or a Temporal-class engine underneath your own loop.
  • Multi-day human-in-the-loop pauses → checkpointed state with resume → LangGraph, MAF.
  • You need the whole stack to be typed and testable inside an existing Python service → Pydantic AI.
  • You're .NET / Azure → Microsoft Agent Framework. This is now the only maintained Microsoft path.
  • You're Google Cloud / Vertex, or need Java/Go → Google ADK 2.0.
  • You're AWS/Bedrock and want a thin, OTel-instrumented loop → Strands.
  • You're OpenAI-native and the shape is triage-and-handoff → OpenAI Agents SDK.

#1C.1 The 2026 landscape has consolidated — verify before you cite a 2025 comparison

Three facts invalidate most framework comparisons published before mid-2026:

  1. AutoGen and Semantic Kernel are gone as separate products. Microsoft merged them into Microsoft Agent Framework: public preview October 2025, Release Candidate 19 February 2026, 1.0 GA 3 April 2026 with stable APIs, an LTS commitment, and native MCP and A2A interop. AutoGen and Semantic Kernel are in maintenance mode — bug fixes and security patches, no new features. Migration guides and a bridge exist; the SK→AF migration doc was updated to AF 1.0 GA in May 2026. (devblogs.microsoft.com/agent-framework; microsoft/semantic-kernel PR #13852, merged 12 May 2026.) ESTABLISHED
  2. LangGraph 1.0 shipped 22 October 2025, a stability release: graph primitives and execution model unchanged, committed to no breaking changes until 2.0. LangChain 1.0 shipped alongside, refocused on create_agent built on the LangGraph runtime. (langchain.com/blog/langchain-langgraph-1dot0; docs.langchain.com/oss/python/releases/langgraph-v1.) ESTABLISHED
  3. Google ADK 2.0.0 hit GA 19 May 2026, moving from a hierarchical agent executor to a flexible execution-graph engine with parallel sub-agent workers, nested hierarchies, and native inter-agent routing. Available across Python, Java, Go and TypeScript. (google/adk-python release PR #5752, merged 19 May 2026.) ESTABLISHED

#1C.3 The serious argument against frameworks

Take it at full strength, because it is largely correct:

  1. An agent loop is not hard; durable execution is. Frameworks bundle the easy thing (the loop) with the hard thing (persistence, resumption, HITL). You can get the hard thing from a general-purpose workflow engine — Temporal, Step Functions, a Postgres state table — which is better tested, not LLM-specific, and which your platform team may already run. You then own a loop you fully understand.
  2. Abstractions leak exactly where you need control. Context engineering is the primary determinant of agent reliability (§1B.3), and it is precisely what frameworks abstract away. When you need to control what enters the window token by token — and you will — you end up fighting the framework's message-assembly logic. Cognition's original complaint about agent frameworks was that they were disappointing for this reason.
  3. Debugging through an abstraction is slower. Agent failures are non-deterministic and trace-dependent. Every layer between your code and the raw request/response makes reproduction harder.
  4. Framework churn is a real cost. AutoGen went to maintenance mode; Semantic Kernel became a migration project; LangChain rewrote its agent abstraction at 1.0. If you'd built deeply on any of these in 2024, you have paid a migration tax.
  5. Latency and token overhead. Every framework adds prompt scaffolding you didn't write and may not want. If you're at sub-200ms budgets or optimising token spend hard, the overhead is measurable.

The counter-argument, also fair: teams that write their own loop reliably rebuild checkpointing, retries, streaming, HITL interrupts and tracing — badly, on a deadline, twice. The value of LangGraph 1.0 is not the graph; it is that durable execution, interrupt(), and time-travel debugging are already correct.

Resolution: the split is not framework-vs-none, it is orchestration vs durability. Write your own orchestration (you understand your control flow better than a framework does). Buy your durability (you do not want to write a correct checkpointing layer). LangGraph is the one product that does the durability well enough to be worth its abstraction; everything else is a matter of ecosystem fit.

#What most teams get wrong here

They choose a framework by GitHub stars and multi-agent feature lists, then discover their actual requirement was "resume a three-day workflow after a deploy." The selection criterion that predicts regret is not the agent abstraction — it is the state and durability model. Ask first: what happens when the process dies at step 14 of 30? If the honest answer is "we start over and that's fine," you need far less framework than you think.

Second: they adopt one framework for the whole company. The right pattern is usually mixed — a fast handoff-shaped front door on a lightweight SDK, and the money-adjacent, long-running, audit-sensitive paths on a durable engine. Migrating specific paths beats re-architecting everything.

#DELIVERABLE — REFERENCE ARCHITECTURES

#(a) Production RAG

                          ┌──────────── INGEST (offline) ────────────┐
  source docs ──► parse ──► chunk (400–800 tok, 10–15% overlap)
                            │
                            ├─► [conditional] contextual prefix (cheap model,
                            │     50–100 tok, prompt-cached over parent doc;
                            │     REJECT prefixes with high lexical overlap)
                            │
                            ├─► embed  ──────────► vector index (HNSW)
                            └─► tokenize ────────► BM25 / inverted index
                                                   + metadata: tenant, ACL,
                                                     source, version, valid_from

                          ┌──────────── SERVE (online) ──────────────┐
  query
    ├─► intent router (embedding classifier, ~10ms)
    │      ├─ out of scope ─────────────────────────► refuse / parametric answer
    │      ├─ aggregate/numeric ────────────────────► text-to-SQL over semantic
    │      │                                          layer (read-only, timeout,
    │      │                                          row cap) ──┐
    │      └─ knowledge ──► [conditional] rewrite               │
    │              (multi-turn → resolve; claim-shaped → HyDE;  │
    │               well-formed domain Q → pass through)        │
    │                                                            │
    ├─► parallel: BM25 top-100  +  dense top-100                │
    ├─► RRF fuse (k=60)  →  top-100 candidates                  │
    ├─► ACL/tenant filter (post-fusion, pre-rerank)             │
    ├─► cross-encoder rerank 100 → top 5–8                      │
    ├─► assemble context (dedupe, order by score, cap tokens) ◄─┘
    └─► generate with citations  →  faithfulness check  →  answer

Non-negotiables: tenant/ACL filtering enforced in the index and re-checked after fusion; every returned chunk carries a source ID and version; retrieval traces logged with query, candidate IDs, fused scores, rerank scores, final selection.

Evaluation metrics — define these before you build:

  • Recall@k = |relevant ∩ retrieved_k| / |relevant| — the ceiling on everything downstream. Measure at k=100 (candidate pool) and k=5 (final).
  • nDCG@k = DCG@k / maxDCG@k, where DCG@k = Σᵢ₌₁..ᵏ (2^lᵢ − 1) / log(1 + i) — ranking quality.
  • Context precision@k — fraction of returned chunks actually used in the answer. Your token-waste metric.
  • Faithfulness — fraction of answer claims entailed by retrieved context. Catches the failure users report as "it made things up."
  • Out-of-scope rejection rate — the metric almost nobody has. Baseline for always-retrieve is 66.7 F1 by construction.
  • p95 end-to-end, decomposed. Expect ~45–50% generation, ~45% rewriting, ≤5% retrieval, ≤2% rerank.

Failure signatures:

Symptom Likely cause First check
Fails on IDs, codes, names dense-only retrieval Is BM25 in the fusion?
Right document, wrong passage chunk too large, or no reranker Rerank depth ≥50?
Fluent answer, wrong numbers vector search answering an aggregate Route to SQL
"The company grew 3%" — which company? referent lost at chunk boundary Contextual prefix or parent-child
Confidently answers off-topic questions no intent router Add one; measure OOS rejection
Generic context sentences dominating results contextualised prefixes are retrievable and near-duplicate Exclude prefix-only matches
Latency fine at p50, terrible at p95 rewrite + generate serialised on the tail Parallelise; cache head-query rewrites

Runbook — recall regression: (1) Confirm on a frozen eval set, not production anecdotes. (2) Recall@100 or Recall@5? If @100, it's retrieval/fusion — check index freshness, embedding-model version drift, BM25 analyzer changes. If @5, it's the reranker — check candidate depth and model version. (3) Diff the corpus: new document types with different structure? (4) Diff the query distribution: new intent that needs a different rewrite path? (5) Only then touch the chunker.

#(b) Single agent with tools

system prompt (role, success criteria, explicit stop condition)
  + tool schemas (≤10–15 visible; namespace-routed if the catalogue is larger)
  + retrieved context (from architecture (a), as a TOOL not a preamble)
       │
       ▼
   ┌───────────────── loop ─────────────────┐
   │ model → reason → tool call(s)          │
   │   ├─ parallel if independent           │
   │   └─ sequential if dependent           │
   │ execute: validate args → run →         │
   │   structured error OR compact result   │
   │ append to state                        │
   │ ── budget checks every iteration ──    │
   │   step ≤ N (10–25) · tokens ≤ T ·      │
   │   wall-clock ≤ W · loop detector ·     │
   │   no-progress detector                 │
   │ ── context management ──               │
   │   clear stale tool results             │
   │   compact at TASK boundary (not %)     │
   │   write plan/notes to external memory  │
   └────────────────────────────────────────┘
       │
       ▼
   done | budget exhausted (partial + provenance) | escalate to human

Checkpoint after every state transition if a lost run is an incident. Idempotency key = hash(run_id, step_index) on every write tool.

Loop detector, concretely:

key = sha256(tool_name + canonical_json(normalized_args))
seen[key] += 1
if seen[key] == 2: inject("You already called {tool} with these arguments and
                           got {result_summary}. Try a different approach or stop.")
if seen[key] >= 3: halt(reason="repeated_tool_call")

Metrics: task success (pass^1), pass^k for k=3–8, tool-selection accuracy (tracked against tool count), steps-per-task distribution (p50/p95/max), tokens-per-task, error-recovery rate (fraction of tool errors the agent recovers from without human help), budget-exhaustion rate.

Failure signatures: wrong tool chosen → tool count or near-synonym names; same call repeated → no loop detector; runs to step ceiling on easy tasks → no explicit stop condition in the prompt; quality degrades mid-run → context rot, compact earlier; duplicate side effects → missing idempotency keys.

#(c) Supervisor multi-agent

                        ┌──────────────┐
     user request  ───► │ ORCHESTRATOR │  plans; writes plan to EXTERNAL memory
                        │  (strong     │  decomposes ONLY if independent
                        │   model)     │  hard limits: fan-out ≤ F, depth ≤ 2
                        └──┬────┬───┬──┘
             ┌─────────────┘    │   └──────────────┐
             ▼                  ▼                  ▼
      ┌────────────┐     ┌────────────┐     ┌────────────┐
      │ WORKER 1   │     │ WORKER 2   │     │ WORKER 3   │   ◄── READ-ONLY
      │ own context│     │ own context│     │ own context│       own step budget
      │ own tools  │     │ own tools  │     │ own tools  │       own token budget
      └─────┬──────┘     └─────┬──────┘     └─────┬──────┘
            └──────── compressed findings ────────┘
                              ▼
                    ┌──────────────────┐
                    │  ORCHESTRATOR    │  synthesise, reconcile, cite
                    └────────┬─────────┘
                             ▼
                    ┌──────────────────┐
                    │ VERIFIER         │  ◄── CLEAN CONTEXT. Sees only the
                    │ (clean context)  │      output + an external oracle
                    └────────┬─────────┘
                             ▼
                  orchestrator filters findings against
                  full user context → single-threaded WRITE

The three invariants: 1. Workers read; the orchestrator writes. One writer. Always. 2. The verifier gets a clean context and an external oracle (tests, schema, policy, a second retriever). A verifier with neither is a token multiplier. 3. Every agent carries its own step, token and wall-clock budget, and every message carries a correlation ID and emits an OTel span.

Shared state: a checkpointed store for durable run state, correlation IDs, and audit. Not as a coordination mechanism.

Metrics: everything from (b), per agent and aggregated, plus: orchestrator decomposition quality (are sub-tasks actually independent?), worker result-utilisation rate (findings that survive into the final answer — low means you're paying for discarded work), verifier catch rate and false-positive rate, cost per resolved request, and the multi-agent-vs-single-agent A/B on the same eval set. That last one is the only number that justifies the architecture.

#Escalation criteria and the cost of each step up

Step Escalate when Do NOT escalate for Cost/latency penalty (source)
Naive RAG → hybrid + rerank (a) Any production deployment — +1 index; +10–40ms fusion; rerank ~$0.002–0.0025 per search (Cohere Rerank 4 Fast/Pro, OpenRouter listings, retrieved 4 Sep 2026); rerank latency single-digit ms/doc on GPU up to seconds for heavy cross-encoders (SciRerankBench, arXiv 2508.08742)
(a) → single agent with tools (b) The task needs conditional multi-step tool use; the user's request cannot be answered by one retrieval + one generation Ordinary Q&A. A fixed pipeline is faster, cheaper and more testable Agentic vs enhanced pipeline: 3.3× input tokens, 1.9× output tokens, 1.5× wall-clock, up to 3.6× cost, measured with a 3-turn cap (Ferrazzi et al., arXiv 2601.07711v2, Apr 2026). Agents generally ~4× a chat turn (Anthropic, Jun 2025)
(b) → supervisor multi-agent (c) ①genuinely parallel independent threads, ②context isolation is itself the win (generator-verifier), or ③cross-model capability routing Sequential dependencies · shared write state · most coding · cost-sensitive workloads · when a bigger tool budget or better compaction would do ~15× the tokens of a chat interaction, with token usage explaining ~80% of performance variance (Anthropic, Jun 2025, VENDOR CLAIM). Plus a new failure class: 14 documented modes across 3 categories (MAST, arXiv 2503.13657)
(c) → hierarchical / manager-of-managers Work spans many artefacts over days-to-weeks and the manager has deep enough context to delegate without being over-prescriptive Anything under a day of work; any recursion without a hard depth cap Superlinear; no reliable public numbers. Cognition reports this is live in Devin and required more context engineering than expected, with cross-agent communication not happening by default (Apr 2026). EMERGING

The two questions that gate every escalation: 1. What is the failure mode I am buying? Each step adds a documented class of failure. Step 2 adds loops and runaway cost. Step 3 adds coordination failures that better models will not fix. 2. Have I measured the previous step at its ceiling? Most systems escalate from a badly tuned version of the prior step. A well-optimised enhanced pipeline can match or beat an agentic one at a third of the cost — that is the explicit finding of the only controlled comparison available (arXiv 2601.07711v2). Tune before you escalate.

#Gaps I could not close, and the experiments that would settle them

Named honestly rather than estimated:

  1. No reliable public number for contextual retrieval's benefit outside Anthropic's own eval suite. Reported third-party gains (5–15% precision) are an order of magnitude below the headline. Experiment: on 200 labelled queries from your corpus, measure Recall@20 with and without prefixes, and separately measure the lexical-novelty rate of generated prefixes. Report both — the second explains the first.
  2. No independent replication of the 90.2% multi-agent uplift on a public benchmark with published methodology. Experiment: same task set, same total token budget, single-agent vs orchestrator-worker. Controlling for tokens is the whole experiment; without it you are measuring spend.
  3. Tool-count degradation thresholds come from one organisation's production traffic plus secondary compilations whose underlying methodology I could not verify. Experiment: hold the task set fixed, pad the tool list with plausible distractors at 5/10/15/20/30/50, measure selection accuracy and position bias. One afternoon, and the result is specific to your tool surface.
  4. A2A production adoption is unquantified. Supporter counts are published; deployment counts are not.
  5. LLM-judged comprehensiveness/diversity win rates (the basis for most GraphRAG claims) have documented position bias capable of >30-point swings. Any comparison resting on them should be re-run with randomised presentation order and a retrieval metric alongside.
  6. Reranker pricing could not be confirmed from the vendor's own rendered pricing page; per-search figures are from a third-party host and disagree in unit with other secondary sources. Confirm on a Production key before it enters a budget.
