The harness itself is free — you pay only for underlying resources.

#The billing model is the actual news

AgentCore Runtime charges for active CPU consumption, not allocated capacity. Agent workloads typically sit in I/O wait 30–70% of the time waiting on model responses and tool calls, and that wait is free for CPU; memory bills on peak consumed up to each second. AWS's worked example: a 60-second session at 70% I/O wait, 1 vCPU active, memory ramping 1GB → 2GB → 2.5GB, costs $0.0007235, and 10 million sessions come to $7,235/month. AWS estimates pre-allocated pricing would be up to 3.3x higher on CPU and 1.4x on memory for the same work.

This is the correct billing model for agents and it is a real differentiator against running the same agent on Fargate or a provisioned container. Take the vendor's 3.3x claim as vendor-published, but the mechanism is sound and independently checkable against your own traces.

#Runtime microVMs vs Instances

  • microVMs: request/response agents, bursty concurrency, session isolation, scale to thousands of sessions in seconds.
  • Instances: long-running multi-agent sessions sharing a filesystem — AWS's example is a code-modernization pipeline with writer, reviewer and test-runner agents on one repo, 3-hour sessions on c7g.2xlarge, at $0.97 per session including the 12% fee. Your EC2 Savings Plans and RIs apply to the compute; the management fee is always calculated on the public On-Demand rate, so discounts never reduce it.

#Cost traps in the agent layer

  1. Web Search at $7 per 1,000 queries is the most expensive line item per unit on the platform. AWS's own example — 200,000 research queries a month — costs $1,400, while the 600,000 accompanying tool invocations cost $3.00. Search is 466x the cost of the tool calls around it. If your agent searches speculatively, cap it.
  2. Gateway Search API is 5x InvokeTool ($0.025 vs $0.005 per 1,000). Semantic tool-matching on every turn is a real cost at 50M interactions — AWS's example bills $1,250 for Search against $1,000 for four times as many invocations.
  3. Built-in Evaluations bill on the full evaluated context. AWS's example evaluates 15,000 interactions with 3 evaluators against 15,000-token contexts and reaches $1,782/month. Sampling rate is the only real lever; production sampling at 2% is the example's own assumption.
  4. Memory long-term storage bills hourly on a 31-day month basis, and the "built-in with override" strategy drops storage from $0.75 to $0.25 per 1,000 records — a 3x saving — at the cost of paying for model usage in your own account. That is usually the better trade above a few hundred thousand records.

#Managed vs roll-your-own

You gain: session isolation, identity federation with Cognito/Okta/Entra, MCP-server creation over existing APIs without writing code, policy enforcement at the tool boundary in Cedar, OTel-compatible traces landing in CloudWatch, and a memory service you did not have to build.

You give up: portability. Runtime, Gateway, Memory and Policy are proprietary surfaces. The escape hatch is that Strands Agents SDK is open source, so agent logic written against Strands can in principle move; the platform services around it cannot.

When to roll your own on Step Functions or ECS/EKS: when your orchestration is deterministic enough to be a state machine, when you already operate a container platform, or when you need durable execution semantics Step Functions gives you natively. A supervisor agent that is really a workflow with an LLM at three nodes should be a Step Functions state machine, not an agent framework. Most "multi-agent systems" in production are this.

Bedrock Agents (the original service) vs AgentCore: UNVERIFIED — I did not confirm the current positioning, deprecation status, or migration path between the two in this pass. Given AgentCore's evident investment, confirm whether classic Bedrock Agents remains a recommended path before starting new work on it.

#5. Guardrails and safety VERIFIED

Billing unit is a text unit of up to 1,000 characters — characters, not tokens. A 5,600-character input bills as 6 text units.

Filter Price per 1,000 text units
Content filters (text) $0.15
Content filters (image) $0.00075 per image
Denied topics $0.15
Sensitive information filters $0.10
Sensitive information (regex) Free
Word filters Free
Contextual grounding checks $0.10
Automated Reasoning checks $0.17 per policy

Standalone InvokeGuardrailChecks API: content filters $0.07, prompt attack $0.08, sensitive information $0.10. Pricing is identical for standard and classic tiers.

Three things that matter here:

  1. Contextual grounding is the expensive one on RAG. It bills the combined characters of source, query and response. With a long retrieved context, the source dominates: 20,000 characters of retrieved passages is 20 text units per call, $0.002 per request, $2,000 per million requests — for one filter.
  2. The prompt attack filter is only separable via InvokeGuardrailChecks. That API separation is what lets you run injection detection on retrieved documents and tool outputs, not just user input. Use it that way — see the gap below.
  3. Automated Reasoning checks bill per policy. Five policies is five times the cost. AWS's clinical example runs 5,000 cases at 8 text units each for $6.80/month, which makes formal verification of model outputs remarkably cheap for high-stakes narrow domains. This is the most under-used capability on the platform.

The gap: Bedrock Guardrails is built around filtering the user's input and the model's output. Indirect prompt injection — instructions embedded in a retrieved document or a tool response — is not what the prompt attack filter was designed for, and running it over every retrieved chunk is your own architectural decision with its own cost. Do not assume Guardrails covers this. [Reasoning from the documented filter set; confirm against current AWS security guidance.]

Comprehend PII detection, Macie and WAF pricing: UNVERIFIED.

#6. Evaluation VERIFIED

Bedrock Model Evaluation: algorithmic scores are free; you pay only model inference. Human evaluation with your own workstream costs $0.21 per completed task plus inference. LLM-as-a-judge and RAG evaluation bill judge tokens at on-demand Standard rates, and the judge prompts are published in AWS documentation — which is unusually good practice and means you can audit and reproduce the judge.

AgentCore Evaluations: 13 built-in evaluators plus custom ones, with CI/CD integration and configurable quality thresholds, production sampling rules, and results flowing into Observability. Batch evaluations get a 25% discount.

Where you still need third-party tooling:

  • Dataset curation and annotation workflow. Neither service gives you a real labelling UI, inter-rater reliability tracking, or a golden-set management workflow. This is the actual bottleneck in evaluation practice and AWS does not solve it.
  • Judge validation. Nothing here helps you measure your judge's agreement with human labels. You need to build that.
  • Local CI ergonomics. promptfoo, DeepEval and RAGAS run on a laptop in seconds against a git-tracked YAML file. Running evaluation through a cloud service is a slower inner loop, and inner-loop speed is what determines whether evaluation actually gets used.
  • Retrieval-specific metrics. Context precision/recall, nDCG, MRR over a labelled retrieval set — RAGAS territory.

SageMaker Clarify and MLflow on SageMaker: UNVERIFIED.

#7. Observability and ops

AgentCore Observability writes OTel-compatible telemetry into your own CloudWatch account, billing ingestion, storage, queries and PII masking at CloudWatch rates. AWS's worked example: 200,000 agent invocations producing 10 GB of spans (~10 million spans at 1KB) plus 6 GB of event logs costs $6.50/month — span ingestion $0.35/GB, event logging $0.50/GB. VERIFIED

Observability is cheap. There is no cost argument for not instrumenting. At $6.50 for 200,000 invocations, the objection is never money — it is that nobody set it up. AgentCore Optimization's Insights feature, free during public preview, analyses those OTel traces to surface failure and trajectory patterns across hundreds of sessions.

Cost allocation tags, Budgets, Cost Anomaly Detection and X-Ray specifics: UNVERIFIED — but note that token spend is not natively attributable per tenant or per feature. You get that only by emitting your own dimensions into CloudWatch or by inference-logging to S3 and joining downstream. Build this on day one; retrofitting per-tenant cost attribution onto a live system is miserable.

#8. Security posture

[Largely UNVERIFIED in this pass — I did not fetch current IAM, PrivateLink, KMS or Bedrock data-handling documentation. The following are the questions to answer, not answers.]

Verify each of these against current AWS documentation before an architecture review:

  • Bedrock training and retention terms — AWS's stated position on whether prompts and completions are used for model training, retention periods, and how this differs by model provider. This is the first question every enterprise legal team asks and the answer must come from the AWS Trust Center, not a blog.
  • VPC endpoints and PrivateLink coverage for Bedrock, AgentCore Runtime and Gateway. Note AgentCore Gateway charges $0.006/GB for egress to customer-owned VPCs VERIFIED, which confirms the path exists and is metered.
  • KMS and BYOK support per service — inconsistent across the GenAI service surface.
  • IAM for tool-calling identities. AgentCore Identity issues OAuth tokens and API keys on behalf of users or the agent itself with pre-authorized consent. The least-privilege design problem is that an agent's effective permissions are the union of every tool it can reach — Policy at the Gateway boundary is the intended mitigation and is priced at $0.000025 per authorization check, effectively free at $12.50 for 500,000 checks. There is no cost reason to skip per-tool-call authorization.
  • Data residency — recall the ~10% premium on in-region inference profiles versus Global. Residency has a permanent line-item cost.
  • GovCloud: NVIDIA Nemotron models are listed in GovCloud US-East/West at roughly a 20% premium VERIFIED; other model availability there needs checking.

#9. Reference architectures and estimated bills

All estimates us-east-1, September 2026 rates, Claude Sonnet 5 Global at $3/$15 as the reasoning model. Assumptions are stated so you can substitute yours — the totals are worthless without them.

#A. Lean startup — RAG chat, 100,000 requests/month, 5 GB corpus

Line Assumption Monthly
Model inference 4k input, 500 output per request $1,950
Managed Knowledge Base 5 GB storage + 100k retrievals $125
Guardrails Content + denied topics, 3 text units/request $90
Observability CloudWatch, low volume ~$5
Lambda, API Gateway, S3 ~$20
Total ~$2,190

89% of the bill is model tokens. Every infrastructure decision at this scale is noise. The only optimizations that matter are a smaller model for easy queries and prompt caching. Swapping the reasoning model for a Nemotron- or Gemma-class model on the easy path cuts the dominant line by roughly an order of magnitude [rates VERIFIED, the routing benefit is reasoning].

Do not build: a self-managed vector store, a custom evaluation platform, a multi-agent orchestrator. Managed KB at $125/month is cheaper than the engineering week you would spend replacing it.

#B. Mid-scale — agent product, 500,000 sessions/month, 50 GB corpus

Line Assumption Monthly
Model inference 8k input, 1.5k output per session $23,250
— with 60% of input from prompt cache cache read ≈ 10% of input rate SECONDARY, verified only for Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2 −$6,480
AgentCore Runtime AWS's $0.0007235/session example $362
Gateway 1 Search + 4 InvokeTool per session $23
Memory 500k events, 50k records, 200k retrievals $262
Managed Knowledge Base 50 GB + 500k retrievals $750

Evaluations 2% sampling, 3 built-in evaluators $1,188
Observability ~$16
Total ~$19,996

Model tokens are 84% even after caching. The entire agent platform — runtime, gateway, memory, identity — costs $647, or 3%. Anyone optimizing infrastructure here instead of token consumption is optimizing the wrong thing.

At 500,000 retrievals you are just below the Managed-KB-to-OpenSearch crossover. Do not migrate yet.

#C. Regulated enterprise — 5,000,000 sessions/month, residency and audit requirements

Line Assumption Monthly
Model inference as B ×10, in-region profile (+10%) ~$184,470
AgentCore Runtime $3,618
OpenSearch Serverless NextGen 4 sustained OCU + 200 GB storage — replaces Managed KB ~$705
Guardrails, standard filters 5 text units × 5M $6,250

Two decisions carry this architecture. Moving retrieval off Managed KB saves roughly $4,300/month at 5M retrievals ($5,000 versus $705) — but you now own parsing, embeddings, reranking and index tuning, which is at least a part-time engineer. At this scale that trade is clearly worth it; at scale B it clearly is not.

The in-region inference premium costs roughly $16,770/month versus Global profiles. That is the price of data residency, and it should appear as a line item in the compliance business case rather than disappearing into the model bill.

#Where AWS's own reference architectures are over-engineered for a small team

The Well-Architected Generative AI Lens (published 15 April 2025, announced 17 April 2025, available as an official lens in the Well-Architected Tool lens catalogue) covers all six pillars across six lifecycle phases and is genuinely good as an assessment checklist. VERIFIED

It is a review framework, not a build order. A three-person team that implements every practice in it before shipping will not ship. The lean version:

  1. Bedrock on-demand plus Managed Knowledge Base.
  2. Guardrails with content filters and sensitive-information filters. Skip contextual grounding until you have measured hallucination.
  3. AgentCore Observability from the first commit — it costs single-digit dollars.
  4. A 50-example golden set in a git repo, run in CI with promptfoo.
  5. Everything else when a metric forces it.

Add Automated Reasoning, human evaluation workflows, Policy, multi-account isolation and PrivateLink when compliance or scale demands them — not because the lens lists them.

#10. Where AWS-managed is currently weaker than best-of-breed

Ranked by how much it should influence a decision.

  1. Prompt-iteration developer experience. LangSmith, Langfuse and Braintrust are built around the inner loop of changing a prompt and seeing what broke. AgentCore Observability is CloudWatch-shaped: excellent for production monitoring and audit, wrong for the tight iteration cycle where prompt engineering actually happens. Most serious teams run one of the specialists alongside AWS rather than instead of it.
  2. Evaluation dataset and annotation workflow. No labelling UI, no inter-rater reliability, no golden-set lifecycle management. This is the bottleneck in real evaluation practice and it is unaddressed.
  3. Provisioned Throughput price opacity. Not being able to model a cost without a sales call is a genuine platform weakness, and the competitors publish their rates.
  4. Indirect prompt injection. Guardrails is oriented to user input and model output. Defending against instructions inside retrieved documents and tool results is left to you.
  5. Reranking cost. Cohere Rerank 3.5 at $2 per 1,000 queries — where a query is only 100 chunks of ≤512 tokens — is expensive against a self-hosted cross-encoder, and the managed KB reranker (free, but not model-selectable without extra charge) is a black box you cannot tune.
  6. Model availability lag and gating. Frontier models reach first-party APIs before Bedrock, and the Mythos tier requires provider approval. If you need day-one access to the newest model, Bedrock is structurally second.
  7. Lock-in at the agent platform layer. Gateway, Memory and Policy have no portable equivalents. Strands being open source partially mitigates this for agent logic only.
  8. Per-tenant cost attribution. Not native. You build it.

Where AWS is genuinely ahead: Automated Reasoning checks have no real equivalent elsewhere; AgentCore Runtime's consumption-based billing is the right economic model for agents and competitors mostly still charge for allocated capacity; and S3 Vectors' storage economics at $0.06/GB-month are hard to argue with for large, infrequently-queried corpora.

  • Neptune Analytics, DocumentDB and MemoryDB vector pricing and limits

The two highest-value unresolved questions: published Managed KB retrieval latency (which would settle whether it belongs in interactive paths at all) and the Bedrock Agents versus AgentCore migration story (which determines whether existing Bedrock Agents work is an asset or a liability).

#4.0 The one-paragraph version, and the ordering rule

Evaluate in this order, and stop when your remaining budget is better spent elsewhere:

  1. Retrieval, against labelled qrels. Cheap, deterministic, no judge required, and it caps everything downstream. Most teams skip it and then spend months tuning prompts against a retrieval ceiling.
  2. Generation, grounded in what was retrieved. Faithfulness and citation support first; "quality" last.
  3. The judge itself, before you trust any number it produces. An unvalidated judge is not a metric, it's a mood.
  4. Agents: outcome first, trajectory second. Task completion and cost-per-successful-task are the numbers that decide anything; trajectory metrics tell you why.
  5. Statistics. n≥3 trials, paired comparison, confidence intervals, per-item flip analysis. Without these you cannot distinguish a regression from noise.
  6. Business linkage. The last step and the one almost nobody does: prove that a movement in your eval score corresponds to a movement in something the business cares about.

The single most important structural fact in this module: public benchmark rank does not predict performance on your task, and there is now good evidence for why (§4C). Benchmarks tell you which model to shortlist. Only your own eval tells you whether your system works.

#4A — RETRIEVAL EVALUATION

#4A.1 Metric definitions

Notation: for query q, let R_q be the set of relevant (ground-truth) documents/chunks, D_k the ranked top-k returned, rel_i ∈ {0,1,2,3} the graded relevance of the item at rank i, and Q the query set.

Metric Formula Answers the question Use when
Recall@k |R_q ∩ D_k| / |R_q| Did we retrieve the evidence at all? The ceiling metric. Measure at candidate depth (k=50–100) and final depth (k=5–10)
Precision@k |R_q ∩ D_k| / k How much of what we sent the model is junk? Token-waste and context-rot proxy
Hit rate@k (1/|Q|) Σ_q 1[|R_q ∩ D_k| > 0] What fraction of queries have any usable evidence? Blunt, honest, great for exec dashboards
MRR (1/|Q|) Σ_q 1 / rank_q(first relevant) How high is the first good result? Single-answer lookups; navigational queries
MAP (1/|Q|) Σ_q [ (1/|R_q|) Σ_{i=1..k} P@i · rel_i ] Overall ranking quality across all relevant items Multi-answer retrieval
DCG@k Σ_{i=1..k} (2^{rel_i} − 1) / log₂(i + 1) Graded gain, discounted by position Intermediate; you report nDCG
nDCG@k DCG@k / IDCG@k, where IDCG is DCG of the ideal ordering Ranking quality with graded relevance, normalised to [0,1] The default ranking metric. Comparable across queries
Context precision@k Σ_{i=1..k} (P@i · rel_i) / (number of relevant items in top-k) Are the relevant chunks ranked above the irrelevant ones? RAG-specific; what the generator actually experiences
Context recall (claims in the reference answer supported by retrieved context) / (total claims in the reference answer) Does the retrieved context contain everything needed to answer? RAG-specific; requires reference answers, not just relevant-doc labels

Two distinctions that matter and are usually blurred:

  • Recall@k vs context recall. Recall@k is document-level and needs qrels (which documents are relevant). Context recall is claim-level and needs reference answers. They fail differently: you can have Recall@5 = 1.0 (you got the right document) and context recall = 0.4 (the specific facts needed were in a different chunk of it). Measure both if you can afford it; if you can only afford one, start with Recall@k because it needs cheaper labels.
  • Precision@k vs context precision. Precision@k counts relevant items; context precision weights by position. Since the generator is position-sensitive (Module 1: lost-in-the-middle, context rot), context precision is closer to the thing you actually care about.

Which k to report: always at least two. Recall@100 (or whatever your candidate depth is) tells you whether the evidence exists in your pipeline at all; nDCG@5 or Recall@5 tells you whether it survives to the generator. When a number regresses, knowing which of the two moved localises the fault immediately (Module 2, §2.3).

#4A.2 Building a labelled retrieval set without a labelling team

You need triples: (query, relevant_chunk_ids, [optional] reference_answer). Four sources, in descending order of quality-per-dollar:

#Source 1 — Production traces (best; requires that you instrumented retrieval)

If your traces carry retrieval.candidate_ids and the final answer, you can label retroactively: show a human the query and the top-10, ask which chunks were used. This is 30–60 seconds per query. 200 queries is a day of work and is worth more than anything below it, because the queries are real.

#Source 2 — Reverse-engineered from documents (cheap, biased — see below)

Sample chunks, generate a question each chunk uniquely answers, and take the source chunk as the gold label. Free, scales infinitely, and produces a coverage eval — good for catching total failures, not for ranking systems.

#Source 3 — Existing artefacts you already have

Support ticket → resolution links, FAQ → source-doc mappings, "was this article helpful" data, search-click logs, sales enablement Q&A. These are real queries with real relevance signals and cost nothing to label. Almost every organisation has more of this than it realises.

#Source 4 — Public benchmarks (BEIR, MTEB, domain sets)

Useful for choosing an embedding model in the abstract. Useless for predicting your system's behaviour on your corpus. Use to shortlist, never to gate.

#4A.3 Synthetic query generation, and its measured bias problems

This is the most common shortcut, and it has real, quantified failure modes. Use it — but know what it's lying to you about.

The distributional bias is measured. Rahmani et al. (CIKM 2025; arXiv 2506.10301) compared real vs LLM-generated queries on TREC DL and found real user queries are consistently shorter than synthetic ones, with different frequent-term distributions — users minimise typing and expect the system to cope with incomplete input; LLMs write grammatical, complete questions. ESTABLISHED

The magnitude, from a production system. Airbnb's natural-language search work (arXiv 2605.21812) quantified it precisely: median real query = 4 words (e.g. "pet friendly cabin"), median synthetic = 6 words, with 33% of real users using 1–2 words. An unguided contrastive baseline produced a mean length of 13.6 words with 97.6% exceeding 8 words — a KL divergence from the real distribution of 4.95. Seeding generation with real query templates cut that to 0.66, a 7.5× improvement, and the shape mattered as much as the mean: real and seed queries were right-skewed with σ ≈ 4, while unguided synthetic queries were tightly concentrated (σ = 2.5, 84% in the 3–8 word band). EMERGING — single company, one domain, but it is production data with published methodology.

The judgment bias compounds it. The same CIKM line of work found LLMs used as relevance judges are more lenient than human experts, inflating absolute system performance, and showing preference for systems aligned with their own generative patterns. EMERGING A partial reassurance: an earlier study (arXiv 2405.07767) found that synthetic collections built with GPT-4 queries did not systematically overestimate GPT-based systems, and T5-generated queries showed almost no bias toward T5-based systems — so the "same-family self-preference" fear is weaker than the leniency effect. EMERGING

What this means operationally:

Use synthetic queries for Do NOT use them for
Coverage floor — "is any part of my corpus unretrievable?" Absolute score reporting ("our Recall@5 is 0.87")
Regression detection on a fixed set Comparing two systems where the margin is small
Cold start before you have traffic Anything that gates a release on its own
Generating candidates for human labelling Replacing human relevance judgments

How to de-bias, concretely: 1. Seed with real queries. Even 20–50 real queries used as few-shot style templates collapses the length/shape gap by most of the way (the Airbnb 7.5× result). 2. Constrain length explicitly and enforce a target distribution — sample the target word count from your real distribution, then generate to it. 3. Include the ugly ones. Typos, fragments, all-lowercase, missing question marks, mixed language, one-word queries. Real traffic is full of these and generated traffic never is. 4. Validate the distribution before you trust the eval. Compute KL divergence on query length between synthetic and a real sample. This is a 20-line check and it tells you whether your eval set represents your users at all. 5. Filter with a second model. Generate query → ask a separate LLM whether the source passage actually answers it → drop the failures. This removes the largest class of bad synthetic items (queries the "gold" chunk doesn't actually answer). 6. Anchor absolute numbers to a small human-labelled set. Report synthetic scores as relative movement, and calibrate the level against 50–100 human-labelled queries.

#4A.4 Why this is the highest-ROI eval most teams skip

Four reasons, and they compound:

  1. It's deterministic. No judge, no temperature, no variance. Same index + same query = same qrels comparison. This is the only part of your eval stack that behaves like a normal software test.
  2. It's cheap to run. No generation tokens. You can run 500 queries in CI in seconds against a local index.
  3. It caps everything downstream. If Recall@k is 0.6, no prompt engineering will produce correct answers on the missing 40%. Teams routinely spend a quarter tuning the generator against a retrieval ceiling they never measured.
  4. It localises faults. When end-to-end quality drops, the first question is "retrieval or generation?" Without retrieval metrics that question takes days; with them it takes one query.

The counterargument — "we don't have labels" — is answered by §4A.2: you almost certainly have Source 3 artefacts sitting in a support system, and Source 1 costs one engineer-day for 200 items.

#What most teams get wrong here

They evaluate the whole pipeline end-to-end with an LLM judge and never separate retrieval from generation. The end-to-end score is the only number they have, so every regression investigation starts from zero, and every improvement is attributed to whatever they happened to change last. Splitting the metric is a day of work and permanently halves your debugging time.

The second, more specific error: generating synthetic queries from chunks and then evaluating retrieval of those same chunks. This measures whether your embedding model can match a question to the passage it was written from — a task it will ace — while telling you nothing about whether a real user's four-word fragment finds anything. If your synthetic Recall@5 is 0.95 and users are complaining, the eval is the problem, not the users.

Third: reporting one k. A single Recall@5 number conflates "we never retrieved it" with "we retrieved it and the reranker buried it," which have completely different fixes.

#4B — GENERATION EVALUATION

#4B.1 The metrics that matter, with formulas

All of these are claim-decomposed: split the answer into atomic claims, then check each. That decomposition is where the noise lives, and it is why these metrics need validation (§4B.3).

Metric Formula Detects
Faithfulness / groundedness supported_claims / total_claims, where a claim is supported if entailed by the retrieved context Hallucination relative to context
Hallucination rate (response-level) (1/|Q|) Σ_q 1[any claim in answer_q is unsupported] The user-facing failure. Binary per response, not an average
Answer relevance RAGAS-style: generate n questions from the answer, take mean cosine similarity to the original question Evasive, padded, or off-topic answers
Completeness / answer recall (reference claims covered by the answer) / (total reference claims) Partial answers — the failure faithfulness cannot see
Citation precision (citations that support their attached claim) / (total citations) Fabricated or decorative attribution
Citation recall (claims needing a citation that have one) / (claims needing a citation) Unsourced assertions
Citation resolvability (citations resolving to a real retrieved chunk ID) / (total citations) Deterministic — put it in Tier 1 CI (Module 2, §2.3)
Refusal rate / over-refusal rate refusals / queries, split by whether refusal was correct Both directions of a prompt change

Faithfulness and completeness are orthogonal and both are needed. A system that answers "I found some information about that" is perfectly faithful and useless. A system that answers thoroughly by drawing on parametric knowledge is complete and unfaithful. Gating on faithfulness alone produces the first failure mode, reliably.

Citation resolvability is the cheapest high-value check in this whole module. It's a set membership test — does the cited chunk ID appear in retrieval.candidate_ids? — costs nothing, has no judge, and catches fabricated provenance, which is among the most damaging failures in any product where users check sources.

#4B.2 Where classical NLP metrics are actively misleading

BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore should not be used to evaluate RAG or open-ended generation. This is not a stylistic preference; it's measured.

A 2025 crowdsourcing study of RAG evaluation (arXiv 2504.15689) took human pairwise-judgment rankings per topic, designated the top-ranked response as reference, and asked whether BLEU, ROUGE-L and BERTScore could reproduce the human ranking of the remaining candidates. Across all metrics and all utility dimensions, correlation with human ranking remained low, with an absolute maximum of 0.477 (BLEU on logical coherence). Their conclusion is unambiguous: none of the utility dimensions are accurately measurable by any of the three metrics. ESTABLISHED

Why they fail here specifically: - N-gram overlap assumes one correct surface form. A correct answer phrased differently scores near zero; a fluent wrong answer that reuses the reference's vocabulary scores well. - BERTScore rewards topical similarity, not factual correctness. "The contract terminates in 2027" and "The contract terminates in 2029" are near-identical in embedding space and opposite in meaning. This is the single most dangerous property for any domain where numbers, dates or negations matter. - They cannot see the retrieved context at all, so they are structurally incapable of measuring faithfulness.

Where they're still legitimate: translation with human references, summarisation against a fixed abstract in a research setting, and as a cheap regression tripwire on tasks with genuinely canonical outputs (structured extraction, code with fixed formatting). Even there, treat a change as a signal to investigate, never as a gate.

The safe replacements, in order: deterministic assertions (schema, citation resolvability, exact-match on extracted fields), then claim-level entailment (an NLI model or a validated LLM judge), then pairwise human/judge preference for holistic quality.

#4B.3 The uncomfortable part: RAG metric frameworks have documented validity problems

If you are going to gate releases on RAGAS-style scores — and many teams do — you should know what has been measured about them.

Discriminant validity failure. A 2026 measurement-validity analysis (arXiv 2605.23024) tested whether RAGAS faithfulness can distinguish where a failure occurred. On 500 Natural Questions instances, faithfulness shifted by 19.3 percentage points under retrieval degradation and 15.9 points under generation degradation — comparable magnitudes for two entirely different faults. A metric that moves the same amount whether your retriever broke or your generator broke cannot tell you which one broke. EMERGING — single study, but the experiment design is clean and directly falsifies a common assumption.

Correlation with humans is moderate, not high. A 2026 survey reports that correlation between RAGAS metrics and human evaluation yields a harmonic mean of only 0.55 — well below what reliable automated gating would require (reported in arXiv 2601.08847, citing prior empirical work). EMERGING

Component-level failure modes are documented. A telecom-domain evaluation of the four RAGAS metrics (arXiv 2407.12873) found the claim-decomposition step can misclassify sentences — paraphrasing a simple statement into multiple sentences changes the score, irrelevant statements sometimes get included, relevant sentences sometimes fall into no group — and that the cosine-similarity component of answer relevance inherits all the known problems of cosine similarity as a semantic measure. EMERGING

What follows from this, practically: 1. Use RAGAS-family metrics for relative movement on a fixed dataset, not for absolute claims. "Faithfulness went from 0.82 to 0.79 on our 200-item set" is a usable signal. "Our system is 82% faithful" is not a defensible statement. 2. Do not use a single metric to localise a fault. Pair faithfulness with retrieval metrics (§4A) so you have an independent read on which stage moved. 3. Validate on your own data. RAGChecker (arXiv 2408.08067) is the useful template here: it annotated a human judgment dataset specifically to meta-evaluate its own metrics against human correlation. That is the standard — meta-evaluate the metric, then use it. 4. Prefer entailment over similarity wherever the framework offers a choice. NLI-based claim checking degrades more gracefully on numbers and negations than cosine similarity does.

#What most teams get wrong here

They install a metric library, take the default metrics, and treat the outputs as ground truth. These metrics are themselves LLM pipelines with their own error rates — and the published correlation with human judgment is moderate at best. Running an unvalidated metric to three decimal places produces false confidence with a professional-looking dashboard attached.

The second error is subtle and pervasive: gating on faithfulness alone, which selects for evasiveness. Faithfulness is trivially maximised by saying less. Always pair it with completeness, and watch the two together — a change that raises faithfulness while lowering completeness has usually made the product worse.

Third: still reporting ROUGE. It survives in eval suites because it is cheap and familiar, and its maximum measured correlation with human ranking on RAG utility dimensions is 0.477. It is not a quality metric; at best it is a change detector.

#4C — AGENT AND TOOL-USE EVALUATION

#4C.1 Trajectory vs outcome: use both, and know which decides

Outcome evaluation Trajectory evaluation
Question Did the world end up in the right state? Did it get there sensibly?
Example Order status is cancelled in the DB; the PR's tests pass; the correct row was updated Called lookup_order then cancel_order with correct args, in 4 steps, no retries
Cost to build Needs an environment with checkable state Needs a reference trajectory or a rubric
Failure it misses Right answer by luck, at 40 steps and $3 Perfect-looking trajectory that achieved nothing
Use it to Gate releases Diagnose regressions and set budgets

The rule: outcome decides, trajectory explains. A trajectory metric should never block a release on its own, because there is usually more than one correct path and penalising divergence from a reference trajectory punishes legitimate strategies. The exception is policy compliance — "did the agent verify identity before issuing a refund" is a trajectory property that is genuinely a pass/fail requirement, and it should be a Tier 1 assertion.

#4C.2 Metric definitions

Metric Formula Notes
Task completion (outcome) (runs reaching the correct terminal state) / (total runs), verified against DB/filesystem/test-suite state — not against the agent's own claim of success Agents self-report success generously. Check state, never text
pass^k E_task[ C(c,k) / C(n,k) ] for c successes in n trials Report this, not pass@1. The reliability number
pass@k 1 − E_task[ C(n−c,k) / C(n,k) ] Capability ceiling. Useful for "could this ever work"
Tool selection accuracy (calls choosing the correct tool) / (total tool-call decisions) Track against tool count (Module 1, §1B.4)
Parameter accuracy Three tiers: schema_valid, exact_match, semantically_correct Report all three; schema-valid-but-wrong is the dangerous middle
Invalid-tool / hallucinated-tool rate (calls to nonexistent tools) / (total calls) Should be ~0. Non-zero means your schema surface is confusing
Correct abstention (correctly declined to call a tool) / (queries where no tool applies) The mirror of the retrieval out-of-scope metric. Almost never measured
Step efficiency optimal_steps / actual_steps (bounded ≤1), or report the raw distribution Report p50/p95/max, not the mean — the tail is where cost lives
Cost per successful task total_cost_all_runs / successful_runs The single most important agent metric. Includes the cost of failures
Recovery rate (tool errors after which the run still succeeded) / (runs encountering a tool error) Directly measures whether your error surfacing works (Module 1, §1B.4)
Loop rate (runs with ≥2 identical (tool, normalised_args) calls) / runs Step repetition was among the largest MAST failure modes
Stall rate (runs with ≥N consecutive steps producing no state change) / runs Catches semantic loops that vary args cosmetically
Budget exhaustion rate (runs terminated by step/token/time ceiling) / runs Reliability and cost signal
Latency to first useful action wall-clock to the first state-changing call User-perceived responsiveness for long-running agents

Cost per successful task deserves emphasis because it is the only metric that resists gaming. Accuracy improves by spending more; step efficiency improves by giving up early; cost-per-success punishes both. It is also the number that determines whether the product has unit economics (Module 2, §2.8). If you adopt one new metric from this module, adopt this one.

#4C.3 Multi-turn and stateful evaluation

Single-turn agent evals are the norm and they miss most production failures. What multi-turn adds:

  • A user simulator, which is itself a model with its own biases. Pin it (model snapshot + prompt hash) exactly as you pin the judge (Module 2, §2.2). An unpinned user simulator makes your agent scores drift for reasons that have nothing to do with your agent.
  • Information asymmetry. The realistic setup is that the simulated user does not see the agent's tool calls — they only see what the agent says. This is what makes τ-bench's design useful, and it is the property that surfaces "the agent silently did the wrong thing and reported success."
  • State verification at every turn, not just at the end. A run that reaches the right final state through an illegal intermediate state (a refund issued before identity verification) has failed a policy check even though outcome evaluation passes.
  • Context accumulation effects. Turn 12 behaves differently from turn 2 because the context is longer (Module 1: context rot). Your eval must include long conversations or it will not see this.
  • Interruption and correction. "Actually, no, I meant the other order" is extremely common in real traffic and almost absent from eval sets.

Practical minimum: 30–50 multi-turn scenarios with scripted user goals, a pinned simulator, database state assertions per turn, and n≥3 runs each. That's a week of work and it catches a class of failure nothing else will.

#4C.4 Public benchmarks: what each measures, and how it breaks

Benchmark What it actually measures Contamination / validity risk Use it for
τ-bench / τ²-bench (Sierra) Tool-agent-user interaction under policy, in retail/airline/telecom; verifies final DB state, not text; introduced pass^k Original board frozen at late-2024 models; τ²-bench v1.0.1 (July 2026) fixed banking_knowledge grading, so pre-1.0.1 scores are not comparable. Task set is public → learnable The best public proxy for customer-facing agent reliability. Steal its methodology even if you don't run it
BFCL v4 (Berkeley/Gorilla) Function-calling: correct tool, correct args, correct types, plus refusing to call when nothing fits. v4 reweighted to Agentic 40% / Multi-Turn 30% / Live 10% / Non-Live 10% / Hallucination 10% AST-graded static cases are public and learnable. Scores are not comparable across versions — v4 is substantially harder than v1's AST-only tests Shortlisting models for tool use. Its category structure is a good template for your own tool eval
SWE-bench / SWE-bench Verified Resolving real GitHub issues, graded by the repo's test suite The most documented validity problems of any agent benchmark. Re-analysis attributed a substantial share of reported successes to solution leakage and weak test suites — one representative SWE-agent configuration fell from ~12.5% to ~4% after correction (Aleithan et al., 2024). Adding stronger auto-generated tests changed leaderboard rankings in ~25–41% of cases across Lite and Verified (Yu et al., arXiv 2506.09289) Coding-agent shortlisting, with heavy discounting. Never as a proxy for your codebase
GAIA General-assistant reasoning with tool use; questions easy for humans, hard for agents Public answers; search-time contamination is a live problem (below) Directional capability signal only
WebArena Multi-step tasks in realistic self-hosted web environments Environment-specific; brittle to site changes; expensive to run Browser-agent shortlisting
AgentBench Agent behaviour across multiple interactive environments Broad but shallow per environment Coarse comparison
HAL (Princeton, ICLR 2026) Not a benchmark — a cost-controlled leaderboard and standardised harness across benchmarks Its purpose is to fix the others' problems Read this before you read any leaderboard

#The four reasons benchmark rank rarely predicts your performance

1. Cost is usually unreported, and it dominates. "AI Agents That Matter" (Kapoor et al., TMLR 2025; arXiv 2407.01502) showed that simple baseline strategies achieve Pareto efficiency over complex state-of-the-art agents once cost is controlled, and that accuracy-only leaderboards reward spending without reporting what the spending bought. HAL was built as the response: 21,000+ standardised agent rollouts across nine models and nine benchmarks, at roughly $40,000, with cost-adjusted comparison by default (Kapoor et al., arXiv 2510.11977, ICLR 2026). One of its findings should give any team pause: higher reasoning effort reduced accuracy in the majority of runs studied. ESTABLISHED

2. Contamination, in two forms. - Training contamination: benchmark items in pretraining data. Detection methods that work in 2026 include time-based partition (pre- vs post-cutoff subsets of a longitudinal benchmark), Min-K% probability, guided-completion attacks, ConStat performance gaps on rephrased items, and BIG-Bench canary GUID reproduction. Documented magnitude: up to 13 percentage points of overfit on GSM8K measured against the freshly-constructed GSM1k. ESTABLISHED - Search-time contamination (STC): search-enabled agents look up the benchmark answers. HAL's authors observed agents searching Hugging Face for benchmark answers; a dedicated study found accuracy dropping ~15% on the contaminated subset once Hugging Face was blocked (arXiv 2508.13180). EMERGING This is new, specific to agents, and invisible in an accuracy number.

3. Reproducibility is weak. The same paper documented inconsistent task ordering, non-standard evaluation setups, missing evaluation scripts, and benchmark subsets modified differently by different authors — with results from incompatible methods aggregated onto the same leaderboard. ESTABLISHED

4. Construct mismatch. Your task is not the benchmark's task. A model that tops BFCL has demonstrated function-calling competence on public schemas; it has demonstrated nothing about your 23 semantically overlapping internal tools with terse descriptions. Module 1's production data makes the point: tool-selection accuracy is a function of your tool surface, and degrades between 10 and 15 tools for some models.

Use benchmarks to shortlist three models. Use your own eval to choose one.

#What most teams get wrong here

They evaluate agents on outcome only, then cannot explain any failure. Outcome tells you the pass rate; the trajectory metrics tell you whether the fix is tool descriptions, error surfacing, step budget, or the model. Without trajectory instrumentation, every agent regression becomes a re-run-and-stare exercise.

The second, and it is the expensive one: reporting pass@1 on a system that takes irreversible actions. A 90% single-run success rate is a ~57% chance of eight consecutive clean runs. Your on-call engineer experiences pass^k; your dashboard shows pass@1; the gap between them is the gap between your confidence and reality.

Third, specific to 2026: treating a leaderboard position as a purchasing decision without checking cost or contamination. Given documented solution leakage, ranking flips from stronger tests, and agents that search for their own answers, the honest read of a headline benchmark number is "this model is in the right tier," not "this model is better."

#4D — LLM-AS-JUDGE, DONE PROPERLY

#4D.1 Choosing the judge format

Format How it works Reliability Use when
Binary reference-based "Given this reference answer, does the response correctly and completely answer the question? Yes/No" Highest. The reference does the hard work You have reference answers. Default choice
Binary rubric (reference-free) "Does every claim in this answer appear in the provided context? Yes/No" High for narrow, checkable properties Faithfulness, citation support, policy compliance
Pairwise preference "Which of A and B better answers the question?" Medium — requires position swapping Comparing two system versions holistically
Graded rubric (1–5 Likert) "Rate helpfulness 1–5" Lowest. Judges cluster on 3–4, ordinal distances are meaningless, agreement inflates Avoid for gating. Decompose into binary checks instead

The single highest-leverage design choice is decomposing one vague judgment into several checkable binary ones. "Rate this answer's quality 1–5" is unanswerable and unvalidatable. "Is every factual claim supported by the context? / Does it answer the question asked? / Does it cite sources for claims that need them? / Does it follow the required format?" is four binary questions with high inter-rater agreement that you can actually validate.

Judge prompt design checklist: - State the criterion, then the definition, then the edge cases you care about — the same discipline as annotation guidelines (Module 2, §2.7), because it is an annotation guideline - Provide 2–4 few-shot examples including at least one near-miss - Ask for the verdict in a structured field, with reasoning before the verdict (post-hoc rationalisation of an already-emitted verdict is worthless) - Never expose which system produced which output - Temperature 0, and still run n≥3 — providers are not bit-deterministic - Pin the judge model snapshot and prompt hash (Module 2, §2.2)

#4D.2 The biases, with measured magnitudes

The strongest current evidence is a systematic study of 21 judges from nine providers across MT-Bench, JudgeBench and RewardBench — 118 runs, ~541,000 individual judgments, March–April 2026 (arXiv 2606.19544).

Bias Measured Mitigation
Position bias >0.10 in two production-deployed judges, coexisting with test–retest reliability >0.95 — "the most reproducible judges were among the least valid" Always swap positions and average. Report swap-disagreement rate as a health metric
Kappa deflation (not a bias — a measurement error) 33–41 percentage points on MT-Bench between exact-match agreement and chance-corrected Cohen's κ Report κ, never percent agreement
Benchmark-dependence Judge rankings shift by up to 14 positions across the three benchmarks Never inherit someone else's "best judge." Validate on your task
Verbosity bias Small: <0.011 across their cohort under a single pairing protocol A useful correction to folklore. Still control length in pairwise comparisons
Self-preference Reported across the literature; magnitudes vary Use a judge from a different model family than the system under test
Stochastic variance A separate 2026 study found cross-judge κ = 0.51, matching the human inter-annotator range of 0.3–0.6 for subjective NLG tasks (arXiv 2606.13685) Multi-trial aggregation. Bias correction does not reduce random variance

The older, favourable baseline still holds directionally and is worth stating honestly: GPT-4 judges reached >80% agreement with human preferences on MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, comparable to human–human agreement (Zheng et al., 2023) — but that figure is tie-excluded, and retaining ties and inconsistent annotations drops it substantially (arXiv 2307.03025). ESTABLISHED The honest summary: LLM judges are roughly as consistent as humans on subjective tasks, which is to say moderately, and the field's habit of reporting exact match has been overstating that.

Judge model choice, temperature, ensembling: - Different family from the system under test. Non-negotiable if self-preference matters to your decision. - A strong model. Judging is harder than answering. A cheap judge is a false economy on the gating path; sample instead. - Temperature 0 with n≥3. Determinism is not guaranteed. - Ensembling (2–3 judges, majority vote) raises agreement and roughly multiplies cost. Worth it on the release gate, not on 100% of production traffic. - A cheap judge for online sampling, a strong ensemble for the gate. This is the cost-sane split.

#4D.3 Validating the judge — the part everyone skips

A judge you have not validated is not a metric. The protocol:

Step 1 — Build a calibration set. - 100–200 items minimum, stratified across the difficulty and topic distribution of your real eval set (not just easy cases) - Deliberately include borderline items — a judge validated only on obvious pass/fail cases will show high agreement and no discriminative power - Label each by two humans independently, adjudicate disagreements, and record the adjudication reasons (they are your rubric bugs)

Step 2 — Compute human–human agreement first. - Cohen's κ = (p_o − p_e) / (1 − p_e) for two raters, categorical - Krippendorff's α = 1 − D_o/D_e for >2 raters or ordinal scales - This is your ceiling. If your humans agree at κ = 0.55, expecting κ = 0.8 from the judge is incoherent. Calibrate expectations: human IAA for subjective NLG tasks sits around 0.3–0.6.

Step 3 — Compute judge–human agreement on the same items.

Judge κ vs adjudicated human labels Verdict
≥ 0.7 Strong. Safe to gate releases
0.6 – 0.7 Acceptable for gating with a human review of flagged failures
0.4 – 0.6 Directional only. Use for trend monitoring, do not gate
< 0.4 Unusable. Fix the rubric — the problem is almost always an ambiguous criterion, not the model

Also report: agreement relative to the human–human ceiling (κ_judge / κ_human). A judge at 0.55 against humans who agree at 0.58 is doing near-human work; the same 0.55 against humans at 0.85 is not.

Step 4 — Bias audit on the same set. - Position swap: run every pairwise comparison in both orders. Report the disagreement rate. Anything above ~10% means the judge is substantially reading position, not content. - Length control: correlate verdict with response length. If the correlation is material, add an explicit length-neutrality instruction and re-measure. - Self-preference check: if the judge shares a family with any system under test, run a cross-family judge on a subsample and compare. - Test–retest: run the same items twice. High test–retest with high position bias is the documented "consistency–bias paradox" — do not read stability as validity.

Step 5 — Re-validate on a schedule. Every time the judge model snapshot changes, every time the judge prompt changes, every time the task distribution shifts materially, and quarterly regardless. The 2606.19544 authors flag temporal-scope risk explicitly: their own results are scoped to March–April 2026 for judges whose hosted endpoints subsequently drift.

Step 6 — Keep a permanent human sample. 1–5% of judged items, blind-graded, forever. This is your judge's own drift monitor (Module 2, §2.6), and it costs almost nothing.

#4D.4 The serious published criticisms, stated at full strength

You should be able to argue the case against your own method:

  1. Reliability is not validity. The headline finding of arXiv 2606.19544: the most reproducible judges were among the least valid, with test–retest >0.95 coexisting with position bias >0.10. A stable number can be stably wrong.
  2. The standard validation metric overstates competence. Exact-match agreement does not correct for chance and is sensitive to benchmark label distribution; the deflation to κ is 33–41pp. Most published judge validations use exact match.
  3. Judge quality does not transfer. Rankings shift by up to 14 positions across benchmarks. There is no "best judge."
  4. Documented bias taxonomies are long. The CALM framework documents 12 distinct LLM-judge biases including position, verbosity, self-enhancement and authority bias (cited in arXiv 2601.08847).
  5. The circularity objection. Using an LLM to judge an LLM measures agreement with a model's notion of quality, which is a different construct from user value. This is the criticism with no technical fix — the answer is §4F.5, connecting scores to business outcomes.
  6. It is not cheap at scale. Judging 100% of production traffic with a strong judge can cost more than the primary calls being judged.

None of these say "don't use LLM judges." They say: validate, report κ not agreement, swap positions, pin everything, keep humans in a sample, and never let a judge score be the only evidence for a decision that matters.

#What most teams get wrong here

They validate the judge with percent agreement and declare it good. Given 33–41 points of kappa deflation, an "85% agreement" judge on a skewed set can be barely better than chance. This one substitution — report κ, not agreement — invalidates or rescues most judge validations in the wild.

Second: they use a 1–5 Likert rubric. It produces high-looking agreement because judges cluster on the middle, hides the disagreements that matter, and cannot be validated meaningfully. Decompose into binaries.

Third, and it silently corrupts everything downstream: the judge is unpinned. The metric then drifts on the vendor's schedule, and the team spends a week bisecting their own commits looking for a regression they did not cause.

#4E — FRAMEWORKS AND TOOLING

Two market facts that invalidate older comparisons. (1) OpenAI announced the acquisition of Promptfoo on 9 March 2026, integrating it into OpenAI Frontier; the MIT-licensed core remains open source and the team stated OSS development continues. Reported reach at acquisition: ~130,000 monthly active users and >25% of the Fortune 500. Treat the independence question as open — a red-team tool owned by a model provider is a harder sell as a neutral referee, even if the licence doesn't change. (2) ClickHouse acquired Langfuse (announced 16 January 2026) — see Module 2, §2.11.

Red-teaming and adversarial tooling is a separate family — do not expect your eval framework to cover it:

Family Tools What they give you
Orchestrators (adaptive, attacker-LLM driven) PyRIT (Microsoft) — multi-turn and multi-modal chains, crescendo/TAP Attacks that adapt to your refusals; multi-turn escalation over 5–20 turns
Probe libraries (fixed vocabulary, paired detectors) garak (NVIDIA) — broad probe-module coverage Wide, repeatable scans mapped to known weakness classes

Benchmark suites HarmBench, JailbreakBench, AdvBench A common yardstick to compare your defences against
Runtime guards (not eval) Lakera Guard, LLM Guard, NeMo Guardrails Blocking, not measuring — different job

The consensus in this space, which matches Module 2's position: pick one from each family, because probe libraries miss adaptive attacks and orchestrators miss the known-weakness catalogue. And note the ceiling: off-the-shelf probes test generic vulnerabilities; your actual exposure comes from your system prompt, your tools, and your data sources, so a custom suite is mandatory, not optional.

#Choosing — the rules that actually decide

  1. You need CI gating in Python → DeepEval (or RAGAS if you're purely RAG). Both run locally, free, no account.
  2. You need prompt × model matrix testing and adversarial suites → promptfoo, with the acquisition noted.
  3. You need defensible, reproducible, auditable evals (regulated domain, safety claims, external scrutiny) → Inspect AI. MIT, structured logs, sandboxing, and the framework several frontier labs standardised on.
  4. You need self-hosting for residency → Langfuse (MIT), DeepEval, RAGAS, promptfoo, MLflow, TruLens, or Phoenix (check ELv2 against your policy).
  5. Your pain is shipping regressions, not debugging → Braintrust, if SaaS is acceptable.
  6. You're on LangGraph → LangSmith.

Almost everyone needs two tools, and this is the division that works: a lightweight library for CI gating (DeepEval / RAGAS / promptfoo / Inspect) plus a platform for traces, annotation queues and online scoring (Langfuse / Phoenix / Braintrust / LangSmith). Trying to make one tool do both usually means the CI gate is slow and the annotation workflow is homemade.

#What most teams get wrong here

They adopt a metric library and inherit its metrics as their definition of quality. Every one of these tools ships defaults; none of them knows your domain. The framework should be the harness, and the metrics should be yours — derived from real failures (§4F.1) and validated against human labels (§4D.3).

Second: they buy an eval platform before writing 50 labelled examples. The tooling is not the bottleneck and never was. A CSV of 100 labelled cases plus 30 lines of pytest outperforms any platform with an empty dataset, and it tells you what you actually need from a platform when you do buy one.

#4F — MAKING EVALUATION REAL

#4F.1 Building the golden dataset

#Size

Purpose Items Trials per item Rationale
Smoke test (pre-commit) 20–30 1 Seconds; catches catastrophic breakage
CI gate (per PR) 100–200 3 The workable floor for detecting a meaningful regression
Nightly regression 300–1,000 3–5 Broader coverage, slower budget
Release / model migration 500–1,000+ 5 You're making a two-year decision
Judge calibration 100–200 (double-labelled) — §4D.3
Adversarial / safety 100–300 3 Separate suite, separate gate

Do not start by trying to build the big one. 50 real, well-labelled cases from production beat 5,000 synthetic ones, and you will learn more from labelling those 50 than from any amount of generation.

#Stratification

Deliberately allocate, and track coverage per stratum: - By query type (factual lookup / multi-hop / aggregate / comparison / out-of-scope / ambiguous) - By difficulty — target roughly 20% easy / 50% medium / 30% hard. An all-easy set shows a flat 0.95 and detects nothing; an all-hard set shows 0.3 and swamps signal in noise - By business value — your highest-revenue segment deserves proportionally more items than its traffic share - By failure mode — one representative per distinct production failure you've fixed (this is your regression suite) - Out-of-scope items — 10–15% of the set. Almost nobody includes these, and they're the only way to measure over-triggering and over-refusal - By recency — items sourced after your models' training cutoffs, as a contamination control

#Sourcing from production traces

The pipeline from Module 2, §2.7, applied: mine candidates daily (explicit negatives, escalations, retries, low online scores, schema violations, budget exhaustions, high-cost outliers, plus a stratified random sample so you don't only learn from complaints) → dedupe and cluster → triage weekly → annotate → split into regression suite / eval set / few-shot pool.

The leakage rule, restated because it is violated constantly: items used as few-shot examples or fine-tuning data must never appear in the eval set. Both pools come from the same mining pipeline, which is exactly why the mistake is easy.

#Refresh cadence and contamination hygiene

  • Add continuously from production mining; retire items that no longer represent live traffic (with a changelog entry, never silently)
  • Version the dataset and never edit in place — an eval score is only comparable to another score on the same dataset version
  • Keep a held-out slice that is never used for prompt iteration. If you tune against the whole set, you have a training set, not an eval set — and the score will drift upward while product quality doesn't
  • Never publish your golden set. Once public, it's a candidate for the next model's training data (§4C.4). If you must share, share the methodology, not the items
  • Add a canary item — a unique, meaningless string in a few items. If a model reproduces it, you have evidence of contamination
  • Track item age relative to model cutoffs, and watch for the tell: much better performance on pre-cutoff items than on equally difficult post-cutoff ones

#4F.2 Offline vs online: what belongs where

Layer Answers Metrics Cadence
Pre-commit "Did I break something obviously?" Schema validity, citation resolvability, smoke set Seconds, every commit
CI gate (PR) "Is this change safe to merge?" Tier 1 assertions (100%) · retrieval Recall@k/nDCG@k · faithfulness · completeness · per-item pass→fail flips · cost/latency ceilings Minutes, every PR
Nightly "Has anything drifted, including the vendor?" Full regression suite · safety/adversarial suite · frozen canary on the pinned endpoint · judge drift sample Nightly
Shadow "Does this work on the real query distribution?" Score distributions of old vs new on live inputs, never served Per release candidate
Canary "Does this hold up with real users at 1%?" Online quality score · refusal rate · fallback share · budget exhaustion · cost per request Per release, with auto-rollback
A/B "Does this make the product better?" Business metrics — resolution rate, escalation rate, task completion, time-to-resolution, retention Weeks

The boundary that matters: offline eval tells you whether the system is correct; only A/B tells you whether it is better for users. Those come apart more often than teams expect — a more thorough answer can score higher on completeness and lower on user satisfaction because it's now too long to read.

#4F.3 Statistical rigour

#Sample size and detectable effect

Treat eval questions as drawn from a super-population (Miller, Anthropic, arXiv 2411.00640). Then, for an unpaired comparison at significance α and power 1−β:

n  ≈  2 (z_{1−α/2} + z_{1−β})² · σ² / δ²

and inverting for the minimum detectable effect at a fixed n:

MDE  ≈  (z_{1−α/2} + z_{1−β}) · sqrt(2σ²/n)

With α=0.05, β=0.2: (1.96 + 0.84)² ≈ 7.85. For a binary metric with p≈0.8 (σ² = p(1−p) = 0.16), detecting a 5-point absolute difference needs roughly 2 × 7.85 × 0.16 / 0.05² ≈ 1,005 items unpaired. This is why unpaired comparison on a 100-item set cannot detect anything smaller than about a 16-point swing. Most teams are running underpowered evals and calling the noise a result.

Two things rescue you:

1. Pair everything. Run both systems on the same items and analyse the differences d_i = score_A(i) − score_B(i):

d̄ = (1/n) Σ d_i        SE(d̄) = sqrt(s_d² / n)        CI = d̄ ± 1.96 · SE(d̄)

Because much of the variance is item difficulty (shared by both systems), s_d² ≪ 2σ², often by a large factor. Pairing is free and typically the difference between a usable eval and an unusable one.

2. Multiple trials per item. Miller's paper shows resampling answers per question reduces the MDE materially — his worked example moves it from 13.2% to 7.5%. ESTABLISHED Sampling more answers on the same questions attacks the within-question variance that non-determinism introduces.

#Small-N reality

Miller's framework assumes thousands of items; a typical custom developer eval has 20–100. Practitioner work on small-N eval statistics recommends: Wilson intervals for binary single-sample coverage, Bayesian paired methods below N≈100 (they become overconfident and unreliable past N≈200), and smooth bootstrap with KDE as the general-purpose method for non-binary scores at larger N. EMERGING — practitioner simulations, not peer-reviewed, but the direction (don't use normal-approximation intervals on 40 binary items) is uncontroversial.

#Clustering

If your eval items are drawn from a smaller set of source documents, conversations, or users, they are not independent. Use clustered standard errors, clustering at the source level. Ignoring this understates your uncertainty — sometimes badly — and it is the most common silent statistical error in RAG evals, because 200 questions generated from 20 documents look like n=200 and behave like n=20.

#Multiple comparisons

A scorecard of 12 metrics × 2 systems at α=0.05 gives you roughly a 46% chance of at least one spurious "significant" difference. Fix it: - Designate one primary metric before you run. This is the decision metric; everything else is diagnostic. - Apply Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control across the secondary metrics rather than Bonferroni, which is too conservative for correlated eval metrics. - Pre-register the threshold. Deciding what counts as a regression after seeing the numbers is how teams talk themselves into shipping.

#Reporting standard

Every eval result should carry: dataset version · n items · k trials · model snapshot · judge snapshot + prompt hash · point estimate · CI · paired difference vs baseline with CI · per-item flip counts. If a result cannot be stated in that form, it is an anecdote.

#4F.4 Safety and adversarial evaluation

A separate suite, a separate gate, a separate cadence.

Suite Contents Pass criterion
Direct prompt injection Instruction override, role reassignment, delimiter escape, encoding tricks, multilingual variants Attack success rate below threshold; trending down
Indirect prompt injection Payloads planted in retrievable documents, tool outputs, web pages, file contents, image alt text The critical one for agents. Test the retrieval and tool paths, not just the user input
Exfiltration paths Markdown image auto-fetch, ANSI escape in terminal/IDE sinks, URL-taking tools, webhook/email tools, generated SQL/HTML/shell Zero tolerance. Any success is a Tier 1 failure
Jailbreak batteries HarmBench / JailbreakBench / AdvBench sets, plus multi-turn crescendo escalation over 5–20 turns Attack success rate below threshold
PII leakage Cross-tenant retrieval attempts · training/system-prompt extraction · PII in outputs · cache-scoping tests (Module 2, §2.5) · PII in traces Zero tolerance on cross-tenant
Bias and fairness Counterfactual substitution of protected attributes in otherwise identical inputs; measure outcome-rate differences Pre-declared parity thresholds; document the metric choice
Robustness Typos, truncation, very long inputs, rare languages, Unicode edge cases, empty and adversarially long prompts Graceful degradation, no crash, no policy bypass

Three design points that matter: 1. Attack success rate is statistical, not binary. Report ASR per category with confidence intervals and track the trend; "we're secure" is not a finding. 2. Multi-turn escalation is the coverage gap. Single-message probes miss crescendo attacks that build over 5–20 turns, and most eval suites are single-message. 3. RAG poisoning is a real and cheap attack. PoisonedRAG (USENIX Security 2025) is reported to manipulate responses ~90% of the time with 5 crafted documents injected into the corpus. EMERGING — cited secondhand; verify against the paper before quoting. Your adversarial suite should include corpus poisoning, not just prompt attacks.

Cadence: the full battery pre-deployment, after every model or prompt change, after every tool or MCP server change, and on a monthly or quarterly schedule regardless, because the attack literature moves faster than your system does.

#4F.5 Connecting eval scores to business metrics

This is the step almost everyone skips, and it is what makes the whole apparatus defensible.

The problem: you improved faithfulness from 0.82 to 0.89. Nobody outside the team knows whether that matters, including you.

The method, in order:

Step 1 — Name the business metric. One primary, measurable, owned by someone outside engineering. Support: deflection rate, escalation rate, time-to-resolution, CSAT. Search: task success, session abandonment, repeat-query rate. Coding: PR acceptance rate, review-cycle count, revert rate. Sales: qualified-lead conversion.

Step 2 — Establish the correlation once, retrospectively. Take 200–500 historical production sessions where you know the business outcome. Score them offline with your eval metrics. Compute the correlation, per metric, between the offline score and the business outcome. - A metric with near-zero correlation to the outcome is not measuring anything you care about — retire it or demote it to diagnostic. This single exercise usually kills two or three metrics on a typical scorecard. - A metric with strong correlation earns the right to gate.

Step 3 — Fit the translation. From the same data, estimate the slope: how much business-metric movement per point of eval movement. Even a crude linear fit converts "faithfulness +7 points" into "roughly X fewer escalations per thousand sessions," which is the sentence that gets you budget.

Step 4 — Validate causally with an A/B. Correlation from step 2 establishes plausibility; only the A/B establishes that moving the eval metric causes the business metric to move. Run it once per major change class, not once per change.

Step 5 — Publish the chain. eval metric → business metric → dollars, on one dashboard, with the correlation and the date it was last validated. Re-validate quarterly, because the relationship drifts as the product and users change.

The uncomfortable finding you should expect: some of your metrics will show no relationship to anything. That is a good result — you've found the ones that were costing judge tokens and dashboard attention for nothing.

#What most teams get wrong here

They run an underpowered, unpaired eval and treat a 3-point move as a result. On 100 items unpaired, a 3-point move on a binary metric is indistinguishable from noise; the fix — pair the comparison and run n≥3 — is free and changes what you can detect by roughly an order of magnitude.

Second: they tune against the entire eval set. Held-out discipline is standard practice in ML and gets abandoned the moment the "model" becomes a prompt. Without a held-out slice, your score rises and your product doesn't, and you have no way to detect the difference.

Third, and the most consequential: no business linkage at all. A scorecard that has never been correlated with an outcome is a set of numbers that go up. When the eval investment gets questioned — and it will — the only defensible answer is "moving this metric by N points reduced escalations by M%, and here is the A/B that showed it."

#The day-one scorecard — 10 metrics

If you have nothing today, build exactly these, in this order. Every one is either deterministic or cheap, and together they cover the failure classes that actually take systems down.

# Metric Why it's on the list Deterministic?
1 Schema / format validity Free, 100% threshold, catches the loudest breakage ✅
2 Citation resolvability (or tool-schema validity for agents) Free, catches fabricated provenance and hallucinated tools ✅
3 Recall@k at candidate depth The ceiling on everything downstream ✅
4 Recall@k (or nDCG@k) at final depth Separates "never retrieved" from "reranker buried it" ✅
5 Faithfulness (validated judge) The hallucination signal users experience judge
6 Completeness (validated judge) Stops #5 selecting for evasiveness judge
7 Task success / pass^3 Capability and reliability in one number depends
8 Cost per successful request The only cost metric that resists gaming ✅
9 p95 latency The SLO your users feel ✅
10 Per-item pass→fail flip count vs previous version Catches the regressions a stable mean hides ✅

Seven of the ten are deterministic and need no judge. Two need a judge — and before you trust either, run the §4D.3 validation on 100 double-labelled items and report κ.

Build them against 100 real production cases, run n=3, pair every comparison, and report confidence intervals. That is a week of work, and it is more evaluation rigour than most production GenAI systems have.

#Gaps I could not close, and the experiments that would settle them

  1. No public study establishes the correlation between offline eval metrics and business outcomes for production GenAI systems. This is the largest hole in the entire literature, and it is the thing §4F.5 exists to make you build privately. Experiment: 300 historical sessions with known outcomes, scored offline, correlation per metric. One week, and it will retire at least one metric on your scorecard.
  2. RAGAS validity findings rest on single studies — the discriminant-validity result is 500 Natural Questions instances, one paper; the 0.55 harmonic-mean correlation is reported secondhand. Treat as a strong caution, not a settled fact. Experiment: meta-evaluate your own metrics against 100 human-labelled items, RAGChecker-style.
  3. Judge validation targets (κ ≥ 0.7 to gate) are my synthesis of standard κ interpretation plus the measured human ceiling, not an established standard. No consensus threshold exists. Calibrate against your own human–human agreement rather than against my table.
  4. Synthetic query bias is quantified in only a handful of domains (TREC DL, Airbnb search). The 4-vs-6-word gap is not a universal constant. Experiment: KL divergence on query length between your synthetic set and a real sample — 20 lines, and it tells you whether your eval set represents your users.
  5. Search-time contamination is new and under-measured. One study, ~15% effect on one benchmark. The base rate across benchmarks and agents is unknown.
  6. No public data on how much benchmark rank predicts application performance. Everyone asserts the gap; nobody has published the correlation. Experiment: rank 5 models on a public benchmark and on your own eval, and report the rank correlation. If enough teams published this, the field would have the number it currently only gestures at.
  7. Eval framework comparisons are dominated by vendor-authored content, including several sources in §4E. Licence facts and acquisition dates are verified against primary sources; relative quality judgments are not, and should be treated as a starting hypothesis for a two-day bake-off, not a conclusion.
