MODULE 5 — FIELD GUIDE: PROBLEMS, SIGNATURES AND COMPETING FIXES

Compiled: 4 September 2026. Weighted toward practitioner postmortems, engineering blogs, framework issue trackers and honest retrospectives; vendor marketing is labelled where it appears. CONTEXT block: not supplied. General purpose; thresholds are starting points.

Confidence tags: ESTABLISHED · EMERGING · CONTESTED · VENDOR CLAIM

Per-problem format: signature → root causes → 2–4 competing strategies with trade-offs → the diagnostic that picks between them → residual risk after fixing.

The meta-rule for this whole module: most teams apply the expensive fix to a cheap problem, because the expensive fix is the one that got written up in a blog post. The cheap-fix/correct-fix table at the end exists to interrupt that reflex.

#PART 1 — RETRIEVAL AND DATA

#R1 — Retrieval returns plausible but wrong chunks; recall looks fine, answers do not

Signature. Users say "it's confidently wrong." Your Recall@k looks healthy. The retrieved chunks are all topically related to the query and none of them contains the answer. Answers are fluent, on-subject, and factually off.

Root causes. - Recall is measured at the wrong k. Recall@100 is 0.92; Recall@5 is 0.61. The evidence is in the pipeline and the reranker isn't surfacing it. - Semantic similarity ≠ answer-bearing. Dense retrieval finds text about the topic; the answer may live in a table, a footnote, or a differently-phrased passage. - Distractor dominance. Many near-identical chunks (versions, regions, product variants) and the wrong one ranks first. - Label mismatch. Your qrels mark "relevant documents," but the user needs a specific claim. Document-level recall can be 1.0 while claim-level context recall is 0.4.

Strategy Trade-off
Increase candidate depth, rerank harder (retrieve 100, rerank to 5–8) Cheapest and usually the answer. On a 2026 text-and-table benchmark, Recall@5 went 0.458 (20 candidates) → 0.826 (50) → 0.888 (100), while returning 10 vs 20 barely mattered (arXiv 2604.01733). Costs one rerank call ESTABLISHED
Add BM25 + RRF if you're dense-only Fixes the identifier/rare-term class specifically. On the same benchmark BM25 beat text-embedding-3-large on every metric except Recall@20. One day of work
Switch to claim-level evaluation (context recall against reference answers) Tells you the truth, costs reference answers. Do this if the two strategies above don't move the user-visible problem
Distractor pruning / dedup at index time Fixes the version-collision class. Requires knowing which document is canonical (see R4)

Diagnostic. Run the failing queries and compute Recall@100 and Recall@5 separately. - High@100, low@5 → reranker problem. Increase depth first, then check the reranker is in-domain (off-the-shelf cross-encoders trained on web search have been measured degrading nDCG by 0.3–3.1% on technical/scientific corpora, arXiv 2604.15484). - Low@100 → retrieval problem. Hybrid, chunking, or the content genuinely isn't indexed. - High@100 and high@5 but wrong answers → not a retrieval problem at all. Go to G1/G2.

Residual risk. Reranking raises precision and cannot invent evidence that was never indexed. You will still fail on questions whose answer requires synthesis across documents (R3) and on content that exists only in a format your parser mangled (R2).

#R2 — Chunk boundaries destroy meaning; tables, code and figures shredded

Signature. Failures cluster by document type, not by topic. Financial and legal queries fail while narrative queries succeed. Retrieved chunks contain half a table, a function signature without its body, or a figure caption with no figure. Answers cite real chunks and get numbers wrong.

Root causes. A character-count splitter applied to structured content; PDF extraction that linearises multi-column layouts and flattens tables into word soup; code split mid-function; the referent problem (Module 1) where "the company grew 3%" loses its subject.

Strategy Trade-off
Structure-aware parsing before chunking — never split inside a table, code block, or list; keep the table header with every row-group The correct fix for structured content. Requires a real parser per format, which is unglamorous engineering nobody wants to own
Parent-child / hierarchical — index small, return large Fixes the "right chunk, missing surroundings" case cheaply. Doubles index storage; can reimport noise if parents are large
Contextual prefixes (LLM-generated 50–100 tokens per chunk) Fixes the referent class. One LLM call per chunk at index time (cacheable). Only works if the prefix adds tokens the chunk lacks — a 2026 legal audit found prefixes that were near-verbatim paraphrases added nothing, and the generated context chunks themselves outranked targets in 15–17 of 22 audited queries (arXiv 2606.21676) EMERGING
Vision-first retrieval (ColPali/ColQwen family) for visually complex documents Skips OCR entirely and wins on charts/tables/scans. Costs on the order of 1,000+ patch vectors per page — budget the index before prototyping

Diagnostic. Sample 30 failing queries and read the retrieved chunks. This is the single most valuable hour in RAG debugging and teams skip it because it isn't automatable. Classify: mid-table split → parser; missing surrounding context → parent-child; missing subject/date/section → contextual prefix; content never extracted → the PDF pipeline, not retrieval.

Residual risk. Better chunking cannot fix content that was never extracted. Run an extraction-coverage check — what fraction of source pages produced zero text? — separately, because a broken parser looks exactly like a retrieval problem from the outside.

#R3 — Multi-hop questions no single chunk can answer

Signature. Failures on queries containing "compare," "across," "which of," "how many total," "changed between." Retrieved chunks are individually relevant and collectively insufficient. The model answers using whichever hop it found and states it confidently.

Root causes. One-shot top-k retrieval structurally cannot gather evidence whose second hop is only identifiable after the first. Also frequently a classification failure: nobody detected that this query needed a different pipeline.

Strategy Trade-off
Query decomposition — split into sub-queries, retrieve each, fuse Works when sub-queries are genuinely independent. Degrades ranking precision on true multi-hop where hop 2 depends on hop 1's answer — a 2026 study found decomposition helped a structured DevOps domain (+0.17 MRR) but hurt on MuSiQue (arXiv 2606.05658) EMERGING
Iterative/agentic retrieval — retrieve, read, retrieve again Handles dependent hops. Expensive and unreliable: agentic RAG cost 3.3× input tokens, 1.9× output, 1.5× latency with only a 3-turn cap, and the agent re-retrieved just 10% of the time with 53% of documents unchanged when it did (arXiv 2601.07711v2) EMERGING
Graph / entity-linked retrieval Genuinely good at relation-chain queries. Full GraphRAG indexing runs an LLM over every chunk (~10K tokens per document); LazyGraphRAG-style deferral cuts that dramatically VENDOR CLAIM on magnitude
Route to SQL/structured for aggregates and comparisons The correct fix for "how many," "total," "as of date." A vector index cannot do arithmetic

Diagnostic. Classify your failing multi-hop queries into three buckets: (a) enumerable independent parts → decomposition; (b) dependent chain over entities/relations → graph or iterative; (c) numeric aggregate/filter → SQL. The most common error is applying (a) to (b) queries and concluding decomposition doesn't work.

Residual risk. Every option above raises latency and cost on every query if applied unconditionally. Put a router in front. Iterative retrieval remains the weakest option relative to its cost.

#R4 — Conflicting or duplicate documents; stale content outranking current

Signature. Two users get contradictory answers to the same question. The system cites a real document that was superseded 18 months ago. Answers reference deprecated APIs, old pricing, or a policy that changed. Often reported as "hallucination" and is not.

Root causes. Corpus hygiene, not model behaviour: superseded documents never removed; near-duplicates across drafts/regions/versions; no recency or authority signal in ranking; no canonical-source designation; and — critically — retrieval that surfaces both versions and lets the model pick.

Strategy Trade-off
Corpus governance: canonical flags, valid_from/valid_to, owner per document The correct fix and the least popular, because it's data ownership work, not ML. Nothing else survives without it
Recency/authority boost post-fusion (e.g. multiply RRF score by a decay term) Cheap, immediate, no labels. Silently wrong for content where the old version is correct (historical records, prior-year filings)
Hard filter on is_current = true Deterministic and safe. Requires the metadata to exist and be maintained — which is R4's whole problem
Surface the conflict to the model explicitly ("these two sources disagree; the later one is authoritative") Preserves both, lets the model reason. Adds tokens and depends on instruction-following

Diagnostic. Take 20 contradictory answers, look at the retrieved set. If both versions were retrieved, it's a ranking/instruction problem — boost or filter. If only the stale one was retrieved, it's an index-freshness problem (R5). If the current one doesn't exist in the index at all, it's an ingestion problem. Three different fixes, one symptom.

Residual risk. Recency boosting introduces a new failure class — legitimately historical queries now get current documents. Any deployment of a recency boost needs a query class that opts out of it, and a test for that class.

#R5 — Corpus updates, re-embedding cost, and index drift

Signature. Two shapes. Slow: retrieval quality decays over months with no deploy and no errors. Fast and catastrophic: quality collapses overnight after an infrastructure change, while every health check stays green.

Root causes. The canonical one — query encoder upgraded, index not re-encoded — is a silent, total failure. Others: ANN parameters differing subtly between index builds, changing neighbour rankings; corpus growth pushing the embedding model out of distribution; deletions never propagating; partial re-index leaving mixed vector spaces.

Strategy Trade-off
Index manifest + query-time assertion — store {embed_model_id, dimension, build_id, corpus_snapshot} with the index, assert the query encoder against it on every search, fail loud ~15 lines of code. Converts a month of silent degradation into a startup error. This is the highest value-per-line fix in this entire module
Frozen-query neighbour stability, weekly — 200 fixed queries, measure top-k overlap vs baseline Detects slow drift. Practitioner-reported ranges: stable systems 85–95% neighbour persistence, drifting 25–40% loss EMERGING — treat the method as sound, calibrate the threshold yourself
Blue/green index with pointer flip Makes re-embedding safe and rollback instant. Doubles storage during the swap
Incremental re-embed only changed documents Cheapest ongoing. Only valid while the embedding model is unchanged; a model change requires a full rebuild, no exceptions

Diagnostic. Embed a fixed canary document with the production encoder daily and compare to its stored vector. Practitioner-reported thresholds: stable ≈ 0.0001–0.005 cosine distance, unstable ≥ 0.05 EMERGING. A jump means the encoder changed. One documented post-mortem puts the query-encoder/index mismatch bug at ~$15K of emergency re-encoding plus 2–5 engineer-days to diagnose.

Residual risk. The manifest catches model and dimension mismatches, not quality drift from corpus change. You still need the neighbour-stability check and a labelled qrels run to catch "the corpus moved away from what the model was trained on."

#R6 — Long-tail and out-of-domain queries; queries with no good answer

Signature. Head queries are excellent; the tail is terrible. The system confidently answers questions your corpus cannot answer. Users ask things you never anticipated, in four words, with typos.

Root causes. Two independent failures conflated: (a) no out-of-scope detection, so retrieval runs unconditionally and returns the least-bad chunks, which the model then treats as evidence; (b) real query distribution ≠ eval query distribution, so the tail was never tested.

The evidence that this is a distribution problem, not a model problem. A production RAG deployment on the Danish National Encyclopedia (~240,000 curated articles, real users) named this the "coverage illusion" — a structural mismatch between synthetic and real query distributions, with real users submitting short keyword phrases unlike the verbose conversational queries dominating English RAG benchmarks. Crucially, they found pre-retrieval routing cannot resolve it, because whether augmentation is needed is only revealed after searching the index. Their post-retrieval cascade — run workflows cheapest-first, escalate to LLM augmentation only when a step returns nothing — improved quality by +0.140 composite points over always-HyDE, cut latency 31.8%, and served 72.2% of real queries without LLM augmentation at all (arXiv 2605.27220). EMERGING — single production system, but it is real users at scale with published numbers.

Strategy Trade-off
Explicit "I don't know" path with a confidence threshold (retrieval score floor + no-answer instruction) The single most valuable fix. A naive always-retrieve pipeline is wrong on 100% of out-of-scope queries by construction. Costs some over-refusal (see G5)
Out-of-scope router (embedding classifier over labelled valid/invalid examples) ~10ms, no LLM call. Measured F1 84–96 across three domains vs 64.6–99.8 for an LLM agent doing the same job — the agent won on tight domains and lost by 28.8 F1 points on a loose one (arXiv 2601.07711v2) EMERGING
Post-retrieval cascade (cheap path first, escalate only on empty results) The coverage-illusion result above. Best measured cost/latency profile; needs the escalation ladder built
Fallback to human / search / documentation link Honest, and often the right product answer for the tail

Diagnostic. Sample 200 real production queries (not your eval set) and hand-classify: answerable-and-answered / answerable-and-missed / not-answerable-but-answered-anyway. The third bucket is your out-of-scope failure rate, and most teams have never measured it. Separately, compute the query-length distribution of your eval set against real traffic — if the medians differ by 2+ words you are not testing your users (Module 4, §4A.3).

Residual risk. A confidence threshold trades false answers for refusals. Tune it against both rates, publish both, and expect to move it as the corpus grows.

#R7 — Metadata filtering and permission-aware retrieval

Signature. Best case: a user sees a document they shouldn't. Worst case: nobody notices for months. Intermediate and very common: after adding permission filtering, recall collapses and users say "it can't find anything anymore."

Root causes. ACLs treated as an application-layer feature added before launch rather than a retrieval-layer property; permissions going stale relative to the source system; post-filtering used for security; ANN indexes behaving badly under highly selective filters.

The recall-collapse arithmetic, because it explains the intermediate symptom. With post-filtering, if a principal is authorised on 1% of the corpus, a top-50 retrieval by pure similarity contains ~0.5 authorised documents in expectation. The user experiences "the search is broken"; the cause is filter selectivity, not retrieval quality.

Strategy Trade-off
Pre-filter with expanded ID list (fetch authorised object IDs, then filtered vector search) The only defensible design for access control — restricted content is never retrieved. Cost is O(number of authorised objects), which is painful for broadly-permissioned principals
Post-filter (retrieve then check) Simple, and not a security boundary — restricted content was retrieved and existed in memory before being discarded, so any bug in the discard step is a disclosure. Also collapses recall under selectivity
Partition by namespace/tenant Strong isolation, simple reasoning, no filter cost. Doesn't handle overlapping per-document permissions within a tenant
Metadata filter on chunk-level ACL fields, re-synced from source Practical middle ground. Depends entirely on metadata correctness — the permission model still lives in the source system, and the filter's job is to faithfully mirror it

Diagnostic. Two tests, both of which should be in CI. 1. Negative retrieval test: for a low-privilege principal, issue queries whose best answers are in restricted documents. Any restricted chunk ID appearing in retrieval.candidate_ids is a Tier-1 failure — including if it was later filtered out. 2. Selectivity test: measure Recall@k as a function of filter selectivity. If recall craters at 1–5% selectivity, you're post-filtering.

Residual risk. Permissions go stale between syncs. Set an explicit freshness SLO on ACL sync, alarm when it's breached, and log every retrieval decision with the principal set used — you will need that audit trail. Note also that highly selective pre-filters can degrade ANN performance because the index was built over the whole corpus; test with realistic selectivity rather than assuming, since behaviour varies significantly by vector store.

#PART 2 — GENERATION

#G1 — Hallucination despite correct retrieved context

Signature. You check the trace: the right chunk was retrieved, in the top 3, and the answer still contains a fabricated detail. Usually a specific number, date, name or condition — the surrounding prose is correct.

Root causes. Context too long or the evidence buried mid-context (G3); the required fact spans two chunks and the model bridges the gap by inventing; conflicting chunks in context (R4); a prompt that rewards completeness over abstention; and the parametric-conflict case (G2).

Strategy Trade-off
Shrink the context: rerank harder, return 5–8 chunks not 20 Frequently improves accuracy while cutting cost, because context rot is real. First thing to try
Require inline citations per claim, then verify resolvability Deterministic verification, catches fabricated provenance for free. Doesn't stop a claim that's wrong but correctly cited
Claim-level entailment check post-generation (NLI or validated judge), regenerate or flag on failure Real reduction in shipped hallucinations. Adds a full pass of latency and cost; needs a validated checker (Module 4, §4D)
Instruct explicit abstention ("if the context does not contain the answer, say so") Free. Raises refusal and over-refusal rates (G5); measure both

Diagnostic. For each failure, ask: was the fabricated fact present anywhere in context? - Present but stated differently → the model paraphrased incorrectly. Tighten the extraction instruction; consider structured output for the critical field. - Absent, and the context couldn't support the claim → abstention/entailment gap. - Present in a contradicting chunk → R4. - Evidence present but positioned in the middle of a long context → G3.

Residual risk. Entailment checking verifies grounding in the retrieved text, not truth. If the corpus is wrong, a perfectly faithful system confidently propagates the error. Faithfulness is not correctness, and no generation-side fix changes that.

#G2 — Ignoring provided context in favour of parametric memory

Signature. The model answers from what it "knows" rather than from the documents. Classic tell: it gives the pre-update answer — old pricing, old leadership, superseded API — while the correct current document sits in the context window.

Root causes and the non-obvious finding. The folk model is "models over-trust their weights." The best evidence with real documents is more specific and more actionable. Kortukov et al. studied context-memory conflicts using factual real-world documents rather than synthetic conflicts, and found that models readily update their answers from real context — contrary to the synthetic-conflict literature. The remaining failures had a consistent cause they named parametric bias: if the model's incorrect parametric answer appears anywhere in the retrieved documents, even as a distractor, the model is much more likely to stick with it. This held across six QA datasets and five LLMs (arXiv 2404.16032). EMERGING — one study, but a well-designed one that inverts the standard prescription.

Related: a "Dunning-Kruger" pattern has been reported in stronger models showing higher confidence in incorrect parametric knowledge than in external context, plus availability, majority and confirmation biases in how models weigh conflicting evidence (surveyed in arXiv 2506.06485). EMERGING

Strategy Trade-off
Remove the distractor — dedup and prune chunks containing the stale answer before generation The fix the evidence actually points at, and almost nobody does it. Requires knowing which is stale (R4)
Prompt for context primacy ("answer only from the provided context; your prior knowledge may be outdated") Free, helps, depends on instruction-following, and does not adapt at the token level
Contrastive decoding (amplify context-conditioned distribution against context-free) Real mechanism, active research area. Needs logit access — off the table for most API deployments. Will also faithfully follow wrong evidence EMERGING
Structured extraction instead of free generation for the volatile field (price, version, effective date) Very effective for the fields where this hurts most. Only applies to extractable facts

Diagnostic. Run the failing query twice: once with the correct context, once with the correct context plus a chunk containing the stale answer. If the second run flips to the stale answer, you have parametric bias and the fix is corpus hygiene, not prompting. If both runs give the stale answer with only the correct context present, it's a genuine instruction-following failure and prompting or extraction is the lever.

Residual risk. Prompt-level context primacy is not a guarantee, and suppressing parametric knowledge too hard has been observed to undermine the model's ability to interpret the context correctly. The durable fix is not having stale content in the corpus.

#G3 — Lost-in-the-middle and degradation as context grows

Signature. Quality is fine at 5 chunks and worse at 20. Long conversations degrade after N turns. The model misses a fact that is demonstrably in its context window. Agents get worse the longer they run.

Root causes. Degradation with input length is continuous and starts well before the window limit — a model with a 200K window can show meaningful degradation at 50K. Chroma's study found it across all 18 frontier models tested VENDOR CLAIM, corroborated by NoLiMa, where at 32K tokens 10 of 12 models fell below half their short-context baseline and GPT-4o dropped from 99.3% to 69.7% (arXiv 2502.05167) ESTABLISHED.

For agents this is measured too: long-context web agents with success rates of 40–50% on short-horizon task variants fell below 10% once the same task was embedded in a longer interaction history — even when the relevant information remained technically present in the context window (arXiv 2512.04307, cited in 2607.05775). EMERGING

Strategy Trade-off
Send less: rerank to 5–8 chunks; trim tool results; drop stale turns Cheapest, usually improves quality and cost simultaneously. The default
Position the critical evidence at the start or end Free, real effect, brittle — it's exploiting a positional artefact, not fixing anything
Compaction at task boundaries + external notes/plan file The right fix for long agent runs. Aggressive compaction loses subtle context whose importance appears later; compaction at a token threshold rather than a task boundary does this maximally
Sub-agents with clean contexts Turns context isolation into a capability. Costs ~15× chat tokens for full orchestration VENDOR CLAIM; brings coordination failure modes (A5)

Diagnostic. Sweep it. Run the same eval set at 5, 10, 20, 40 chunks and plot the score. If the curve peaks and declines, you have context rot and your top-k is above the peak — a 30-minute experiment that most teams have never run. For agents, log per-step success against horizon length: a declining curve means decay (compaction helps); a flat-and-high failure rate means a capability gap (compaction will not help).

Residual risk. Compaction is lossy by construction. Keep the raw session log outside the context window and queryable, so a compaction decision is retrievable rather than irreversible.

#G4 — Inconsistent output format breaking downstream parsing

Signature. Intermittent parse errors, a few per thousand. Markdown fences appearing around JSON. A field that is usually a string and occasionally an array. Extra prose before the object. Failures spike after a model version bump.

Root causes. Free-form generation used where a schema was required; format instructions buried mid-prompt; few-shot examples inconsistent with the stated schema; and the underlying issue that formatting is a soft constraint the model trades off against other objectives.

Strategy Trade-off
Provider-native structured output / constrained decoding The correct fix where available — makes malformed output structurally impossible. Constrains you to providers that support it; can interact badly with reasoning modes
Tool/function calling as the output channel Well-trodden path, schema-validated by the provider. Slightly awkward when the "tool" is just "return the answer"
Parse-validate-repair loop (validate; on failure, return the error and retry once) Works everywhere, adds latency and cost on the failure path only. Cap the retries
Reason in prose, emit the structure last Free and effective. Older work found requiring JSON output cut GSM8K accuracy by 27.3pp vs natural language CONTESTED, likely dated as models improve — but the principle holds: don't make the model reason inside a JSON field

Diagnostic. Log the raw output on every parse failure. Ninety percent of the time you'll find one of three things: a code fence, a preamble sentence, or a type inconsistency in one optional field. All three have targeted fixes; none needs a prompt rewrite.

Residual risk. Constrained decoding guarantees the shape, not the content. A schema-valid object with a wrong enum value or a hallucinated ID passes every format check. Validate semantics — especially IDs — against the real data (see A2).

#G5 — Refusals and over-cautious behaviour on legitimate queries

Signature. Users in a legitimate domain — security, medicine, legal, finance, HR — report "it won't help me." Often invisible in your metrics, because a refusal is a fluent, well-formed, non-error response.

Root causes. Lexical overfitting in safety alignment (refusal triggered by surface features like "kill," "bomb," "exploit" regardless of context); a defensively-written system prompt compounding the model's own caution; a model swap to a more safety-conservative model; a retrieval failure being expressed as a refusal.

The magnitudes are large and measurable. XSTest (250 hand-crafted safe prompts) identified lexical overfitting as the primary cause of false refusals; on it, Llama-2 falsely refused 38% of safe prompts, dropping to 14% when the system prompt was removed — while GPT-4 sat at 6.4% safe-prompt refusal against 99.5% unsafe-prompt refusal. OR-Bench (ICML 2025) scaled this to 80,000 benign-but-toxic-seeming prompts across 10 categories plus a ~1,000-item hard subset and 600 genuinely toxic controls, across 32 models and 8 families. A 2026 healthcare benchmark found safety-optimised frontier models refusing up to 80% of "hard" benign prompts, with larger frontier models showing more "safety-pessimism" than smaller ones. ESTABLISHED

Strategy Trade-off
Audit your own system prompt first The Llama-2 result — 38% → 14% by removing the system prompt — says your defensive instructions may be the dominant cause. Free to test
Context-setting in the prompt (state the legitimate professional purpose and audience) Cheap and effective. Doesn't survive an adversarial user claiming the same context — which is a policy decision, not a technical one
Model selection on the refusal frontier OR-Bench's core contribution is that over-refusal and unsafe-compliance trade off measurably; pick a point deliberately. Costs a migration
Distinguish "I can't" from "I don't know" in the pipeline Not a refusal fix — it prevents misdiagnosing retrieval failure as refusal, which sends you fixing the wrong thing

Diagnostic. Build a 100–200 item benign-but-triggering set from your domain (XSTest/OR-Bench methodology, your vocabulary), and report four numbers: over-refusal rate, under-refusal rate, correct-refusal rate, correct-compliance rate. Reporting only one of the four is how teams optimise one direction into the ground.

Residual risk. This is a genuine trade-off frontier, not a bug to eliminate. Every reduction in over-refusal moves you toward more unsafe compliance. Pick the point, document why, and re-measure on every model change — because the point moves without you.

#G6 — Prompt brittleness; a working prompt collapsing on a model version bump

Signature. Nothing in your repo changed and quality dropped. Or you upgraded the model deliberately and a prompt tuned over months stopped working: format drift, tone change, different refusal behaviour, reasoning appearing where it wasn't before.

Root causes. Prompts over-fitted to one model's quirks; reliance on undocumented behaviours; a rolling alias silently repointing; a repoint to a model with different defaults (e.g. mandatory reasoning where it was optional); few-shot examples in a format the new model handles differently.

Strategy Trade-off
Pin immutable snapshots and assert the resolved model ID on every call Prevents the surprise version. Creates scheduled migration debt instead — the vendor lifecycle clock keeps running
Write model-agnostic prompts: explicit structure, no reliance on quirks, few-shot examples that are self-consistent Cheaper migrations forever. Slightly lower peak performance on any single model
Maintain a per-model prompt variant behind one interface Highest quality per model. N× the maintenance and N× the eval surface
Migration harness: run the frozen eval set against the candidate model, diff per item, fix only the items that flipped The correct process. Costs a real eval set — which is the actual prerequisite everyone skips

Diagnostic. Compare the requested model ID to the resolved/served model ID in the API response. If they differ, or if the served version changed, you have a vendor-side event, not a code regression. If they match, run the frozen nightly canary — if that moved on a pinned endpoint with fixed params and seed, the vendor changed something behind the same identifier, which is the case only a canary can catch.

Residual risk. Pinning defers the problem; it does not remove it. Keep a deprecation calendar with a named owner per registry entry, and remember the commonly-missed one: your fallback model must be pinned, eval-tested and calendared too, or the resilience path silently routes to whatever an alias resolves to on the day your primary goes down.

#PART 3 — AGENTS

#A1 — Infinite loops, oscillation between two tools, and stalling

Signature. Runs hit the step ceiling on tasks that should take four steps. Cost spikes with no quality change. Traces show the same call repeated with identical or cosmetically-varied arguments, or ping-ponging between search and read forever. Sometimes the agent just stops making progress while still emitting confident narration.

Root causes. No explicit stop condition in the prompt; a tool returning an unactionable error the model cannot recover from; no loop detection in the harness; and a genuine capability gap where the model cannot do the task and keeps trying. Note that the two largest single failure modes in the MAST-derived taxonomy are step repetition and unawareness of termination conditions — both control-flow bugs, not intelligence problems.

Strategy Trade-off
Loop detector: hash (tool_name, canonical_args); on 2nd repeat inject a message naming the repetition; on 3rd, halt ~10 lines. Directly addresses the largest documented failure mode. Almost nobody ships it
Explicit success criteria + remaining-step budget in the prompt ("You are done when X. If you cannot achieve X, say so and stop.") Free. Models under-recognise completion; telling them the condition and their remaining budget is the cheapest intervention available
No-progress detector: N consecutive steps with no state change → escalate or halt Catches semantic loops where args vary cosmetically. Needs a definition of "state change" for your domain
Improve the error message the tool returns Often the actual root cause. {"error":"invalid_date_format","expected":"YYYY-MM-DD","received":"March 3rd","hint":"call resolve_date first"} gets fixed; 400 Bad Request gets retried identically until the budget dies

Diagnostic. Group failing runs by tool.args_hash (Module 2, §2.4). If a small number of hashes dominate, it's a loop → detector plus error-message work. If hashes are all distinct and no state changes, it's a stall → no-progress detector and stop condition. If the trajectory is varied and sensible and the task is simply not getting done, it's a capability gap and none of these help.

Residual risk. A step limit bounds cost; it doesn't prevent burning the whole budget on a doomed approach. Budget-exhaustion rate is a quality metric, not just a cost metric — alert on it.

#A2 — Wrong tool selection and malformed parameters

Signature. The agent calls search_orders when it needed search_shipments. Arguments are schema-valid and semantically wrong — a plausible-looking but nonexistent order ID, a date in the wrong field. Accuracy degrades as your tool catalogue grows, with no single change to blame.

Root causes. Too many tools in one reasoning context; near-synonym tool names; vague descriptions that don't say when not to use the tool; free-form string parameters where an enum belonged; and position bias — tools in the middle of a long list are selected less reliably.

Production data on the threshold. Measured against human-confirmed ground truth in a production voice deployment (Wilson 95% CIs within ±4pp): Claude Haiku 4.5 held 91% at 10 tools and dropped to 87% at 15; Claude Sonnet 4 held ≥90% up to 20 tools and fell below 90% at 30 (arXiv 2606.30317). EMERGING — one organisation, observational, but real traffic. Secondary compilations put success above 90% only to ~30 candidate tools with sharp degradation beyond ~100, and report a 7–85% accuracy drop as catalogues grow. EMERGING

Strategy Trade-off
Cap visible tools at 10–15 per reasoning context via namespace routing, tool-RAG, or specialist sub-agents The fix that matches the evidence. Adds a routing layer; tool-RAG needs a relevance threshold tuned (too high → no tool called at all)
Rewrite descriptions to say when NOT to use the tool, and rename near-synonyms Free, immediate, and the highest-yield hour available. If you can't distinguish two tools by name alone, the model can't
Tighten the schema: enums over strings, few required fields, flat over nested Removes whole classes of argument error structurally
Semantic validation at the boundary — verify IDs exist before executing, return structured errors Catches schema-valid-but-wrong, which format validation cannot. Costs a lookup per call

Diagnostic. Plot tool-selection accuracy against visible tool count on a fixed task set — pad the list with plausible distractors at 5/10/15/20/30 and measure. One afternoon, and it tells you whether you have a tool surface problem (partition it) or a description problem (rewrite them) rather than a model problem.

Residual risk. Partitioning fixes selection accuracy and introduces routing errors: if the router picks the wrong namespace, the right tool is invisible. Measure router accuracy separately, and make "no namespace fits" a first-class outcome.

#A3 — Error cascades: one bad tool result poisoning every later step

Signature. One malformed or empty tool result early in the run, then twenty steps built on it. The agent never revisits the assumption. The final answer is confidently wrong in a way that traces cleanly back to step 3.

Root causes. Tool results treated as ground truth; errors returned as prose the model reads as data ("No results found for..." becomes evidence that the thing doesn't exist); no re-validation of environment state after the first read; and the general property that agents don't reconsider committed decisions — the Ferrazzi et al. result that an agent re-retrieved only 10% of the time and changed nothing half of those times is the retrieval instance of the same behaviour.

Strategy Trade-off
Distinguish "empty result" from "error" from "data" structurally in the tool return type Free and often sufficient. An error field the harness surfaces differently from a results: [] prevents the most common poisoning
Environment re-validation before irreversible actions (re-read state, don't trust the cached read) The correct fix for long-horizon agents, where cached assumptions about UI state, schemas or protocols go stale mid-run. Costs a call per checkpoint
Checkpoint + rollback to a prior state on detected inconsistency Powerful, needs a durable-execution substrate (Module 1, §1C)
Clean-context verifier reviewing the output Catches cascade-derived errors because it reasons backward from the result without the poisoned context. Cognition report their reviewer catches an average of 2 bugs per PR on Devin-written PRs, ~58% of them severe, and works best when coder and reviewer share no context EMERGING

Diagnostic. Take a failed run and find the first step whose output was wrong. If everything downstream is a coherent consequence, it's a cascade — fix error surfacing and add re-validation. If failures are scattered and independent, it's per-step accuracy — a different problem (A4).

Residual risk. Verifiers add cost and produce false positives. Track verifier false-positive rate alongside catch rate; a verifier that flags 40% of good runs will be ignored within a month.

#A4 — Compounding error over long horizons

The arithmetic, first. For H dependent steps at per-step reliability (1−ε), success ≈ (1−ε)^H. That is unforgiving:

Per-step reliability H=5 H=10 H=20 H=50
99% 95% 90% 82% 61%
95% 77% 60% 36% 8%
90% 59% 35% 12% 0.5%

A 95%-accurate agent — which sounds excellent — completes a 20-step task about a third of the time. One survey notes the corollary: P(success) = (1−ε)^H drops below 0.5 once ε > 0.014 at horizons around the 128K-context/SWE-bench-task scale. EMERGING on the specific threshold; the algebra is not in dispute.

Signature. Short tasks work; long ones fail disproportionately, not linearly. Per-step metrics look fine while task completion is poor.

The empirical curve. METR's time-horizon analysis timed human experts on the same multi-step software and research tasks: frontier models achieve near-100% success on tasks taking skilled humans under ~4 minutes, and under 10% on tasks taking more than ~4 hours, with the 50%-reliability task length doubling roughly every seven months since 2019 (Kwa et al., arXiv 2503.14499). ESTABLISHED

Strategy Trade-off
Shorten the horizon: decompose into independently-verifiable sub-tasks with checkpoints between The highest-leverage structural fix. Requires the task to actually decompose
Insert verification steps (tests, schema checks, state assertions) that reset the error budget Turns one long chain into several short ones. Adds cost per checkpoint; the verifier needs an external oracle or you're paying for self-critique, which degrades reasoning
Human checkpoints at irreversible boundaries The honest answer for high-stakes work. Caps autonomy, which is often the point
Raise per-step reliability (better tools, tighter schemas, better errors) Compounds favourably — small per-step gains produce disproportionate horizon gains. Slow, unglamorous, durable

Diagnostic. Log per-step success against horizon length and look for a curve. A declining curve is decay — decomposition and compaction help. Flat-and-high failure at all horizons is a capability gap — none of these patterns help and you should change model or scope. These two look identical from the outside and have opposite fixes.

Residual risk. Decomposition adds hand-off boundaries, and hand-offs lose information (A5). You are trading compounding error for coordination error; measure end-to-end task completion, not sub-task completion, or you will optimise into a worse system.

#A5 — Multi-agent: hand-off loss, duplicated work, deadlock, diffusion of responsibility, unbounded cost

Signature. Sub-agents produce individually reasonable, mutually incompatible output. Two workers do the same search. The orchestrator waits on a worker that already failed. Nothing is anyone's job and the final answer has a hole in it. Cost rises far faster than quality.

Root causes. The two principles Cognition named: sub-agents given only a summary lack the upstream context to interpret their task, and actions carry implicit decisions — parallel agents make incompatible choices about style, edge cases and patterns. The systematic evidence is MAST: 1,600+ annotated traces across 7 popular MAS frameworks, 14 failure modes in 3 categories (system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification), κ = 0.88, with the conclusion that failures stem from system design, not model limitations — meaning better models will not fix them (Cemri et al., NeurIPS 2025). ESTABLISHED

Strategy Trade-off
Keep writes single-threaded: N agents read, one writes The one rule both sides of the multi-agent debate now agree on. Caps parallelism to read-heavy work
Share full context, not summaries — fork the parent's context to the child Cognition found forking the full context was the pragmatic 80/20 for cross-agent consultation. Costs tokens and reintroduces context rot
Map-reduce-and-manage (manager splits, children execute, manager synthesises) rather than unstructured swarms The practical shape; unstructured agent networks are described by practitioners as "mostly a distraction" EMERGING
Per-agent budgets + fan-out and depth caps + correlation IDs on every message Bounds cost and makes failures reconstructible. Doesn't fix coordination quality

Diagnostic — and this is the one that decides whether to keep the architecture at all: run a token-controlled A/B against a single agent. Same tasks, same total token budget. Anthropic's own reporting is that token usage explained ~80% of the performance variance in their multi-agent research system, at ~15× the tokens of a chat interaction VENDOR CLAIM. If your multi-agent system doesn't beat a single agent given equal spend, you have bought 14 documented coordination failure modes and paid a large multiple for them.

Residual risk. Even a well-structured system loses information at hand-offs. Measure worker result-utilisation rate — the fraction of worker findings that survive into the final answer. A low number means you are paying for discarded work, which is the quiet way multi-agent cost gets out of hand.

#A6 — State and memory corruption across turns; context exhaustion mid-task

Signature. The agent contradicts something it established ten turns ago. It re-reads a file it already read. It hits the context limit mid-task and either hard-stops or, worse, silently compacts away the plan and continues confidently on a different task. Behaviour changes after a compaction event.

Root causes. Unbounded accumulation of raw tool output; compaction at a token threshold rather than a task boundary; no external plan file so the objective is lost at compaction; and the failure mode where an agent that perceives its context limit terminates prematurely and declares partial progress a success.

The magnitude. In an Anthropic cookbook example, an unmanaged research agent's context reached ~335,000 tokens over five turns, of which ~96% was raw file-read results. On a 200K-token model that run hard-stops mid-task. VENDOR CLAIM on the specific figures; the shape is universal.

Strategy Trade-off
Tool-result clearing — drop raw outputs once consumed Lightest-touch and highest-yield. There is rarely a reason for a 40K-token file read to stay in the window after extraction
Compact at task boundaries, not at a % threshold Compacting at 90% of the window means compacting mid-reasoning, where subtle-context loss does the most damage
External plan/todo file + structured notes re-read after every compaction Preserves the objective across resets. Costs a read per cycle
Session log outside the window, queryable (rewind, re-read before an action) Turns an irreversible lossy compaction decision into a retrievable one. Materially better reliability posture for long-horizon work; needs harness support

Diagnostic. Plot context size against step index for a failing run and identify what's consuming it. If it's raw tool output, clearing solves it. If it's genuinely accumulated reasoning, you need compaction plus external notes. If failures cluster immediately after compaction events, your compaction prompt is dropping something load-bearing — tune it by first maximising recall on real traces, then improving precision.

Residual risk. Compaction is lossy by construction; you are choosing what to lose. Test the compaction prompt against real agent traces with probe questions about facts established early in the run, and treat "the agent forgot the constraint from turn 2" as a compaction bug, not a model failure.

#A7 — Non-determinism making bugs unreproducible

Signature. "Works on my machine, and also sometimes on yours." A failing production trace re-run against the identical inputs and temperature 0 produces a different, working output. Flaky CI. Bug reports that cannot be closed.

Root causes — and the usual explanation is wrong. The folk model is "GPUs + floating-point non-associativity." Thinking Machines Lab showed the primary cause for inference endpoints is batch invariance: server load varies, batch size varies with load, and several kernels are not batch-invariant — so your output depends on what other requests happened to be batched alongside it. This is not GPU-specific; CPU- and TPU-served endpoints have it too. Measured: sampling 1,000 completions from Qwen3-235B at temperature 0 produced 80 distinct outputs, diverging at token 103. With batch-invariant kernels the same runs were bitwise identical. Reported throughput cost ~61.5% in the reference implementation, reduced to ~34.35% by SGLang with CUDA graphs. (thinkingmachines.ai, Sep 2025; overhead figures via arXiv 2606.03019.) ESTABLISHED

Strategy Trade-off
Accept it and change your methodology: n≥3 trials, report pass^k, gate on distributions with confidence intervals, not single runs The right default for almost everyone. Costs 3× eval spend and a change of habit
Capture the full trace as the reproduction artefact — inputs, retrieved chunk IDs, tool args and results, resolved model ID, params Makes the bug analysable even when it isn't re-runnable. This is what on-call actually needs
Batch-invariant kernels on self-hosted inference Genuine bitwise reproducibility. Only available if you serve the model yourself, and costs meaningful throughput
Replay harness: re-run a trace with tool results stubbed from the recorded run Isolates model non-determinism from environment non-determinism. The single most useful debugging tool for agents, and rarely built

Diagnostic. Re-run the failing trace 10 times. If it fails 10/10, it's deterministic-given-inputs and something in the recorded environment differs — chase the retrieval results and tool responses. If it fails 3/10, it's genuinely stochastic and your question is not "why did this fail" but "what is the failure rate and is it acceptable" — which is a pass^k question, not a debugging one.

Residual risk. Even with batch-invariant kernels, full reproducibility is not guaranteed across framework versions or hardware. Pin the software stack if reproducibility is a requirement you're actually accountable for, and note that in long-horizon tasks error compounds regardless of temperature — determinism does not buy you reliability.

#PART 4 — OPS AND ORG

#O1 — Latency budget blown by retrieval + rerank + multi-hop reasoning

Signature. p50 is acceptable, p95 is not. Users abandon. Adding a "quality improvement" made the product feel worse.

Root causes — and the counter-intuitive part is where the time isn't. Measured on an Enhanced RAG pipeline: 45–50% of end-to-end latency is answer generation, a similar share is query rewriting, 0–5% is retrieval, and 0–2% is reranking (arXiv 2601.07711v2). EMERGING Every instinct to optimise the vector index is aimed at ~5% of your p95. LLM calls are the budget.

Strategy Trade-off
Remove an LLM call: make query rewriting conditional instead of unconditional The largest single win available, since rewriting is ~45% of latency and helps only some query shapes. Requires a cheap router
Parallelise: run un-rewritten retrieval concurrently with the rewrite; run BM25 and dense concurrently Free latency, extra compute. Use whichever candidate set is ready and usable
Cascade cheapest-first and escalate only on empty results The coverage-illusion result: −31.8% latency with quality up, serving 72.2% of real queries without LLM augmentation EMERGING
Stream Fixes perceived latency only, and complicates validation — you cannot schema-check what you haven't finished receiving. Decide up front whether a stream can be retracted

Diagnostic. Break p95 down by span. If retrieval and rerank together are under 10%, stop optimising the index. Then ask of each LLM call: what fraction of queries does this call actually improve? Unconditional stages that help 30% of traffic are latency you're paying 100% of the time.

Residual risk. Conditional stages introduce router errors, and a router that misroutes a hard query produces a fast wrong answer. Measure quality per route, not just aggregate.

#O2 — Cost blowup: retries, oversized context, step explosion, per-user abuse

Signature. The bill triples with no traffic change. Or it's fine on average and a small number of runs consume enormous budget. Or one tenant consumes more capacity than a thousand others.

Root causes. Retry storms at the step ceiling; full-price static prefixes because a rotating token invalidated the cache; unconditional agentic loops (3.3× input tokens, 1.9× output, 1.5× time vs a fixed pipeline, with a 3-turn cap); multi-agent orchestration at ~15× chat tokens; and per-request rather than per-token quotas.

Strategy Trade-off
Prefix-discipline audit (30 min): log cache-read tokens, walk the prompt from the top for the first varying element Usually the biggest single win, and free. One timestamp or session ID above the static block invalidates the cache on every request, silently
Hard caps: retries ≤2, step ceiling, per-run token budget, wall-clock timeout Removes the tail that blows up the bill. Also the top reliability control (A1)
Trim context: rerank harder, return fewer chunks Proportional saving, and often improves quality via context rot
Per-tenant token quotas + weighted fair queuing The only thing that stops noisy neighbours. Requires cost attribution to exist first

Diagnostic. Compute cost per request at the step ceiling, not at the average. Then group spend by budget.terminated_by and by tenant. Two numbers usually explain most of the surprise: the share of runs that hit a ceiling, and the top tenant's share of tokens.

Residual risk. Caps convert cost incidents into quality incidents — a capped run returns partial results. Make the partial-result path return provenance and a clear "incomplete" signal, and track budget-exhaustion rate as a quality metric.

#O3 — Rate limits, throttling and provider outages

Signature. 429s under load, cascading retries making it worse, an outage taking your feature down entirely, or — the quiet one — 30% of traffic silently served by an untested fallback model.

Strategy Trade-off
Client-side token bucket + jittered exponential backoff + circuit breaker, respecting Retry-After Table stakes. Naive retry-on-429 amplifies an incident
Fallback chain with every tier pinned, eval-tested and calendared The commonly-missed one: the fallback is usually a bare alias nobody evals. When it fires you route to whatever the alias resolves to that day, with no baseline
Multi-provider abstraction Real resilience. Costs an abstraction layer, N× prompt maintenance, and N× eval surface
Exploit caching as a rate-limit multiplier — cache reads may not count toward input-token-per-minute limits on current models Free headroom on cached workloads. Verify against current provider docs, it's model-dependent

Diagnostic. Log which tier served every request and alert when fallback share exceeds a threshold. A silent 30% fallback rate is a quality incident nobody is looking at.

Residual risk. Multi-provider fallback means two prompt variants and two eval baselines, forever. Budget for it or accept degraded quality on the fallback path — but know which you chose.

#O4 — Model deprecation and forced migration

Signature. A sunset email with a fixed clock. Or your fallback model quietly stops existing.

Root causes. Pinning buys stability today and creates scheduled migration debt tomorrow. OpenRouter states more than 70 models have been pulled or deprecated by providers in recent years VENDOR CLAIM, unverified independently, but directionally consistent with everyone's experience.

Strategy Trade-off
Registry entry per model with a named owner and retirement date Turns a surprise into a scheduled task. Requires someone to own the calendar
Migration harness: frozen eval set, run candidate, diff per item, fix only what flipped The correct process. Prerequisite is a real eval set — which is why migrations hurt teams that skipped Module 4
Model-agnostic prompts (G6) Cheaper migrations forever, marginally lower peak quality
Standing migration budget (e.g. 5% of team capacity) Prevents migration always being an emergency. Costs 5% of capacity

Diagnostic. Inventory every model reference in your codebase — including fallbacks, judges, embedders, rerankers and user simulators. Most teams find three or four they had forgotten, and the judge and embedder are the two most consequential unpinned entries.

Residual risk. Migration is never free. A model that scores identically on your eval set can behave differently on the query distribution the eval set doesn't cover. Shadow the new model on live traffic before cutting over.

#O5 — Eval-set overfitting: scores rise, users complain

Signature. Every metric on the dashboard is up and to the right, and support volume isn't falling. New model versions score well and feel worse.

Root causes. Tuning against the whole eval set with no held-out slice; an eval set built only from complaints, so it doesn't represent the silent majority; a stale set that no longer matches live traffic; and a scorecard of metrics nobody ever correlated with an outcome.

Strategy Trade-off
Held-out slice never used for iteration Standard ML practice, abandoned the moment the "model" becomes a prompt. Free
Continuous promotion of production failures into the set, including a stratified random sample Keeps the ruler current. Costs an hour of triage weekly
Correlate every metric with a business outcome once, retrospectively (200–500 historical sessions) Kills the metrics that measure nothing. One week, and it is the step that makes the eval program defensible
Shadow deployment on live inputs Tests against the real distribution instead of your sample. No user exposure

Diagnostic. Compute coverage: what fraction of last month's production queries fall into a cluster represented in your eval set? Then compute the query-length and topic distributions of both. If they differ materially, your eval set is measuring a different product than the one you shipped.

Residual risk. Even a well-maintained set lags reality. Treat online quality scoring on sampled production traffic as the ground truth, and offline evals as the fast proxy — not the reverse.

#O6 — Prompt injection through retrieved documents and tool outputs

Signature. Best case: your red-team finds it. Worst case: a security researcher does. Intermediate: an agent takes an action nobody asked for, and the instruction traces to a document, a web page, or a tool result.

Root causes. The model cannot separate instructions from data because both arrive as text. OWASP has kept prompt injection at #1 since the list first appeared, and its own prevention guidance opens by stating no reliable prevention mechanism exists. Filters degrade against adaptive attackers; a second model policing the first is another model that can be talked around.

Strategy Trade-off
Break the lethal trifecta — an agent is exploitable only when it has private-data access and untrusted-content exposure and an egress channel. Remove one leg The only structural fix. Costs architectural constraint: segregate the reader-of-untrusted-content from the holder-of-private-data
Egress allowlisting + renderer hardening (no auto-fetch of Markdown images, no ANSI escapes in terminal/IDE sinks) Closes the exfiltration half specifically. Frequently forgotten because the renderer isn't thought of as attack surface
Capability scoping per step + human approval for irreversible actions Bounds blast radius. Caps autonomy
Guardrail classifier Helps at the margin, is not a boundary, gets bypassed the week it ships. Have one; don't rely on it

Diagnostic. For each agent, answer three questions: does it read untrusted content (including tool output), does it touch private data, can it communicate outward? Three yeses means assume injection will eventually succeed and design for blast radius. Then run an indirect-injection suite against the retrieval and tool paths, not just the user input field — that's where the live attacks are. Include corpus poisoning: PoisonedRAG is reported to manipulate responses ~90% of the time with 5 crafted documents EMERGING, cited secondhand — verify before quoting.

Residual risk. Permanent. The correct posture is bounded damage, not prevention: least privilege, approval gates on irreversible actions, egress control, and monitoring for anomalous tool sequences and data movement.

#O7 — PII leaking into traces, logs, caches and eval datasets

Signature. A compliance review finds customer data in the trace store. A cached response is served to the wrong tenant. An eval dataset built from production traces contains real names.

Root causes. In GenAI observability the payload is the signal — you need prompts and completions to debug, and they're the most sensitive data you have. Default instrumentation logs tool arguments and results wholesale. Semantic caches without tenant-scoped keys serve across boundaries. Golden datasets are built from production traces without redaction.

The cache case is a documented incident shape: threshold 0.88, global namespace, one customer's summary served into another's session, full revert within a week. "What's the status?" from user A about order #4521 and user B about #7893 have near-identical embeddings.

Strategy Trade-off
Redact in the collector, before egress The trust boundary must be inside your network. "The vendor deletes it" is a contract, not a control
Two-tier storage: redacted traces broadly + raw content in a short-retention, access-controlled store for a sampled fraction Preserves debuggability with bounded exposure. Costs a second store
Tenant/user in every cache key, and exact-match caching before semantic Exact caching has zero correctness risk; semantic has a measured 1–15% false-positive rate depending on threshold
Redact at dataset creation, and treat golden datasets as production data Cheap. Almost always skipped, because the dataset feels like an internal artefact

Diagnostic. Grep your trace store for secret patterns and PII patterns. Then check three specific places teams forget: tool results (a DB tool returns customer rows), cache keys (is tenant in there?), and eval datasets. Anything found is an incident, not a finding — rotate and report.

Residual risk. Redaction is pattern-based and imperfect. Pair it with short retention on raw content and access controls on the trace store, so that imperfect redaction has a bounded window and a bounded audience.

#O8 — Demo works, production does not: the 80% → 95% gap

Signature. The pilot impressed everyone. Six months later the infrastructure runs idle, the AWS line item has no owner, and someone asks "whatever happened to that thing?"

On the headline statistics, honestly. The most-cited number is MIT NANDA's mid-2025 report describing roughly 95% of enterprise GenAI pilots showing no measurable P&L impact. That is a pilot-to-revenue gap, not a claim that 95% of systems broke technically — a distinction most citations drop. Other estimates for "pilots that never reach durable production" range from 70% to 95% depending on analyst, cohort and success definition. CONTESTED on the specific number; not contested that the share is large.

Root causes — why the last mile costs more than everything before it. A pilot succeeds because governance was minimal, data was curated, scope was controlled, and a developer was watching the logs. Production removes all four conditions simultaneously. Concretely, the last 15 points are consumed by: the long tail of queries nobody anticipated (R6); permission and multi-tenancy (R7); the failure paths (A1, A3, O3); observability sufficient to debug non-deterministic failures (A7); adversarial hardening (O6); cost engineering at real volume (O2); and evaluation rigorous enough to ship changes safely (Module 4). Each of those is weeks. None of them appear in a demo.

Strategy Trade-off
Scope to a narrow slice and take it all the way to production first The single best structural decision. Builds the whole pipeline — evals, observability, ACLs, rollback — on a problem small enough to finish. Feels less ambitious than it is
Pilot on the real query distribution from day one (shadow-mode against live traffic) Kills the coverage illusion before you've built on it. Requires access to real traffic early, which is an organisational fight
Budget the last mile explicitly — plan for the post-demo work to exceed the demo work Sets expectations honestly and is usually the thing leadership most resists hearing
Define the production-readiness bar before the demo (accuracy floor, latency SLO, cost ceiling, security review, rollback, on-call owner) Converts "is it good enough?" from a judgment call into a checklist. Costs a conversation nobody wants to have early

Diagnostic. Take 100 real production-representative queries — not curated demo cases — and measure end-to-end task success with the actual permission model applied. That number, not the demo, is your baseline. If it's 20 points below what the demo suggested, that gap is the project.

Residual risk. Even a well-run production system has a tail it handles badly. The goal is a known, bounded, monitored tail with a graceful fallback, not the absence of one.

#O9 — Scope: when the honest answer is "this should not be an LLM feature"

Signature. The team keeps building guardrails around the model to force deterministic behaviour. Accuracy plateaus below the bar and no amount of prompting moves it. Someone proposes a fifth validation layer.

The tests that say "don't."

Test If true →
Is the task deterministic with a known rule? (tax calculation, eligibility from stated criteria, routing on a fixed taxonomy) Write the rule. An LLM is a probabilistic approximation of code you could have written
Does the answer require arithmetic or aggregation over records? SQL. A vector index cannot count, and the failure signature is fluent prose with wrong numbers
Is the per-error cost catastrophic and unrecoverable, with no human in the loop? Either add the human, or don't ship. (1−ε)^H does not go to zero, and pass^k tells you what your on-call will experience
Is the required accuracy above ~99% on an open-ended task? Extremely hard. Be sure the requirement is real before committing quarters to it
Is a search box, a form, a filter, or a template sufficient? Ship that. It's faster, cheaper, deterministic, and users often prefer it
Do you lack any way to tell whether an output is right? You cannot evaluate it, therefore you cannot improve it or safely ship it. This is disqualifying

Where an LLM genuinely earns its place: unstructured input that must become structured; open-ended language generation; tasks with many valid answers; semantic matching where lexical rules fail; and workflows where the LLM orchestrates deterministic tools rather than replacing them. That last pattern — model decides, code executes — is where most durable production value has landed.

The honest reframe that usually works: most failing LLM projects are not "wrong technology," they're "wrong division of labour." Move the deterministic parts into code, keep the model for the genuinely ambiguous step, and the accuracy bar usually becomes reachable.

Residual risk. Saying no is politically expensive. Make it evidential: 100 real cases, measured end-to-end success, and the cost per successful request. A number is easier to argue with than an opinion, and easier to defend.

#DELIVERABLE 1 — DIAGNOSTIC DECISION TREE

Start at the symptom. Follow to the diagnostic. The diagnostic tells you which branch you're on.

SYMPTOM: "The answer is wrong"
│
├─ Check the trace: was the correct evidence in the retrieved context?
│  │
│  ├─ NO ──► Compute Recall@100 vs Recall@5 on failing queries
│  │         ├─ high@100 / low@5 ─► RERANKER  → depth 50–100; check in-domain (R1)
│  │         ├─ low@100 ──────────► RETRIEVAL → +BM25/RRF, chunking, parsing (R1,R2)
│  │         ├─ content not in index at all ─► INGESTION → extraction coverage (R2)
│  │         └─ query needs 2+ documents ────► MULTI-HOP → classify a/b/c (R3)
│  │
│  └─ YES ─► Was the wrong fact present anywhere in context?
│            ├─ present in a CONTRADICTING chunk ─► STALE/DUPLICATE corpus (R4)
│            ├─ present as the model's own prior ─► PARAMETRIC BIAS → remove
│            │                                       the distractor, not more
│            │                                       prompting (G2)
│            ├─ absent, unsupported claim ────────► HALLUCINATION → shrink context,
│            │                                       citations, entailment (G1)
│            └─ evidence buried mid-long-context ─► CONTEXT ROT → sweep top-k (G3)

SYMPTOM: "It says it can't help"
├─ Retrieval returned nothing? ─────► OUT-OF-SCOPE / long tail (R6)
├─ Retrieval returned good chunks? ─► OVER-REFUSAL → audit YOUR system prompt
│                                      first; build a benign-trigger set (G5)
└─ Only for certain users? ─────────► PERMISSION FILTER over-restricting (R7)

SYMPTOM: "It found nothing / recall collapsed after a change"
├─ After adding permission filtering? ─► POST-FILTER selectivity collapse (R7)
├─ After an infra/embedding change? ───► INDEX MISMATCH → assert manifest (R5)
└─ Gradually over months? ─────────────► DRIFT → neighbour stability (R5)

SYMPTOM: "Costs exploded"
├─ Group by budget.terminated_by
│  ├─ ceiling hits dominate ────► LOOPS / step explosion (A1, O2)
│  └─ normal terminations ──────► check cache_read_tokens
│      ├─ near zero ────────────► PREFIX DISCIPLINE — 30-min audit (O2)
│      └─ healthy ──────────────► context size or agentic loop count (G3, R3)
└─ Concentrated in one tenant? ─► QUOTA / noisy neighbour (O2)

SYMPTOM: "It's too slow"
└─ Break p95 down by span
   ├─ generation + rewriting ≈ 90% ─► REMOVE AN LLM CALL; make rewriting
   │                                   conditional; cascade cheapest-first (O1)
   ├─ retrieval + rerank < 10% ─────► STOP optimising the index (O1)
   └─ many agent steps ─────────────► step budget, decomposition (A4)

SYMPTOM: "Agent misbehaves"
├─ Same call repeated? ─────────────► LOOP → detector + better errors (A1)
├─ No state change for N steps? ────► STALL → no-progress detector (A1)
├─ Wrong tool chosen? ──────────────► plot accuracy vs tool count (A2)
├─ Everything after step k wrong? ──► ERROR CASCADE → error surfacing,
│                                      re-validation, clean-context verifier (A3)
├─ Fails only on LONG tasks? ───────► plot per-step success vs horizon
│   ├─ declining curve ─────────────► DECAY → decompose, compact (A4, A6)
│   └─ flat high failure ───────────► CAPABILITY GAP → change model or scope (O9)
└─ Sub-agents incompatible? ────────► token-controlled A/B vs single agent (A5)

SYMPTOM: "It changed and we didn't change anything"
├─ resolved model ID ≠ requested? ──► VENDOR REPOINT → pin snapshots (G6)
├─ IDs match, nightly canary moved?─► SILENT VENDOR CHANGE on same ID (G6)
├─ index build changed? ────────────► RE-INDEX / manifest mismatch (R5)
├─ judge unpinned? ─────────────────► YOUR METRIC drifted, not the system (O5)
└─ nothing moved? ──────────────────► input distribution shift (R6, O5)

SYMPTOM: "Scores are up, users complain"
├─ eval-set coverage of live queries low? ─► STALE EVAL SET (O5)
├─ no held-out slice? ─────────────────────► OVERFITTING (O5)
├─ metrics never correlated to outcomes? ──► MEASURING NOTHING (O5)
└─ faithfulness up, completeness down? ────► optimised into evasiveness (G1)

#DELIVERABLE 2 — CHEAP FIX VS CORRECT FIX

The cheap fix buys time and is often enough. The correct fix is what you owe the system if the problem recurs. The failure mode this table exists to prevent is reaching for the right-hand column first, because that's the one with the conference talk.

Problem Cheap fix (hours–days) Correct fix (weeks) Do the cheap fix when
R1 wrong chunks Raise candidate depth to 100, rerank to 5–8 Claim-level eval + in-domain reranker + distractor pruning Always try first — it's usually sufficient
R2 shredded structure Parent-child retrieval Structure-aware parsing per format; vision-first for visual docs Failures are "missing surroundings," not "mangled extraction"
R3 multi-hop Route aggregates to SQL; decompose enumerable queries Graph/entity retrieval or iterative loop with budgets Most of your "multi-hop" is actually aggregation
R4 stale content Recency boost post-fusion Corpus governance: canonical flags, validity windows, owners You have no historical-query class that the boost would break
R5 index drift Index manifest + query-time assertion (~15 lines) Blue/green re-index pipeline + weekly neighbour stability Always. This is the best value-per-line fix in the module
R6 long tail Retrieval-score floor + explicit "I don't know" Out-of-scope router + post-retrieval cascade Always start here; measure the OOS rate first
R7 permissions Namespace/tenant partition Pre-filter with expanded ID list from the authz system Permissions are tenant-shaped, not per-document
G1 hallucination Return 5–8 chunks instead of 20; require citations Claim-level entailment gate with regenerate-or-flag Always try context shrinking first — it's free and often improves quality
G2 ignores context Prompt for context primacy Remove the stale distractor from the corpus You need it working today; the corpus fix is the durable one
G3 context rot Sweep top-k and pick the peak Compaction at task boundaries + external plan file Non-agentic, single-turn
G4 format Parse-validate-repair with one retry Provider-native structured output / tool-calling channel Your provider lacks constrained decoding
G5 refusals Audit and soften your own system prompt Domain benign-trigger suite, all four rates, model selection on the frontier Always first — the system prompt is often the dominant cause
G6 brittleness Pin the snapshot; assert resolved ID Model-agnostic prompts + migration harness on a frozen eval set Immediately, then build the harness
A1 loops Loop detector + explicit stop condition in the prompt Fix the tool error messages that cause the loop Always. Ten lines against the largest documented failure mode
A2 tool selection Rewrite descriptions; rename near-synonyms Namespace routing / tool-RAG / specialist sub-agents Under ~15 tools — descriptions are usually the whole problem
A3 cascades Structurally distinguish error / empty / data in tool returns Checkpointing + re-validation + clean-context verifier Poisoning traces to an ambiguous "no results" string
A4 long horizons Cap steps; add a verification checkpoint Decompose into independently-verifiable sub-tasks Horizon under ~20 dependent steps
A5 multi-agent Single-thread the writes Map-reduce-and-manage + budgets + correlation IDs, justified by a token-controlled A/B Always single-thread writes first
A6 context exhaustion Tool-result clearing Compaction at task boundaries + external session log Raw tool output dominates the context
A7 non-determinism n≥3 trials, report pass^k, capture full traces Replay harness with stubbed tool results; batch-invariant kernels if self-hosting Always. Methodology change beats an engineering project
O1 latency Parallelise retrieval with rewriting Conditional rewriting + cheapest-first cascade You need the win this week
O2 cost Prefix-discipline audit + hard caps Per-tenant token quotas, fair queuing, routing/cascade Always. Audit before you negotiate pricing
O3 rate limits Token bucket + jittered backoff + circuit breaker Pinned, eval-tested fallback chain; multi-provider Immediately
O4 deprecation Pin snapshots; inventory every model reference Registry with owners, retirement dates, migration harness Immediately, then build the process
O5 eval overfitting Carve out a held-out slice today Continuous promotion pipeline + business-metric correlation Always. The held-out slice costs nothing
O6 injection Egress allowlist; disable Markdown image auto-fetch Break the lethal trifecta architecturally; capability scoping; approval gates Renderer hardening is a same-day win; do it regardless
O7 PII Tenant in every cache key; exact-match cache only Collector-side redaction + two-tier storage + retention policy Immediately — the cache key is a one-line change
O8 demo→prod Measure 100 real queries with the real permission model Narrow the scope; ship one slice end to end Always. The number reframes the conversation
O9 wrong tool Move the deterministic parts into code Redesign the division of labour: model orchestrates, code executes The moment you're building a fifth validation layer

Weighted toward postmortems, engineering blogs and empirical studies; vendor material labelled.

#Gaps I could not close, and the experiments that would settle them

  1. Almost no public negative postmortems. Teams publish what worked. The failure knowledge in this module is reconstructed from research papers, two honest practitioner retrospectives (Cognition's self-revision is the notable one) and incident shapes reported secondhand. The field's biggest missing artefact is a public, blameless GenAI incident corpus.
  2. The 70–95% pilot-failure range is not a measurement, it's a family of estimates with incompatible success definitions. Treat any specific figure — including the widely-quoted 95% — as rhetoric, and measure your own pilot-to-production rate.
  3. Tool-count degradation thresholds come from one organisation's production traffic plus secondary compilations whose methodology I could not verify. Experiment: fix the task set, pad the tool list with plausible distractors at 5/10/15/20/30, plot accuracy. One afternoon, and it's specific to your surface.
  4. Neighbour-stability and embedding-canary thresholds (85–95% persistence; 0.0001–0.005 cosine) are practitioner figures with no published methodology. The method is sound; calibrate the numbers on a two-week baseline of your own.
  5. Parametric bias (G2) rests on one study. It is well-designed and inverts the standard prescription, which makes it worth acting on — but the two-run diagnostic (with and without the stale distractor) is how you confirm it applies to your system rather than trusting the finding wholesale.
  6. No public base rate for silent vendor-side model changes behind a pinned snapshot. Everyone recommends the nightly canary; nobody has published how often it fires. Experiment: run one for a quarter and publish the result.
  7. The (1−ε)^H model assumes independent steps, which real agents violate — errors are correlated, and some are self-correcting. Treat the table in A4 as an upper bound on damage and a lower bound on the case for decomposition, not as a prediction.
