MODULE 6 — SYNTHESIS: OPINIONATED RECOMMENDATIONS

Compiled: 4 September 2026. This module takes positions. Where a recommendation runs against the popular choice, it is marked CONTRARIAN and defended. Evidence carries forward from Modules 1, 2, 4 and 5; nothing new is asserted without a source there or here.

#6.0 Twelve positions, stated flatly

Everything below follows from these. Six of them are contrarian.

  1. Retrieval quality is the ceiling on everything, and almost nobody measures it separately. Fix and instrument retrieval before touching the generator.
  2. CONTRARIAN Don't buy a vector database. Use pgvector on the Postgres you already run, until you can name the specific bottleneck forcing a move.
  3. CONTRARIAN Don't adopt an agent framework on day one. Write the loop. Buy durability, not orchestration, and buy it when a lost run becomes an incident.
  4. CONTRARIAN Don't build multi-agent until a token-controlled A/B shows it beating a single agent at equal spend.
  5. CONTRARIAN Don't pick your embedding model from a leaderboard. Pick it from 200 of your own labelled queries.
  6. CONTRARIAN Don't do semantic chunking, and don't apply query rewriting unconditionally. Both are default-on in most tutorials and default-off in the evidence.
  7. CONTRARIAN Don't instrument with a vendor SDK. Instrument with OpenTelemetry and treat the backend as swappable.
  8. The system version — prompt + model snapshot + retriever config + index build + tool schemas + decoding params — is the artefact you ship. Pin all of it, including the judge and the embedder.
  9. An unvalidated LLM judge is not a metric. Report Cohen's κ, not percent agreement.
  10. Report pass^k, not pass@1, for anything that takes an action.
  11. Cost per successful request is the only cost metric that resists gaming, and it belongs on the same dashboard as quality.
  12. Prompt injection has no fix. Design for bounded blast radius by breaking the lethal trifecta, not for prevention.

#1. THREE REFERENCE ARCHITECTURES

#A note on naming models

I deliberately do not name generation models in these architectures. Model lineups turn over faster than any architecture document can track, and my reliable knowledge ends in May 2026. Naming a model in a two-year architecture decision is how you end up with a document that is wrong within a quarter and a codebase pinned to something deprecated.

Instead: specify tiers, pin snapshots at deploy time, and put the model behind one interface.

Tier Role Selection rule
Frontier Orchestration, final generation on high-value paths, judging, verification Shortlist 3 from public benchmarks, choose 1 on your own eval
Mid The default workhorse for generation and most tool calls Where most of your traffic should live
Small/fast Routing, classification, rewriting, extraction, online scoring Sub-200ms paths, high volume
Embedding Retrieval Chosen on your own 200-query eval, never MTEB rank
Reranker Precision Cross-encoder; validate in-domain before trusting

Infrastructure components below are named, because they turn over more slowly.

2–5 engineers, no dedicated ML staff, one product surface, moving fast, cost-sensitive.

Choice Why What would change it
Postgres + pgvector for vectors and BM25 (tsvector) and metadata and ACLs, in one query One database, one backup story, one security model, one thing your team already knows. Joins, row-level security and vector search in the same statement — which is exactly what permission-aware retrieval needs (Module 5, R7). The operator consensus in 2026 is convergent: start here, move only when you can name the bottleneck >10–50M vectors, or p95 vector search dominating your latency budget, or a genuine multi-tenant namespace explosion. Not "we might scale later"
No agent framework — your own loop At this size the framework's abstraction costs more debugging time than it saves build time, and context engineering (the thing that determines reliability) is exactly what frameworks abstract away A lost run becomes an incident, or you need multi-day human-in-the-loop pauses. Then take LangGraph for durability, not orchestration
Thin model gateway you own One place to pin snapshots, assert the resolved model ID, attach prompt-cache breakpoints, and swap providers. ~150 lines Nothing. Build this on day one; it is the cheapest optionality you will ever buy
Exact-match cache + prompt caching. No semantic cache Exact caching has zero correctness risk; prompt caching is the largest cost lever available. Semantic caching has a measured 1–15% false-positive rate depending on threshold and a documented cross-tenant incident shape (Module 2, §2.5) You have measured exact + prompt caching, have an eval loop running, and semantic adds >8pp of hit rate
Langfuse (MIT core, self-hostable) Traces, datasets, prompt management and annotation queues in one place, with a permissive licence and a real self-host path. Note ClickHouse acquired it (Jan 2026) — the MIT core is your protection, not the press release Hard residency rules → self-host it. LangGraph adoption → LangSmith's graph trace ergonomics start to justify the lock-in
DeepEval in pytest CI gating that feels like normal testing, MIT, no account, runs locally Purely-RAG scope → RAGAS is a tighter fit. Regulated/auditable → Inspect AI
OTel instrumentation, not a vendor SDK Backend stays swappable. gen_ai.* attributes are still Development-status, so own the constants in one file and normalise renames at export (~50 lines) Nothing

What this profile deliberately omits: agent framework, dedicated vector DB, semantic cache, multi-agent, GraphRAG, fine-tuning, a second eval platform. Every one of them is a later-trigger item in §2.

Choice Why What would change it
Router in front of everything The single cheapest large win. A naive always-retrieve pipeline is wrong on 100% of out-of-scope queries by construction. An embedding router is ~10ms; on tight domains an LLM agent routes better, on loose domains it loses by 28.8 F1 points (Module 1, §1A.3) Domain so tight that everything is in scope — rare, and verify it
Post-retrieval cascade, not unconditional rewriting Query rewriting is ~45% of end-to-end latency and helps only some query shapes; forced HyDE measurably hurt well-formed domain QA. The Danish encyclopedia production result: cheapest-first cascade improved quality, cut latency 31.8%, and served 72.2% of real queries with no LLM augmentation Your traffic is uniformly one query shape — then hard-code the right transform and skip the cascade
ACL pre-filter in the index Post-filtering is not a security boundary, and it collapses recall: at 1% authorised, a top-50 similarity retrieval holds ~0.5 authorised documents in expectation Tenant-shaped (not per-document) permissions → namespace partitioning is simpler and stronger
Still Postgres, now with attention pgvector plus pgvectorscale extends "just use Postgres" much further than most teams expect. Vendor benchmarks claiming large advantages over managed alternatives are vendor benchmarks — but the operational argument stands on its own >50M vectors, or filtered-ANN behaviour degrading under your real selectivity. Test with realistic filter selectivity before deciding
Single agent only where justified Agentic orchestration costs ~3.3× input tokens, 1.9× output and 1.5× latency versus a fixed pipeline, with a 3-turn cap. Pay it where conditional multi-step tool use is genuinely required; nowhere else See the ladder in §3
Durable execution now At this scale a lost run is an incident. Take LangGraph 1.0 (GA Oct 2025, no breaking changes until 2.0) or put a Temporal-class engine under your own loop Prefer keeping your own orchestration → use the workflow engine, not the agent framework
Per-tenant token quotas Requests-per-minute is the wrong unit; one tenant with 200-page documents outweighs a thousand normal ones Single-tenant product

#Profile 3 — Regulated enterprise

Residency, audit, PHI/PII, procurement, external scrutiny. EU AI Act in scope.

Everything in Profile 2, plus:

Choice Why What would change it
Self-host the observability and eval stack — Langfuse (MIT), or a DIY OTel + ClickHouse + Grafana stack Prompts and completions are your highest-sensitivity data and they are the debugging signal. "The vendor deletes it" is a contract, not a control. Decide this before integration; it eliminates most of the field No residency obligation → the managed options are genuinely less work
Inspect AI (MIT) for the auditable eval track, alongside DeepEval for developer CI Dataset/solver/scorer design, structured logs, sandboxing, reproducible runs — built by the UK AI Security Institute and adopted as the framework of choice by several frontier labs. When an auditor asks "show me the evaluation," this is the artefact Nothing. Keep the developer-CI tool too; they do different jobs
Redaction in your own collector, before egress; two-tier storage Redacted traces broadly available and long-retained; raw content in a short-retention, access-controlled store for a sampled fraction Nothing
Pre-filter ACLs, mandatory; audit log of the principal set per retrieval The retrieval layer is a security boundary and an evidence source Nothing
System-version registry with named owners, retirement dates, approval records This is simultaneously good engineering and most of what EU AI Act Art. 11/12/17 and ISO 42001 evidence discipline require. Build it as a pipeline artefact and the audit becomes an export Nothing
Human approval gates on irreversible actions Art. 14 human oversight, and the correct answer to (1−ε)^H on high-stakes long-horizon tasks regardless of regulation Nothing
Model tier locked to providers with the contractual and residency terms you need Procurement, not engineering, will decide this. Build the gateway so it's a config change Nothing

On the EU AI Act timeline specifically: re-baseline. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 entered into force 27 July 2026, moving Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028 — but Article 50 transparency has applied since 2 August 2026 and was not deferred, and two new Article 5 prohibitions phase in 2 December 2026. The deferral is runway for building the documentation and oversight scaffolding deliberately, not a pause.

#2. BUILD ORDER

#Weeks 1–2 — Make it measurable and reversible

# Build Why now
1 Thin model gateway — pinned snapshots, resolved-ID assertion, retries with jittered backoff, timeout, token accounting Every later decision routes through it. ~150 lines
2 OTel tracing with the full system-version manifest on every request You cannot debug a non-deterministic system from logs. Retrieval candidate IDs and scores are non-optional
3 100 real labelled cases from production, support tickets, or a domain expert's hour The asset. The prompt is disposable; this isn't
4 The simplest thing that could work — a prompt, or a prompt plus naive retrieval Establishes the baseline every later claim is measured against
5 Deterministic assertions in CI: schema validity, citation resolvability, latency and cost ceilings Seven of the day-one ten metrics need no judge
6 Rollback that reverts the whole system version, including the index pointer Rehearse it before you need it

End-of-week-2 test: can you (a) state your baseline score with a confidence interval, (b) reproduce a failing case from its trace, and (c) roll back in under five minutes? If not, do not proceed.

#Weeks 3–6 — Make it good

# Build Trigger
7 Hybrid retrieval: BM25 + dense + RRF(k=60) Any corpus containing identifiers, codes, names or dates — i.e. almost all of them
8 Cross-encoder reranking, 100 candidates → 5–8 Immediately after (7). Recall@5 measured at 0.458 / 0.826 / 0.888 for candidate depths 20 / 50 / 100
9 Retrieval metrics separated from generation metrics (Recall@100 and Recall@5, both reported) Immediately. This is the highest-ROI eval and the most commonly skipped
10 Out-of-scope router + explicit "I don't know" path Immediately. You are otherwise wrong on 100% of out-of-scope queries
11 Prompt-cache prefix discipline + exact-match cache 30-minute audit; usually the largest cost win available
12 Judge validation on 100 double-labelled items, report κ Before any judge-based metric gates anything
13 CI eval gate: n=3, paired, per-item pass→fail flip count Before the second person starts changing prompts
14 Shadow deployment on 1–5% of live traffic Before the first risky release
15 Adversarial suite: indirect injection through retrieval and tool paths; egress/renderer hardening Before any external exposure

#After week 6 — Only on a trigger

The core discipline of this module: each of the following is a real capability that most teams build too early. Each has a stated trigger. Do not build it before the trigger fires.

Do NOT build Until this trigger metric
Dedicated vector database pgvector p95 search latency >20% of your latency budget, or >10–50M vectors, or a named filtered-ANN failure you have reproduced
Agent framework A lost run is an incident (money moved, ticket filed, commit pushed), or you need multi-day human-in-the-loop pauses
Any agent at all A measured class of queries — ≥10% of traffic — that a fixed pipeline provably cannot answer, verified by manual review
Multi-agent A token-controlled A/B where multi-agent beats a single agent on the same tasks at equal total token budget
Semantic cache Exact + prompt caching measured, an eval loop running, and semantic adding >8pp hit rate over exact
GraphRAG / knowledge graph ≥15% of traffic is global ("themes across the corpus") or genuine multi-hop over entity relations, measured by classifying 200 real queries
Fine-tuning Prompting plateaued and the gap is a format/style/routing problem, not a knowledge problem, and the task is stable enough to be worth retraining
Contextual retrieval (LLM prefixes) Manual review of 30 failures shows the referent-loss pattern, and you have a prefix lexical-novelty check
Query rewriting You have measured lift per query shape; deploy conditionally, never globally
Long-context-only architecture (no retrieval) Corpus fits in ~30–50k tokens after filtering. Above that, retrieve then stuff
Multi-provider abstraction A provider outage has actually cost you, and you have budget for N prompt variants and N eval baselines
A second eval platform You have 200+ labelled items and a working CI gate and a named annotation workflow. Tooling is never the bottleneck
Custom reranker / embedding fine-tune Off-the-shelf measured in-domain and found wanting on your 200 queries
Batch-invariant kernels / deterministic inference You self-host and a regulator or auditor requires bitwise reproducibility. Otherwise change methodology (n≥3, pass^k), not kernels
Per-tenant fair queuing One tenant exceeds 20% of tokens, or a noisy-neighbour incident has occurred

What is premature, unconditionally: choosing a vector database in week one; building an agent before a fixed pipeline is measured at its ceiling; adopting a framework before you know which abstraction hurts; and building the "ideal" eval platform before you have 100 labelled examples.

#3. THE COMPLEXITY LADDER

Each rung costs more than the last in four currencies — latency, dollars, reliability, and debuggability. The fourth is the one teams don't price, and it's the one that hurts for two years.

#The ladder, with measured penalties

#Rung 1 → 2: Plain prompt → prompt + retrieval

Trigger. The answer depends on facts that are (a) outside the model's training data, (b) change more often than you can retrain, or (c) must be cited. Any one of these is sufficient. If none holds, do not climb — a prompt with the relevant content pasted in is faster, cheaper and fully debuggable.

Currency Penalty
Latency +1 embedding call, +ANN search: typically 10–40ms. Retrieval is 0–5% of end-to-end latency in measured pipelines — negligible
Cost Embedding at index and query time; storage. Usually amortised to near-zero per request
Reliability Improves — provenance, freshness, citations become possible
Debuggability Modest cost: you now need retrieval candidate IDs and scores in the trace, or a bad answer is undiagnosable

Verdict: climb early. This rung usually pays for itself immediately.

#Rung 2 → 3: Naive retrieval → hybrid + reranking

Trigger. Essentially always, for production. The only reason not to is a corpus with no identifiers, no rare terms and no vocabulary mismatch — which is rarer than teams assume.

Currency Penalty
Latency +1 index and fusion: ~10–40ms. Reranking: single-digit ms/doc on GPU for small cross-encoders, up to seconds for heavy ones
Cost ~$0.002–0.0025 per search for a managed reranker (Cohere Rerank 4 Fast/Pro per OpenRouter listings, retrieved 4 Sep 2026 — verify with the vendor; long documents get chunked and each chunk counts toward the 100-document limit, so billed searches can multiply)
Reliability Improves substantially. Recall@5 measured 0.458 → 0.826 → 0.888 at candidate depths 20 / 50 / 100
Debuggability Slight cost: two retrievers and a fusion step to reason about. Mitigated by logging per-stage scores

Verdict: climb. This is the best quality-per-unit-complexity rung on the entire ladder, and it is the one teams skip in favour of climbing to rung 4.

#Rung 3 → 4: Fixed pipeline → single agent with tools

Trigger. A measured class of queries — I'd want ≥10% of traffic, verified by manual review of 200 real queries — that genuinely requires conditional multi-step tool use: the second action's arguments depend on the first action's result, and the branching cannot be enumerated in advance.

Currency Penalty (measured)
Latency 1.5× wall clock vs an equivalent enhanced pipeline (Ferrazzi et al., arXiv 2601.07711v2)
Cost 3.3× input tokens, 1.9× output tokens, up to 3.6× total — and that was measured with a hard cap of 3 turns. Uncapped is unbounded
Reliability Degrades, and non-linearly. Success ≈ (1−ε)^H: a 95%-reliable agent completes a 20-step task ~36% of the time. New failure classes: loops, stalls, budget exhaustion, error cascades, tool-selection degradation
Debuggability The big one. A pipeline trace has ~3–5 spans; an agent run has 40–75. Bugs become non-reproducible (temperature 0 is not deterministic — 1,000 completions at temp 0 produced 80 distinct outputs in one measurement). You now need a replay harness, loop detection, budget instrumentation and pass^k methodology to work an incident

Verdict: climb reluctantly, and only for the query class that needs it. Route the rest to the fixed pipeline. The most common error at this rung is converting the whole product to an agent because 10% of it needed one — paying 3.3× on 100% of traffic to fix 10%.

Note the specific negative result: an agent given free re-retrieval scored below naive RAG on document-list quality, re-retrieving only 10% of the time and changing nothing in 53% of those cases. Agency is a good substitute for a router and a bad substitute for a reranker. Give the model the routing decision; keep the ranking in a scored, testable component.

#Rung 4 → 5: Single agent → multi-agent

Trigger — and it is a gate, not a judgement call. One of exactly three conditions, plus a passed A/B: 1. Parallel breadth — genuinely independent read/search threads combined at the end. 2. Context isolation as a capability — a clean-context verifier is better because it hasn't seen the first agent's context. 3. Capability routing across models with different strengths.

And then: a token-controlled A/B where the multi-agent system beats the single agent on the same task set at equal total token budget. Without that control you are measuring spend, not architecture — Anthropic's own reporting is that token usage explained ~80% of the performance variance in their multi-agent research system.

Currency Penalty
Latency Improves for parallel breadth; worsens for everything else
Cost ~15× the tokens of a chat interaction for full orchestration (Anthropic, vendor-reported). Observability adds a second multiplier: on unit-priced platforms an agent run with 40–75 spans burns 8–15 billing units against a chat call's one
Reliability 14 documented failure modes across 3 categories (MAST, 1,600+ traces, 7 frameworks, κ=0.88), which the authors attribute to system design rather than model limitations — meaning better models will not fix them
Debuggability Worst on the ladder. Cross-agent causality requires correlation IDs on every message and per-agent budgets, or a failed run is unreconstructible

Verdict: CONTRARIAN do not climb by default. The one rule both sides of the public argument now converge on: keep writes single-threaded; extra agents contribute intelligence, not actions. The pattern with the best evidence is not a swarm — it's map-reduce-and-manage, or a clean-context verifier attached to a single writer.

#The compounding penalty nobody prices

Rung Spans/run Cost multiple Failure classes to own Eval methodology needed
1. Prompt 1 1× wrong output 100 cases, n=1
2. + retrieval 2–3 ~1× + stale/missing/wrong chunks + Recall@k, faithfulness
3. + hybrid & rerank 4–6 ~1.05× + fusion & rerank regressions + nDCG@k, per-item flips
4. Single agent 40–75 ~3.3× input + loops, stalls, cascades, tool selection, budget exhaustion, non-reproducibility + pass^k, trajectory metrics, cost-per-success
5. Multi-agent 100s ~15× chat + 14 coordination modes, hand-off loss, duplicated work, diffusion of responsibility + token-controlled A/B, utilisation rate, verifier catch/FP rates

Quantifying "climbing too early": a team that jumps rung 2 → 4 to fix a retrieval problem pays roughly 3.3× the input-token cost and 1.5× the latency on all traffic, takes on six new failure classes, expands its trace volume by an order of magnitude — and still has the retrieval problem, because agency does not improve ranking. The rung-3 fix would have cost one reranker call and moved Recall@5 from 0.458 to 0.888.

#4. MINIMUM VIABLE EVALUATION AND OBSERVABILITY

Not the ideal. The smallest thing that is actually sufficient — buildable in about a week.

#The minimum that works

Observability (~2 days)

  1. One OTel span tree per request, with these attributes and no more: trace_id · run_id · step_index · tenant_id · feature · system_version{model_snapshot, resolved_model, prompt_sha, index_build, embed_model, top_k, rerank_model} · usage{input, output, cache_read, cache_write} · retrieval{candidate_ids[], scores[]} · tool{name, args_hash, error_type} · budget{steps_used, tokens_used, terminated_by}
  2. Tail sampling: 100% of errors, budget exhaustions, negative feedback, bottom-decile quality and >p99 latency; 1–5% of the happy path. Head sampling discards exactly the traces you need.
  3. Redaction in your collector, before egress. Deny-list credential-shaped fields; redact tool results, not just prompts.
  4. One dashboard, six panels: task success · p95 latency · cost per successful request · schema-violation rate · fallback-tier share · budget-exhaustion rate.

Evaluation (~3 days)

  1. 100 real cases, stratified ~20% easy / 50% medium / 30% hard, with 10–15% out-of-scope. Versioned in git, never edited in place.
  2. The day-one ten metrics (Module 4) — seven deterministic, two judge-based, one comparative.
  3. n=3 trials, paired against the previous version, per-item pass→fail flip count. Gate on flips, not on the mean.
  4. Judge validated once on 100 double-labelled items, κ reported, position swaps run. If κ < 0.4, fix the rubric — don't gate.
  5. Nightly frozen canary on the pinned endpoint: 50 items, fixed seed and params, alert on movement beyond CI. The only detector for silent vendor-side change.
  6. A weekly hour of triage: mine failures, promote to the golden set, log the changelog.

#What this deliberately excludes

No eval platform purchase. No annotation vendor. No synthetic dataset generation. No online LLM scoring on 100% of traffic (sample it — a strong judge on all traffic can cost more than the calls it judges). No drift dashboard beyond the nightly canary and a weekly neighbour-stability check. No custom metrics beyond the ten.

Why this is sufficient: it detects regressions before users do, localises them to a stage, survives a vendor-side model change, bounds cost, and produces the evidence an audit or a postmortem needs. Everything beyond it is optimisation of a working loop.

The trigger to expand: more than one team changing prompts (→ annotation queues and a shared platform), a regulated audit (→ Inspect AI and immutable eval logs), or eval runtime blocking merges (→ tiered suites: smoke on commit, full nightly).

#5. PRE-PRODUCTION READINESS CHECKLIST

Every line is a yes/no with a named owner. "Partially" means no.

Quality gates - [ ] ≥100 real labelled cases, versioned, with a held-out slice never used for iteration - [ ] CI gate: Tier-1 assertions at 100%; retrieval and generation metrics with thresholds; per-item pass→fail flips ≤2% - [ ] n≥3 trials; results reported as point estimate + CI + paired diff vs baseline - [ ] pass^k reported for anything taking an action - [ ] Judge validated, κ reported, judge snapshot and prompt hash pinned - [ ] Baseline measured on 100 real production-representative queries with the real permission model applied — not demo cases - [ ] Out-of-scope rejection rate and over-refusal rate both measured and both acceptable

Safety - [ ] Lethal-trifecta audit per agent: private data? untrusted content (including tool output)? egress? Three yeses → documented mitigation - [ ] Indirect-injection suite run against retrieval and tool paths, not just the user input field - [ ] Egress allowlisted; Markdown image auto-fetch disabled; ANSI escapes stripped from terminal/IDE sinks - [ ] Human approval gate on every irreversible action - [ ] Model output treated as untrusted input to every downstream sink (parameterised SQL, escaped HTML, never to a shell) - [ ] Corpus-poisoning test included (small numbers of crafted documents can dominate retrieval) - [ ] Cross-tenant retrieval negative test in CI — a restricted chunk ID appearing in candidate_ids fails the build even if later filtered - [ ] PII scan of traces, tool results, cache keys and eval datasets

Cost controls - [ ] Cost per successful request computed at the step ceiling, not at the average - [ ] Hard caps: retries ≤2, step ceiling, per-run token budget, wall-clock timeout - [ ] Prompt-cache prefix audit done; cache_read_tokens logged and hit rate monitored - [ ] Per-tenant token quotas (tokens, not requests) and fair queuing - [ ] Cost alerting at 1.3× baseline; budget-exhaustion rate on the quality dashboard

Observability - [ ] Full system-version manifest on every trace; resolved model ID asserted against requested - [ ] Retrieval candidate IDs and scores captured - [ ] Tail sampling configured; errors and budget exhaustions at 100% - [ ] Redaction in the collector, before egress; two-tier storage if sensitive - [ ] Correlation IDs on every inter-agent message (multi-agent only) - [ ] Nightly frozen canary running; weekly neighbour-stability check running - [ ] Index manifest asserted at query time — embed model, dimension, build ID. Fail loud on mismatch

Rollback - [ ] Reverts the whole system version, including the index pointer - [ ] Previous index build addressable and warm - [ ] Rehearsed end to end, timed, under five minutes - [ ] Automatic triggers defined as code: quality >2σ drop, schema violations >0.5%, refusal shift >1.5×, p95 >1.5×, cost >1.3×, budget-exhaustion >1.5×

On-call - [ ] Quality is a pageable condition, not just latency and 5xx - [ ] Fallback-tier share alerting (a silent 30% fallback rate is an unmeasured quality incident) - [ ] One-page incident playbook enumerating the LLM-specific causes: silent model change · prompt/config drift · embedding-index mismatch · context position effects · sampling-param drift · wrong route or tier · cache false positive · tool schema change - [ ] Responder can see retrieved chunk IDs, tool arguments and the resolved model ID for a failing trace - [ ] Named owner for: prompts · eval set · judge · index · corpus freshness · model registry and deprecation calendar · cost per tenant

#6. ANTI-PATTERNS, WITH NAMED ALTERNATIVES

Anti-pattern Why it fails Do this instead
Vector database in week one New vendor, new ops, new security model, for a scale you don't have pgvector on your existing Postgres. Migrate on a named bottleneck
Dense-only retrieval Cannot find "invoice #AZ-4471." BM25 beat a strong dense model on every metric but Recall@20 on one 2026 text-and-table benchmark Hybrid + RRF(k=60). One day of work
Reranking 20 candidates Worst of both worlds — you pay the latency and get almost none of the gain (Recall@5 0.458 vs 0.888 at depth 100) Retrieve 100, rerank hard, return 5–8
Semantic chunking as the default Measured as not justifying its cost; gains cluster on synthetic topic-diverse sets Fixed/recursive 400–800 tokens. Fix the referent problem with contextual prefixes or parent-child if that's the actual failure
Picking the embedding model from MTEB One in-domain report had the MTEB top-3 ranking 5th, 7th and 2nd on their own eval, with the winner ranked 11th Shortlist 3, evaluate on 200 of your own labelled queries
Query rewriting on every request ~45% of latency, and forced HyDE measurably hurt well-formed domain QA Conditional transforms behind a router, or a cheapest-first cascade
Agentic re-retrieval instead of a reranker Measured below naive RAG on document quality at 3.3× input tokens Agent decides whether/how to search; a deterministic hybrid + cross-encoder does the ranking
Multi-agent because the diagram looks right 14 documented coordination failure modes, ~15× tokens Single agent + clean-context verifier. Escalate only on a token-controlled A/B
Parallel agents that all write Implicit conflicting decisions; failures surface at integration when the explaining context is gone N agents read, one writes
Reflection loop with no external oracle Intrinsic self-correction degrades reasoning (GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5% → 91.5% → 89.0%) Name the oracle: tests, schema, compiler, retrieval score, second retriever. No oracle → delete the loop
40 tools on one agent Measured degradation between 10–15 tools (Haiku) and 20–30 (Sonnet) ≤10–15 visible per context via namespace routing, tool-RAG, or specialist sub-agents
Step limit without a loop detector Bounds cost, doesn't stop 25 steps of the same failing call — and step repetition is among the largest documented failure modes Hash (tool, canonical_args); warn at 2, halt at 3. Ten lines
Opaque tool errors (400 Bad Request) The model can't recover from what it can't read; it retries identically until the budget dies Structured errors with expected, received, hint
Semantic cache before exact + prompt caching 1–15% false-positive rate, cross-tenant incident shape, permanent eval loop required Exact cache (zero risk) + prompt-cache prefix audit. Semantic last, if at all
Rolling model aliases in production Silent weight, safety-filter and default changes; schema violations with no deploy Pinned snapshots + resolved-ID assertion + nightly canary + deprecation calendar. Including the fallback, the judge and the embedder
Unpinned judge Your metric drifts on the vendor's schedule; you bisect your own commits for a week Pin judge snapshot and prompt hash; re-validate quarterly
Validating a judge with percent agreement 33–41 points of kappa deflation measured on MT-Bench; "85% agreement" can be near chance Report Cohen's κ; run position swaps; report swap-disagreement rate
Reporting pass@1 for an acting agent 90% single-run success ≈ 57% chance of eight clean runs pass^k, k=3–8
ROUGE / BERTScore for RAG quality Max measured correlation with human ranking 0.477; BERTScore can't distinguish 2027 from 2029 Deterministic assertions → claim-level entailment → validated pairwise judge
Gating on faithfulness alone Trivially maximised by saying less; selects for evasiveness Pair faithfulness with completeness; watch both
Tuning against the whole eval set Score rises, product doesn't, and you can't tell Held-out slice never used for iteration
Post-filtering for access control Not a security boundary, and recall collapses (~0.5 authorised docs in a top-50 at 1% selectivity) Pre-filter in the index; re-check post-fusion; namespace-partition where permissions are tenant-shaped
Head sampling traces at 1% Discards exactly the traces you need Tail sampling: 100% of errors, budget exhaustions, negative feedback, bottom-decile quality
Vendor SDK as your instrumentation Re-instrument every time the market moves — and it does (two acquisitions in this space in 2026 alone) OTel/OpenInference, export to the vendor, own redaction and sampling in your collector
Compacting at a token threshold Compacts mid-reasoning, where subtle-context loss does the most damage Compact at task boundaries; keep the session log outside the window and queryable
A central AI team owning all prompts Prompts encode product decisions; the team becomes a bottleneck immediately Central team owns infrastructure and standards; feature teams own prompts; domain experts own eval sets
Engineers writing the eval rubric for a domain they don't practise Measures fluency instead of correctness Domain expert owns the rubric; engineering owns the harness
Treating compliance as a document Art. 11/12/17 obligations get reconstructed under deadline Build lineage, logging, approval records and eval history as pipeline artefacts; the audit becomes an export
Building an LLM feature for a deterministic task You'll add a fifth validation layer and still miss the bar Write the rule. Use the model to orchestrate deterministic tools, not to replace them

#7. WHERE I'M UNCERTAIN, AND WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND

Stated as falsifiable positions, because a recommendation you can't overturn isn't a recommendation.

Position Confidence What would change it
Don't build multi-agent by default Fairly high A published, token-controlled, independently-replicated benchmark showing multi-agent beating single-agent at equal spend on non-parallel tasks. Anthropic's 90.2% figure is first-party and not token-controlled; Cognition's revision was narrow and explicitly about read-only and single-writer patterns. If the "manager + children" pattern matures as Cognition's 2026 work suggests it might, this is the recommendation most likely to age badly
Don't buy a vector database High for <10M vectors, low above 50M A reproducible independent benchmark on realistic filter selectivity showing pgvector/pgvectorscale failing at a scale you'll actually reach. Most published comparisons are vendor-run in both directions
Write your own agent loop first Medium If durable-execution primitives become genuinely commodity — trivially embeddable, no abstraction tax — the argument for hand-rolling weakens a lot. LangGraph 1.0's stability commitment moves in that direction
Contextual retrieval is conditional, not default Medium Anthropic's 49%/67% figures are first-party on one eval suite; third-party reports are 5–15%; a 2026 legal audit found the prefixes frequently adding nothing. An independent replication at the headline magnitude would move this to "default on"
Query rewriting should be conditional Medium-high The strongest evidence is one industry-track paper plus one production system. A larger multi-domain study showing uniform benefit would change it
Semantic caching last, if at all Medium Hit-rate and false-positive figures come from vendor blogs and practitioner reports, not controlled studies. Verified-cache designs (async LLM-judged promotion) could shift the risk profile materially
Judge κ ≥ 0.7 to gate Low — this is my synthesis, not a standard No consensus threshold exists. Calibrate against your own human–human ceiling, which for subjective tasks is often 0.3–0.6. If your humans agree at 0.55, demanding 0.7 from a judge is incoherent
Long context doesn't replace retrieval High for the architecture, medium for the numbers The Self-Route cost figures (65% / 39%) are from 2024-era models. If effective context length starts tracking advertised context length — NoLiMa and context-rot results both say it doesn't today — the routing threshold moves up and the "retrieve then stuff" pattern shrinks
Tool budget of 10–15 visible Medium One organisation's production data plus secondary compilations. Run the padding experiment on your own surface; if models improve here it's a per-generation number, not a constant
Instrument with OTel, not a vendor SDK High on principle, medium on practice The gen_ai.* conventions are still Development status with no stable attribute and no release from the new dedicated repo as of Aug 2026. If stabilisation stalls another year, the pragmatic case for a vendor SDK strengthens
The eval numbers in Modules 4–5 generalise Medium at best Kappa deflation, RAGAS discriminant-validity failure, parametric bias, synthetic-query length bias — several rest on single studies. They're strong enough to act on and not strong enough to stop measuring your own
pgvector, DeepEval, Langfuse, Inspect as named picks Medium, decaying These are September-2026 picks. Two acquisitions hit this space in 2026 (ClickHouse/Langfuse, OpenAI/Promptfoo). The criteria — permissive licence, self-host path, CI ergonomics, OTel portability — should outlive the names, and are the thing to re-run

#The three things I'd most want measured

  1. A token-controlled, independently-replicated multi-agent vs single-agent benchmark. This is the single largest open question in agent architecture, and every current data point is first-party.
  2. A public correlation between offline eval metrics and business outcomes. Nobody has published one. It's the missing link that makes every eval program defensible, and it's a week of work for anyone with historical sessions.
  3. A public, blameless GenAI incident corpus. Module 5 is reconstructed from research papers and two honest retrospectives because the postmortems mostly don't exist. The field is repeating the same failures privately.

#The one thing I'd tell a team starting Monday

Build the gateway, the traces and 100 labelled cases in the first two weeks — before the prompt, before the retriever, before any architecture decision. Everything in this module is a claim about what to build; those three are what let you find out whether the claims are true for you. Every team that skipped them spent the following quarter unable to tell whether anything they did helped.
